At 11 yr after fire, the grassland consists mainly of a dead, slowly decomposing thatch, with little live above-ground material and a markedly declining productivity. The decline was mirrored below-ground where root biomass was also substantially lower than in areas burnt more recently. McDougall (1989) reported the beginnings of tussock decline in a T. triandra grassland reserve nearby after 10 yr of fire exclusion and we have observed similar processes in other Themeda grasslands in western Victoria, Gippsland and the Australian Capital Territory. Hence, the phenomenon is likely to have some generality in Themeda-dominated grasslands in south-eastern Australia. The rate of tussock decline will undoubtedly vary between sites, and depend chiefly on site productivity. Interestingly, similar responses to fire and grazing exclusion have also been reported for T. triandra elsewhere and this suggests that it is a feature of the species itself, rather than a local effect restricted to southern Australia. Mott and Andrew (1985), for instance, found that T. triandra tussocks senesced rapidly after 3 yr without fire in a tropical savanna in north-west Australia whilst Belsky (1992) has reported that T. triandra can decline in less than 5 yr in the absence of disturbance in a tropical grassland in East Africa.

The causes of Themeda tussock decline with increasing time-since-fire were not studied here and are poorly understood. It is suspected that shading (i.e. light quantity) at the soil surface, due to the increase in above-ground biomass with time-since-fire, may be a primary cause of tussock decline, as has been reported in other productive grasslands (e.g. Hulbert, 1969; Old, 1969; Knapp and Seastedt, 1986). Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) at the ground surface can be <5% of PAR available above the canopy in Themeda grasslands unburnt for >4 yr (Morgan, 1997), due to the reflection and absorption of energy by the standing plant material (Knapp, 1984). Hence, the need to elevate the photosynthetic surface high above the ground increases with time-since-fire as biomass accumulates from the ground up. Some Themeda tillers have the ability to elevate well above the soil surface (described as ‘aerial tillering’ by McDougall (1989)) to reach the light, but many tillers do not successfully compete for light in this way, leading to the loss of live tillers and the resources that are captured by the tussock. A point is reached (by 11 yr after fire) when aerial tillers can no longer be elevated higher on their weak stems and the canopy collapses. The dead material forms a thick thatch that effectively mulches the soil and prevents seedling regeneration (Lock and Milburn, 1971; McDougall, 1989) and new tiller initiation.

Other factors that potentially contribute to Themeda tussock decline with increasing time-since-fire also reflect the effects that standing dead and litter material have on microclimate at the tussock bases. Two factors appear to warrant further consideration, namely: (i) the effects of red:far red light (i.e. light quality) (Deregibus et al., 1985) and, (ii) below- and above-ground temperatures (Old, 1969; Knapp, 1984). Both factors have been implicated in the abilities of other tussock grasses to initiate new tillers, with modifications in light quality by a dense grassland canopy being particularly detrimental to tiller populations of some other C4 grasses (Deregibus et al., 1985).

After a long fire-free period (12 yr), a single fire did not, in the short-term, return the grassland's tussock structure to a state more characteristic of a site with a shorter inter-fire interval (i.e. 4 yr). There were fewer tillers and tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> in the long unburnt site six months after fire relative to the shorter fire-interval site and, in general, the tussock structure resembled that in the pre-fire grassland. The rate of Themeda canopy recovery was also slower in the long unburnt area. This has also been observed in a nearby grassland when fire was reintroduced after 17 yr (Lunt and Morgan, 1998). Slow vegetative recovery probably results because pre-fire tiller health was poor, with many aerial tillers being killed by fire, and hence, the subsequent regrowth is from the relatively few, newly initiated tillers found at the soil surface. Regrowth from tillers in the more frequently burnt areas, however, is more likely to be from the recovery of existing tillers, protected by the densely crowded meristems in the basal tuft (Morgan, 1998b). Whether Themeda tussock recovery in the long unburnt area continues in the subsequent post-fire yr, enabling the grassland to more closely resemble the frequently burnt area, is unknown. At the nearby Laverton North Grassland Reserve, however, areas burnt after 17 yr of fire exclusion appear to retain their differences (i.e. low tussock density, less canopy cover) at 3 yr after burning compared to adjacent areas burnt more frequently (Morgan, pers. observation).

The decline in Themeda health with long time-since-fire intervals has two major implications for conservation management at Derrimut. Firstly, changes in

11	### Abstract
12	
13	Changes in tussock attributes and sward structure with time-since-fire were documented for the dominant tussock grass, *Themeda triandra*, at the Derrimut Grassland Reserve in southern Victoria, Australia. When the inter-fire interval exceeded 6 yr, the number of tillers per tussock and the total number of tussocks declined, and by 11 yr, few live tillers or tussocks remained in the sward. Below-ground biomass was also substantially lower at this time. With increasing time-since-fire, the canopy of live leaves was elevated high above the soil surface and dead leaves accumulated around and over the tussock bases. Productivity declined in long unburnt areas and by 11 yr without disturbance, the canopy “collapsed” upon itself, forming a thick layer of dead thatch over the soil surface. A single fire in an area previously unburnt for 12 yr did not immediately return the tussocks to a state more characteristic of a site with a 4 yr inter-fire interval burnt at the same time. Inter-fire intervals of ≤5 yr would appear necessary to maintain the health and competitiveness of *Themeda triandra*. These findings have important implications for the maintenance of faunal habitat and the potential for weed invasion into remnant grasslands. © 1999 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.

16	
17	### 1. Introduction
18	
19	It is widely recognised that fire and grazing regimes have influenced the diversity of temperate grassland and grassy woodland remnants in south-eastern Australia, as in other grassland regions of the world (e.g. Booysen and Tainton, 1984; Collins and Wallace, 1990; Belsky, 1992; Fensham, 1998). Most species-rich sites in south-eastern Australia have a history of frequent burning (i.e. 1–3 yr intervals) and/or minimal stock grazing (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Stuwe, 1986; Kirkpatrick et al., 1988; Benson, 1994; Lunt, 1995; Prober and Thiele, 1995; Morgan, 1998a). Species-poor remnants, on the other hand, are either grazed by domestic stock or only very infrequently disturbed by fire or grazing (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Tremont, 1994; Prober and Thiele, 1995). Species may be lost in the complete absence of sward disturbance because of competitive exclusion (Scarlett and Parsons, 1990; Gilfedder and Kirkpatrick, 1994; Morgan, 1997), sometimes irreversibly given that few native grassland forbs appear to form large, persistent soil seed banks (Gilfedder and Kirkpatrick, 1993; Lunt, 1995, 1997; Morgan, 1995, 1998a).
20	
21	Fire and grazing regimes can also alter the structure of a grassland community and the population dynamics and vigour of its dominant tussock grasses. Numerous Australian studies have reported the effects of intensive disturbance regimes on dominant grasses, allowing Moore (1970) to summarize the general changes that occur in a variety of native temperate grasslands under heavy and continuous stock grazing. Principally, there is a shift from C4 to C3 grasses, from caespitose perennials to annuals, and from native to exotic species. Frequent, low mowing may also have similar effects on the survival of tall-growing tussock grasses (Chan, 1980).
22	
23	The effects of the total exclusion of stock grazing and burning on dominant tussock grasses, however, are generally less well documented in temperate Australia. In grasslands dominated by *Themeda triandra* (Kangaroo Grass), Groves (1974) suggested that there was a curvilinear relationship between shoot biomass and time-since-fire; by 5 yr after fire, new shoot growth would balance death and decomposition of old leaves to maintain a constant biomass. McDougall (1989) noted that in an undisturbed sward (10 yr since fire or grazing) in southern Victoria, tussocks were fewer, had smaller

McDougall (1989) concluded that without fire or grazing, “long unburnt Themeda tussocks could be expected to disappear from the sward” and seedling recruitment would be minimal under the dead thatch. In the following 10 yr, Themeda health declined further as a result of continued fire exclusion, leading to the death of many tussocks (Lunt and Morgan, 1998).

37	At the Derrimut Grassland Reserve in southern Victoria, Australia, fire is considered a necessary conservation management tool to maintain native species diversity (Craigie and Stuwe, 1992), but it has been applied in an adhoc manner since the creation of the reserve in 1985. Some areas have been burnt three times over the last 12 yr (maximum inter-fire interval of 4 yr), whilst other areas have never been burnt. Lunt and Morgan (1999) reported on the floristic changes that occurred during the first 10 yr of reservation and found that most native species that had survived long-term grazing were also fairly resilient to the variable fire regimes imposed. Surprisingly, the least resilient species to infrequent burning and grazing exclusion appeared to be the dominant tussock grass, Themeda triandra. This finding has important implications for the threatened fauna that rely on the grassland for habitat (e.g. the Striped Legless Lizard, Delma impar), as well as the susceptibility of the grassland community to invasion by exotic perennial grasses (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). In this paper, we investigate how time-since-fire affects the survival, vigour, structure and productivity of Themeda triandra tussocks, and the subsequent ability of tussocks to recover from fire.
38	
39	### 2. Methods
40	
41	#### 2.1. Study site
42	
43	The 154 ha Derrimut Grassland Reserve is 15 km south-west of Melbourne, Victoria (37°48′30″S, 144°47′40″E). Mean annual rainfall is 568 mm. The geology is Early Pleistocene olivine basalt (Douglas, 1982). The reserve is dominated by a Themeda triandra grassland in well-drained areas (Lunt, 1990a) and is a remnant of the Keilor Plains grassland described by Willis (1964). This grassland type is on the verge of extinction (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994). Soils in grassland areas range from silty-clay to clay-loam with pH 7.0 (Lunt, 1990a).
44	
45	The property was grazed by sheep until the 1960s and by cattle from then until 1985, when grazing was removed from the entire site after management changed to the state conservation agency for the purposes of grassland conservation.
46	
47	Early recommendations for management of the reserve suggested that fire at 2–5 yr intervals were necessary to maintain botanical values (Stuwe, 1986; Lunt, 1988). However, owing to perceived negative impacts of frequent burning on endangered fauna (Coulson, 1990), a management plan recommended that the reserve be divided into 10 zones, two of which were to be burnt every year, giving a 5 yr fire interval in each zone (Craigie and Stuwe, 1992). In practice, the management plan has not been consistently implemented. Ten fires occurred between 1986 and 1997 but all had different boundaries and burnt different areas. The number of fires experienced in each zone ranged from 0 to 3 and the maximum inter-fire interval varied from 4 to over 12 yr (in areas which were never burnt).
48	
49	#### 2.2. Study species
50	
51	Themeda triandra (syn. T. australis) is a perennial C4 tussock grass that dominates many grassy woodlands and tropical savannahs in both Australia and Africa. In southern Victoria, T. triandra is the dominant species of natural grassland communities on volcanic soils (Patton, 1935; Willis, 1964; McDougall et al., 1994). It grows primarily from October to January in southern Victoria and is most productive in the first 3–4 yr after fire (McDougall, 1989), after which time productivity declines (Groves, 1974; McDougall, 1989). It has no means of extensive vegetative spread. Tussocks are generally fire-resistant, tillers resprouting after summer fires from protected basal apices, even when burnt annually (Morgan, in prep). Aerial tillers form when swards remain undisturbed and these are easily damaged by trampling (McDougall, 1989). The ability of tussocks and tillers to recover from fire after a long period of fire exclusion is virtually unknown, although in a companion study, Lunt and Morgan (1998) found that post-fire recovery of Themeda in areas unburnt for 17 yr lagged behind that of a grassland burnt more frequently. Longevity of tussocks is unknown in Victorian grasslands; Morgan (1998b) observed little mortality and turnover of Themeda tussocks over a 3 yr period in a biennially burnt grassland. Seed set occurs primarily in mid-summer (January; McDougall, 1989) but germination does not occur until spring (October) when soil moisture is high and soil temperatures are >20°C (Hagon, 1976). A thick litter layer of Themeda inhibits germination; seedlings are generally only observed after fire when the insulating vegetation cover and litter layer has been removed (Lock and Milburn, 1971; McDougall, 1989), or when grazed.

70	Changes in vegetation structure in areas last burnt 0.2, 1, 3, >6 and 11 yr ago were documented using point quadrats (Kent and Coker, 1992). A frame consisting of 10 vertically held 4 mm diameter pins, each 10 cm apart, was randomly placed at 12 locations within each fire zone (n=120 points per fire zone) and all hits of both live and dead T. triandra, and their height of contact (in 3 cm intervals), were recorded.
71	
72	Seasonal changes in above-ground biomass in zones burnt 1, 3 and 11 yr ago were followed for 18 months, from August 1995 to February 1997. At each site, 12 random 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> quadrats were selected at 4–6 week intervals for six months, and then again 12 months later, and all vegetation was cut to ground level, dried at 80°C for 48 h and weighed. It was assumed that most (>90%) of the biomass was that of T. triandra, an assumption likely to be valid given that (1) few other species occurred in the areas sampled and (2) the high representation of T. triandra in the biomass samples hand sorted by McDougall (1989) in a similar grassland nearby.
73	
74	The comparative ability of Themeda tussocks to recover from fire was assessed by burning a 1 ha area, unburnt for 12 yr, and an equivalent area most recently burnt 4 yr previously. Both areas were burnt in November 1997. In April 1998, the total number of rooted tillers and tussocks, tussock basal circumference and visual percent cover were recorded in five randomly placed 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> quadrats at each site.
75	
76	#### 2.4. Statistical analyses
77	
78	The number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> , number of live tillers, average number of tillers per tussock (square root transformed), number of inflorescences (square root transformed), average number of inflorescences per tussock and mean basal circumference were compared between fire zones that differed in their time-since-fire by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's post-hoc comparisons (Zar, 1984). Homogeneity of variance assumptions were tested using Cochrane's Test (Winer et al., 1991). A mixed-model nested ANOVA was used to test whether basal circumference was affected by site history, with quadrats nested within fire zones (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). The G-test of independence was used to test whether basal circumference, when grouped into size classes, was associated with fire history (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). Root biomass differences with fire history were compared using a one-way ANOVA on log transformed data with Tukey's post-hoc comparisons.
79	
80	Attributes of post-fire recovery of areas previously unburnt for 4 and 12 yr (i.e. number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> , number of tillers, average number of tillers per tussock, percent cover) were compared using t-tests (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). Homogeneity of variance assumptions were checked using the F<sub>max</sub>-test (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981) and satisfied in all cases. A contingency table was used to test whether basal circumference, when grouped into size classes, was associated with fire history. Expected values were calculated based on the null hypothesis of independence and tested using the chi-square statistic (Zar, 1984). Standardised residuals were examined to determine the pattern of association between the variables.

87	### 3. Results
88	
89	All of the above-ground tussock attributes, except basal circumference, significantly declined with increasing time-since-fire (Table 1). There were no significant differences in tussock attributes between areas burnt 1 and 3 yr previously. Rather, the effects were significant when grasslands had remained unburnt for ≥5 yr.
90	
91	The total number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> was lowest in the long unburnt area (11 yr; F=7.10, p=0.003) but did not differ significantly between areas burnt more recently (≤5 yr). Total number of tillers and mean number of tillers per tussock were highest in 1 and 3 yr unburnt areas, intermediate, but significantly lower, in the 5 yr unburnt area, and least in the 11 yr unburnt area (F=35.32, p < 0.0001 and F=10.54, p< 0.001 respectively). Inflorescence production (total and mean number per tussock) declined with time-since-fire in a similar way (F=47.91, p< 0.0001 and F=16.82, p< 0.001 respectively). Tussock circumference did not differ within (F=0.926, p=0.540) or between (F=1.464, p=0.224) any of the fire zones, nor was the size class distribution of tussocks significantly associated with time-since-fire (χ<sup>2</sup>=12.07, n=12, p> 0.05). Thus, all tussock size classes were represented in all fire zones in similar ratios.
92	
93	Mean root biomass (±1SE) in the 12 yr unburnt area (0.174 ± 0.019 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup>; F=26.19, p < 0.001) was less than 45% of that in the areas burnt two (0.432 ± 0.016 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup>) and four (0.384 ± 0.023 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup>) years previously, which did not differ from one another (p > 0.05).
94	
95	While the total number of contacts with live Themeda did not increase greatly in the years 1 to >6 after burning in the point quadrat study (Fig. 1), the spatial distribution of live leaves in the canopy changed dramatically (Fig. 2). Immediately after fire, Themeda resprouted rapidly from the base and live leaves were mostly concentrated near the ground level (≤6 cm) during year 1. In years 2 to >6, the canopy of live leaves elevated higher in each year so that by >6 yr, most of the live canopy was >18 cm above ground level. During the same period, live leaves disappeared completely from tussock bases (<3 cm) and dead vegetation accumulated from the ‘bottom up’ (Fig. 2). At >6 yr after fire, 73% of all Themeda leaves in the canopy were dead. After 11 yr without disturbance, the grassland appeared to collapse upon itself (Fig. 2). Dead vegetation remained on the soil surface (in a thick layer to 12 cm deep) whilst almost no live vegetation existed at any layer in the canopy.
96	
97	Over the 18 months in which above-ground biomass was followed, areas unburnt for 1 and 3 yr at the start of observations increased their total biomass by 167% and 152%, respectively (Fig. 3), within the context of large seasonal variation. During the same time, the total biomass of the area unburnt for 11 yr declined to 58% of its original amount. The decline was most dramatic between February 1997 and February 1998 when biomass fell from 707 g m<sup>−2</sup> to 462 g m<sup>−2</sup>, despite large increases in biomass at the other two sites. This decline corresponded with the grassland collapse observed in areas which had remained unburnt for >12 yr.
98	
99	Time-since-fire affected the subsequent ability of Themeda tussocks to recover from fire (Table 2). The canopy of the long unburnt area (12 yr since fire) regrew more slowly (7% versus 35%), had fewer tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup>, had fewer tillers and fewer tillers per tussock than the area that had a shorter inter-fire interval (4 yr since fire; Table 2). 123	### 4. Discussion
124	
125	It has long been recognised that frequent biomass removal by burning is necessary to maintain native plant diversity in ungrazed, species-rich grassland remnants on the western volcanic plains in southern Victoria (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Scarlett and Parsons, 1982; Stuwe, 1986). Where inter-fire intervals exceed 5 yr, even on only rare occasions, competitive exclusion by the dominant tussock grass (T. triandra) has usually been considered to reduce native plant diversity (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Scarlett and Parsons, 1990). This decline may be irreversible given that the soil seed bank type possessed by many native species is a transient one (Lunt, 1995, 1996; Morgan, 1995, 1998a). This study suggests that frequent biomass removal is also necessary to maintain the health and vigour of the dominant grass itself at one of the few reserves dedicated to the conservation of this threatened community (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994).
126	
127	The effect of ‘time-since-fire’ on Themeda was the specific parameter of interest in this study, but it is confounded with another fire regime factor, namely, the fire frequency (Morrison et al., 1995). Some areas experienced no fires in the 12 yr since reservation, others only one fire, and yet other areas experienced three fires in the same period. Although the effects of fire frequency on Themeda tussocks should not be discounted, given that all fire zones were generally similar at the time of reservation and that the number of fires experienced at all sites was low, the parameter of time-since-fire would appear to be a valid one to compare between fire zones.
128	
129	When time-since-fire exceeded 6 yr, the total number of tillers, number of tillers per tussock and number of inflorescences per tussock all declined substantially. Whilst the total number of live leaves in the canopy was relatively constant between yr 2 and 6 after fire, the canopy was raised high above the soil surface with a consequent accumulation of dead leaves around the tussock base. In the prolonged absence of fire (by 11 yr),

152	tussock degeneration becomes substantial; few live tussocks survive in the grassland and the canopy collapses on itself. At 11 yr after fire, the grassland consists mainly of a dead, slowly decomposing thatch, with little live above-ground material and a markedly declining productivity. The decline was mirrored below-ground where root biomass was also substantially lower than in areas burnt more recently. McDougall (1989) reported the beginnings of tussock decline in a T. triandra grassland reserve nearby after 10 yr of fire exclusion and we have observed similar processes in other Themeda grasslands in western Victoria, Gippsland and the Australian Capital Territory. Hence, the phenomenon is likely to have some generality in Themeda-dominated grasslands in south-eastern Australia. The rate of tussock decline will undoubtedly vary between sites, and depend chiefly on site productivity. Interestingly, similar responses to fire and grazing exclusion have also been reported for T. triandra elsewhere and this suggests that it is a feature of the species itself, rather than a local effect restricted to southern Australia. Mott and Andrew (1985), for instance, found that T. triandra tussocks senesced rapidly after 3 yr without fire in a tropical savanna in north-west Australia whilst Belsky (1992) has reported that T. triandra can decline in less than 5 yr in the absence of disturbance in a tropical grassland in East Africa.
153	
154	The causes of Themeda tussock decline with increasing time-since-fire were not studied here and are poorly understood. It is suspected that shading (i.e. light quantity) at the soil surface, due to the increase in above-ground biomass with time-since-fire, may be a primary cause of tussock decline, as has been reported in other productive grasslands (e.g. Hulbert, 1969; Old, 1969; Knapp and Seastedt, 1986). Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) at the ground surface can be <5% of PAR available above the canopy in Themeda grasslands unburnt for >4 yr (Morgan, 1997), due to the reflection and absorption of energy by the standing plant material (Knapp, 1984). Hence, the need to elevate the photosynthetic surface high above the ground increases with time-since-fire as biomass accumulates from the ground up. Some Themeda tillers have the ability to elevate well above the soil surface (described as ‘aerial tillering’ by McDougall (1989)) to reach the light, but many tillers do not successfully compete for light in this way, leading to the loss of live tillers and the resources that are captured by the tussock. A point is reached (by 11 yr after fire) when aerial tillers can no longer be elevated higher on their weak stems and the canopy collapses. The dead material forms a thick thatch that effectively mulches the soil and prevents seedling regeneration (Lock and Milburn, 1971; McDougall, 1989) and new tiller initiation.
155	
156	Other factors that potentially contribute to Themeda tussock decline with increasing time-since-fire also reflect the effects that standing dead and litter material have on microclimate at the tussock bases. Two factors appear to warrant further consideration, namely: (i) the effects of red:far red light (i.e. light quality) (Deregibus et al., 1985) and, (ii) below- and above-ground temperatures (Old, 1969; Knapp, 1984). Both factors have been implicated in the abilities of other tussock grasses to initiate new tillers, with modifications in light quality by a dense grassland canopy being particularly detrimental to tiller populations of some other C4 grasses (Deregibus et al., 1985).
157	
158	After a long fire-free period (12 yr), a single fire did not, in the short-term, return the grassland's tussock structure to a state more characteristic of a site with a shorter inter-fire interval (i.e. 4 yr). There were fewer tillers and tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> in the long unburnt site six months after fire relative to the shorter fire-interval site and, in general, the tussock structure resembled that in the pre-fire grassland. The rate of Themeda canopy recovery was also slower in the long unburnt area. This has also been observed in a nearby grassland when fire was reintroduced after 17 yr (Lunt and Morgan, 1998). Slow vegetative recovery probably results because pre-fire tiller health was poor, with many aerial tillers being killed by fire, and hence, the subsequent regrowth is from the relatively few, newly initiated tillers found at the soil surface. Regrowth from tillers in the more frequently burnt areas, however, is more likely to be from the recovery of existing tillers, protected by the densely crowded meristems in the basal tuft (Morgan, 1998b). Whether Themeda tussock recovery in the long unburnt area continues in the subsequent post-fire yr, enabling the grassland to more closely resemble the frequently burnt area, is unknown. At the nearby Laverton North Grassland Reserve, however, areas burnt after 17 yr of fire exclusion appear to retain their differences (i.e. low tussock density, less canopy cover) at 3 yr after burning compared to adjacent areas burnt more frequently (Morgan, pers. observation).
159	
160	The decline in Themeda health with long time-since-fire intervals has two major implications for conservation management at Derrimut. Firstly, changes in

180	
181	grassland structure may affect the habitat suitability of the site for the endangered Delma impar (Striped Legless Lizard), a species largely dependent on the western volcanic plains grassland community. The animal's habitat requirements have not been conclusively determined (e.g. Coulson, 1990; Moro, 1990) but are presumed to revolve around the dense Themeda cover that develops in the yr after fire. Further research is clearly needed to identify the structural requirements most favoured by D. impar, perhaps using a technique similar to the point quadrat method used here to quantify grassland structure. However, it is apparent from this study that excluding fire for long periods is likely to cause sward deterioration and hence, potential habitat loss for this species in the long-term.
182	
183	Secondly, Themeda sward health may play a role in resisting invasion into the grassland by the aggressive alien perennial grass Nassella neesiana (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). Nassella neesiana is perhaps the most serious environmental weed in remnant native grasslands in southern Victoria (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994; McLaren et al., 1998) and poses a major threat to the conservation of this endangered ecosystem. When Themeda swards are productive and dense (>50% live cover) and tussock densities are high, invasion appears to be inhibited relative to areas where the Themeda sward cover is low and/or unhealthy (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). Leaving grassland areas unburnt for long periods is likely to increase the potential for, and rate of, invasion by N. neesiana because of the decline in vigour and competitive ability of Themeda. Maintenance of a healthy sward of Themeda may prove to be an extremely cost-effective method of slowing (but not preventing) invasion by N. neesiana at Derrimut.
184	
185	In summary, the productive, ungrazed grassland at Derrimut requires frequent biomass removal via fire if the structural dominant (T. triandra) is to remain in a vigourous state. Short inter-fire intervals (i.e. <5 yr intervals) will allow Themeda to maintain its competitiveness and the habitat values it provides for endangered vertebrates in the long-term. Burning will also benefit an inter-tussock native flora that can be rapidly eliminated from grasslands due to severe competition from Themeda in the absence of disturbance. Frequent ecological burning is therefore likely to be a far more cost-effective conservation management option at Derrimut than the current practice of intermittent, and largely unplanned, burning. When the time between ecological burns exceeds 5–6 yr, however, substantial costs are likely to be incurred to (a) restore degenerate Themeda swards again to a healthy condition and, (b) control aggressive perennial weeds that flourish with long inter-fire intervals. Such activities are non-sustainable in the long-term and importantly, they are almost entirely avoidable in the short-term.

# Effects of time-since-fire on the tussock dynamics of a dominant grass (*Themeda triandra*) in a temperate Australian grassland

John W. Morgan<sup>a,\*</sup>, Ian D. Lunt<sup>b</sup>

<sup>a</sup>School of Botany, La Trobe University, Bundoora, Vic. 3083, Australia

<sup>b</sup>The Johnstone Centre, Charles Sturt University, P.O. Box 789, Albury, NSW 2640, Australia

Received 9 June 1998; received in revised form 6 August 1998; accepted 4 September 1998

### Abstract

Changes in tussock attributes and sward structure with time-since-fire were documented for the dominant tussock grass, *Themeda triandra*, at the Derrimut Grassland Reserve in southern Victoria, Australia. When the inter-fire interval exceeded 6 yr, the number of tillers per tussock and the total number of tussocks declined, and by 11 yr, few live tillers or tussocks remained in the sward. Below-ground biomass was also substantially lower at this time. With increasing time-since-fire, the canopy of live leaves was elevated high above the soil surface and dead leaves accumulated around and over the tussock bases. Productivity declined in long unburnt areas and by 11 yr without disturbance, the canopy “collapsed” upon itself, forming a thick layer of dead thatch over the soil surface. A single fire in an area previously unburnt for 12 yr did not immediately return the tussocks to a state more characteristic of a site with a 4 yr inter-fire interval burnt at the same time. Inter-fire intervals of ≤5 yr would appear necessary to maintain the health and competitiveness of *Themeda triandra*. These findings have important implications for the maintenance of faunal habitat and the potential for weed invasion into remnant grasslands. © 1999 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.

Keywords: Australia; Conservation management; Grassland decline; Inter-fire interval; Tillers

### 1. Introduction

It is widely recognised that fire and grazing regimes have influenced the diversity of temperate grassland and grassy woodland remnants in south-eastern Australia, as in other grassland regions of the world (e.g. Booysen and Tainton, 1984; Collins and Wallace, 1990; Belsky, 1992; Fensham, 1998). Most species-rich sites in south-eastern Australia have a history of frequent burning (i.e. 1–3 yr intervals) and/or minimal stock grazing (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Stuwe, 1986; Kirkpatrick et al., 1988; Benson, 1994; Lunt, 1995; Prober and Thiele, 1995; Morgan, 1998a). Species-poor remnants, on the other hand, are either grazed by domestic stock or only very infrequently disturbed by fire or grazing (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Tremont, 1994; Prober and Thiele, 1995). Species may be lost in the complete absence of sward disturbance because of competitive exclusion (Scarlett and Parsons, 1990; Gilfedder and Kirkpatrick, 1994; Morgan, 1997), sometimes irreversibly given that few native grassland forbs appear to form large, persistent soil seed banks (Gilfedder and Kirkpatrick, 1993; Lunt, 1995, 1997; Morgan, 1995, 1998a).

Fire and grazing regimes can also alter the structure of a grassland community and the population dynamics and vigour of its dominant tussock grasses. Numerous Australian studies have reported the effects of intensive disturbance regimes on dominant grasses, allowing Moore (1970) to summarize the general changes that occur in a variety of native temperate grasslands under heavy and continuous stock grazing. Principally, there is a shift from C4 to C3 grasses, from caespitose perennials to annuals, and from native to exotic species. Frequent, low mowing may also have similar effects on the survival of tall-growing tussock grasses (Chan, 1980).

The effects of the total exclusion of stock grazing and burning on dominant tussock grasses, however, are generally less well documented in temperate Australia. In grasslands dominated by *Themeda triandra* (Kangaroo Grass), Groves (1974) suggested that there was a curvilinear relationship between shoot biomass and time-since-fire; by 5 yr after fire, new shoot growth would balance death and decomposition of old leaves to maintain a constant biomass. McDougall (1989) noted that in an undisturbed sward (10 yr since fire or grazing) in southern Victoria, tussocks were fewer, had smaller

0006-3207/99/$ - see front matter © 1999 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.
PII: S0006-3207(98)00112-8


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

380 J.W. Morgan, I.D. Lunt / Biological Conservation 88 (1999) 379–386

basal areas, and were poorly rooted compared to Themeda tussocks in a frequently burnt area. Litter levels were also much greater in the undisturbed area and covered all the intertussock spaces. McDougall (1989) concluded that without fire or grazing, “long unburnt Themeda tussocks could be expected to disappear from the sward” and seedling recruitment would be minimal under the dead thatch. In the following 10 yr, Themeda health declined further as a result of continued fire exclusion, leading to the death of many tussocks (Lunt and Morgan, 1998).

At the Derrimut Grassland Reserve in southern Victoria, Australia, fire is considered a necessary conservation management tool to maintain native species diversity (Craigie and Stuwe, 1992), but it has been applied in an adhoc manner since the creation of the reserve in 1985. Some areas have been burnt three times over the last 12 yr (maximum inter-fire interval of 4 yr), whilst other areas have never been burnt. Lunt and Morgan (1999) reported on the floristic changes that occurred during the first 10 yr of reservation and found that most native species that had survived long-term grazing were also fairly resilient to the variable fire regimes imposed. Surprisingly, the least resilient species to infrequent burning and grazing exclusion appeared to be the dominant tussock grass, Themeda triandra. This finding has important implications for the threatened fauna that rely on the grassland for habitat (e.g. the Striped Legless Lizard, Delma impar), as well as the susceptibility of the grassland community to invasion by exotic perennial grasses (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). In this paper, we investigate how time-since-fire affects the survival, vigour, structure and productivity of Themeda triandra tussocks, and the subsequent ability of tussocks to recover from fire.

### 2. Methods

#### 2.1. Study site

The 154 ha Derrimut Grassland Reserve is 15 km south-west of Melbourne, Victoria (37°48′30″S, 144°47′40″E). Mean annual rainfall is 568 mm. The geology is Early Pleistocene olivine basalt (Douglas, 1982). The reserve is dominated by a Themeda triandra grassland in well-drained areas (Lunt, 1990a) and is a remnant of the Keilor Plains grassland described by Willis (1964). This grassland type is on the verge of extinction (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994). Soils in grassland areas range from silty-clay to clay-loam with pH 7.0 (Lunt, 1990a).

The property was grazed by sheep until the 1960s and by cattle from then until 1985, when grazing was removed from the entire site after management changed to the state conservation agency for the purposes of grassland conservation.

Early recommendations for management of the reserve suggested that fire at 2–5 yr intervals were necessary to maintain botanical values (Stuwe, 1986; Lunt, 1988). However, owing to perceived negative impacts of frequent burning on endangered fauna (Coulson, 1990), a management plan recommended that the reserve be divided into 10 zones, two of which were to be burnt every year, giving a 5 yr fire interval in each zone (Craigie and Stuwe, 1992). In practice, the management plan has not been consistently implemented. Ten fires occurred between 1986 and 1997 but all had different boundaries and burnt different areas. The number of fires experienced in each zone ranged from 0 to 3 and the maximum inter-fire interval varied from 4 to over 12 yr (in areas which were never burnt).

#### 2.2. Study species

Themeda triandra (syn. T. australis) is a perennial C4 tussock grass that dominates many grassy woodlands and tropical savannahs in both Australia and Africa. In southern Victoria, T. triandra is the dominant species of natural grassland communities on volcanic soils (Patton, 1935; Willis, 1964; McDougall et al., 1994). It grows primarily from October to January in southern Victoria and is most productive in the first 3–4 yr after fire (McDougall, 1989), after which time productivity declines (Groves, 1974; McDougall, 1989). It has no means of extensive vegetative spread. Tussocks are generally fire-resistant, tillers resprouting after summer fires from protected basal apices, even when burnt annually (Morgan, in prep). Aerial tillers form when swards remain undisturbed and these are easily damaged by trampling (McDougall, 1989). The ability of tussocks and tillers to recover from fire after a long period of fire exclusion is virtually unknown, although in a companion study, Lunt and Morgan (1998) found that post-fire recovery of Themeda in areas unburnt for 17 yr lagged behind that of a grassland burnt more frequently. Longevity of tussocks is unknown in Victorian grasslands; Morgan (1998b) observed little mortality and turnover of Themeda tussocks over a 3 yr period in a biennially burnt grassland. Seed set occurs primarily in mid-summer (January; McDougall, 1989) but germination does not occur until spring (October) when soil moisture is high and soil temperatures are >20°C (Hagon, 1976). A thick litter layer of Themeda inhibits germination; seedlings are generally only observed after fire when the insulating vegetation cover and litter layer has been removed (Lock and Milburn, 1971; McDougall, 1989), or when grazed.

#### 2.3. Changes in Themeda tussocks with time-since-fire

A chronosequence study was used to assess changes in T. triandra tussock structure with the time since last 


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

J.W. Morgan, I.D. Lunt / Biological Conservation 88 (1999) 379–386 381

fire. Areas of the reserve that originally supported structurally similar species-poor Themeda grassland at the time of reservation in 1985 (Lunt, 1990a), and that subsequently differed in their fire histories, were chosen for comparative study.

The design of this study clearly represents a case of pseudoreplication (Hurlbert, 1984); whilst there was replication of plots within each of the fire history treatments (each >10 ha in size), there was no replication of the treatments (fire histories) themselves. There was no opportunity to achieve a statistically valid design to experimentally test for the effects of time-since-fire on T. triandra but rather, only the chance to study a single grassland that had, by fate of the management over the last decade, differed in fire history (i.e. the “unplanned or natural experiment” of Diamond (1986)). Sharp boundaries between the different fire zones were clearly discernible on the ground and hence, differences in tussock attributes between treatments were unlikely to be due to soil factors. Such a design places restrictions on the application of inferential statistics, but need not prevent ecological interpretation of the data and their implications for management of the Derrimut Grassland Reserve.

In areas that had last been burnt 1, 3, 5 yr ago (number of years are expressed as integers) or had remained unburnt (11 yr since exclusion of disturbance), five 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> quadrats were randomly located in visually homogeneous vegetation over an area of ca. 1 ha and the number of live tussocks, live rooted tillers and inflorescences of T. triandra were counted in December 1996. Basal circumference of tussocks was also measured. Most tussocks usually had an irregular shape that prevented accurate basal diameter estimates.

Total root biomass was determined in November 1997 in areas burnt 2, 4 and 12 yr ago. At 2 m intervals along a single transect in visually homogeneous vegetation in each fire zone, and nearest the closest, large (>10 cm diameter) tussock, one soil core (2 cm diameter × 10 cm depth) was taken within 3 cm of the edge of the tussock. A total of 18 cores were collected per fire zone. The soil samples were then sieved and rinsed under a jet of water before drying the root matter at 80°C for 72 h. It was assumed that most of the roots recovered were from T. triandra, an assumption deemed reasonable given that few other species were observed in the areas sampled.

Changes in vegetation structure in areas last burnt 0.2, 1, 3, >6 and 11 yr ago were documented using point quadrats (Kent and Coker, 1992). A frame consisting of 10 vertically held 4 mm diameter pins, each 10 cm apart, was randomly placed at 12 locations within each fire zone (n=120 points per fire zone) and all hits of both live and dead T. triandra, and their height of contact (in 3 cm intervals), were recorded.

Seasonal changes in above-ground biomass in zones burnt 1, 3 and 11 yr ago were followed for 18 months, from August 1995 to February 1997. At each site, 12 random 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> quadrats were selected at 4–6 week intervals for six months, and then again 12 months later, and all vegetation was cut to ground level, dried at 80°C for 48 h and weighed. It was assumed that most (>90%) of the biomass was that of T. triandra, an assumption likely to be valid given that (1) few other species occurred in the areas sampled and (2) the high representation of T. triandra in the biomass samples hand sorted by McDougall (1989) in a similar grassland nearby.

The comparative ability of Themeda tussocks to recover from fire was assessed by burning a 1 ha area, unburnt for 12 yr, and an equivalent area most recently burnt 4 yr previously. Both areas were burnt in November 1997. In April 1998, the total number of rooted tillers and tussocks, tussock basal circumference and visual percent cover were recorded in five randomly placed 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> quadrats at each site.

#### 2.4. Statistical analyses

The number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> , number of live tillers, average number of tillers per tussock (square root transformed), number of inflorescences (square root transformed), average number of inflorescences per tussock and mean basal circumference were compared between fire zones that differed in their time-since-fire by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey's post-hoc comparisons (Zar, 1984). Homogeneity of variance assumptions were tested using Cochrane's Test (Winer et al., 1991). A mixed-model nested ANOVA was used to test whether basal circumference was affected by site history, with quadrats nested within fire zones (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). The G-test of independence was used to test whether basal circumference, when grouped into size classes, was associated with fire history (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). Root biomass differences with fire history were compared using a one-way ANOVA on log transformed data with Tukey's post-hoc comparisons.

Attributes of post-fire recovery of areas previously unburnt for 4 and 12 yr (i.e. number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> , number of tillers, average number of tillers per tussock, percent cover) were compared using t-tests (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981). Homogeneity of variance assumptions were checked using the F<sub>max</sub>-test (Sokal and Rohlf, 1981) and satisfied in all cases. A contingency table was used to test whether basal circumference, when grouped into size classes, was associated with fire history. Expected values were calculated based on the null hypothesis of independence and tested using the chi-square statistic (Zar, 1984). Standardised residuals were examined to determine the pattern of association between the variables.


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

382 J.W. Morgan, I.D. Lunt / Biological Conservation 88 (1999) 379–386

### 3. Results

All of the above-ground tussock attributes, except basal circumference, significantly declined with increasing time-since-fire (Table 1). There were no significant differences in tussock attributes between areas burnt 1 and 3 yr previously. Rather, the effects were significant when grasslands had remained unburnt for ≥5 yr.

The total number of tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> was lowest in the long unburnt area (11 yr; F=7.10, p=0.003) but did not differ significantly between areas burnt more recently (≤5 yr). Total number of tillers and mean number of tillers per tussock were highest in 1 and 3 yr unburnt areas, intermediate, but significantly lower, in the 5 yr unburnt area, and least in the 11 yr unburnt area (F=35.32, p < 0.0001 and F=10.54, p< 0.001 respectively). Inflorescence production (total and mean number per tussock) declined with time-since-fire in a similar way (F=47.91, p< 0.0001 and F=16.82, p< 0.001 respectively). Tussock circumference did not differ within (F=0.926, p=0.540) or between (F=1.464, p=0.224) any of the fire zones, nor was the size class distribution of tussocks significantly associated with time-since-fire (χ<sup>2</sup>=12.07, n=12, p> 0.05). Thus, all tussock size classes were represented in all fire zones in similar ratios.

Mean root biomass (±1SE) in the 12 yr unburnt area (0.174 ± 0.019 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup>; F=26.19, p < 0.001) was less than 45% of that in the areas burnt two (0.432 ± 0.016 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup>) and four (0.384 ± 0.023 g/100 cm<sup>3</sup>) years previously, which did not differ from one another (p > 0.05).

While the total number of contacts with live Themeda did not increase greatly in the years 1 to >6 after burning in the point quadrat study (Fig. 1), the spatial distribution of live leaves in the canopy changed dramatically (Fig. 2). Immediately after fire, Themeda resprouted rapidly from the base and live leaves were mostly concentrated near the ground level (≤6 cm) during year 1. In years 2 to >6, the canopy of live leaves elevated higher in each year so that by >6 yr, most of the live canopy was >18 cm above ground level. During the same period, live leaves disappeared completely from tussock bases (<3 cm) and dead vegetation accumulated from the ‘bottom up’ (Fig. 2). At >6 yr after fire, 73% of all Themeda leaves in the canopy were dead. After 11 yr without disturbance, the grassland appeared to collapse upon itself (Fig. 2). Dead vegetation remained on the soil surface (in a thick layer to 12 cm deep) whilst almost no live vegetation existed at any layer in the canopy.

Over the 18 months in which above-ground biomass was followed, areas unburnt for 1 and 3 yr at the start of observations increased their total biomass by 167% and 152%, respectively (Fig. 3), within the context of large seasonal variation. During the same time, the total biomass of the area unburnt for 11 yr declined to 58% of its original amount. The decline was most dramatic between February 1997 and February 1998 when biomass fell from 707 g m<sup>−2</sup> to 462 g m<sup>−2</sup>, despite large increases in biomass at the other two sites. This decline corresponded with the grassland collapse observed in areas which had remained unburnt for >12 yr.

Time-since-fire affected the subsequent ability of Themeda tussocks to recover from fire (Table 2). The canopy of the long unburnt area (12 yr since fire) regrew more slowly (7% versus 35%), had fewer tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup>, had fewer tillers and fewer tillers per tussock than the area that had a shorter inter-fire interval (4 yr since fire; Table 2). Whilst there was no significant

difference in the mean basal size of tussocks at each site (Table 2), the size class distribution of regenerating tussocks was associated with time-since-fire (Table 3). Tussock regeneration at the long unburnt site consisted of significantly fewer large tussocks (>25 cm basal circumference) and significantly more intermediate-sized tussocks (5–15 cm) than expected using a null hypothesis of independence, whilst at the 4 yr burn site, large tussocks (>25 cm) were more common than expected.

### 4. Discussion

It has long been recognised that frequent biomass removal by burning is necessary to maintain native plant diversity in ungrazed, species-rich grassland remnants on the western volcanic plains in southern Victoria (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Scarlett and Parsons, 1982; Stuwe, 1986). Where inter-fire intervals exceed 5 yr, even on only rare occasions, competitive exclusion by the dominant tussock grass (T. triandra) has usually been considered to reduce native plant diversity (Stuwe and Parsons, 1977; Scarlett and Parsons, 1990). This decline may be irreversible given that the soil seed bank type possessed by many native species is a transient one (Lunt, 1995, 1996; Morgan, 1995, 1998a). This study suggests that frequent biomass removal is also necessary to maintain the health and vigour of the dominant grass itself at one of the few reserves dedicated to the conservation of this threatened community (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994).

The effect of ‘time-since-fire’ on Themeda was the specific parameter of interest in this study, but it is confounded with another fire regime factor, namely, the fire frequency (Morrison et al., 1995). Some areas experienced no fires in the 12 yr since reservation, others only one fire, and yet other areas experienced three fires in the same period. Although the effects of fire frequency on Themeda tussocks should not be discounted, given that all fire zones were generally similar at the time of reservation and that the number of fires experienced at all sites was low, the parameter of time-since-fire would appear to be a valid one to compare between fire zones.

When time-since-fire exceeded 6 yr, the total number of tillers, number of tillers per tussock and number of inflorescences per tussock all declined substantially. Whilst the total number of live leaves in the canopy was relatively constant between yr 2 and 6 after fire, the canopy was raised high above the soil surface with a consequent accumulation of dead leaves around the tussock base. In the prolonged absence of fire (by 11 yr),

tussock degeneration becomes substantial; few live tussocks survive in the grassland and the canopy collapses on itself. At 11 yr after fire, the grassland consists mainly of a dead, slowly decomposing thatch, with little live above-ground material and a markedly declining productivity. The decline was mirrored below-ground where root biomass was also substantially lower than in areas burnt more recently. McDougall (1989) reported the beginnings of tussock decline in a T. triandra grassland reserve nearby after 10 yr of fire exclusion and we have observed similar processes in other Themeda grasslands in western Victoria, Gippsland and the Australian Capital Territory. Hence, the phenomenon is likely to have some generality in Themeda-dominated grasslands in south-eastern Australia. The rate of tussock decline will undoubtedly vary between sites, and depend chiefly on site productivity. Interestingly, similar responses to fire and grazing exclusion have also been reported for T. triandra elsewhere and this suggests that it is a feature of the species itself, rather than a local effect restricted to southern Australia. Mott and Andrew (1985), for instance, found that T. triandra tussocks senesced rapidly after 3 yr without fire in a tropical savanna in north-west Australia whilst Belsky (1992) has reported that T. triandra can decline in less than 5 yr in the absence of disturbance in a tropical grassland in East Africa.

The causes of Themeda tussock decline with increasing time-since-fire were not studied here and are poorly understood. It is suspected that shading (i.e. light quantity) at the soil surface, due to the increase in above-ground biomass with time-since-fire, may be a primary cause of tussock decline, as has been reported in other productive grasslands (e.g. Hulbert, 1969; Old, 1969; Knapp and Seastedt, 1986). Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) at the ground surface can be <5% of PAR available above the canopy in Themeda grasslands unburnt for >4 yr (Morgan, 1997), due to the reflection and absorption of energy by the standing plant material (Knapp, 1984). Hence, the need to elevate the photosynthetic surface high above the ground increases with time-since-fire as biomass accumulates from the ground up. Some Themeda tillers have the ability to elevate well above the soil surface (described as ‘aerial tillering’ by McDougall (1989)) to reach the light, but many tillers do not successfully compete for light in this way, leading to the loss of live tillers and the resources that are captured by the tussock. A point is reached (by 11 yr after fire) when aerial tillers can no longer be elevated higher on their weak stems and the canopy collapses. The dead material forms a thick thatch that effectively mulches the soil and prevents seedling regeneration (Lock and Milburn, 1971; McDougall, 1989) and new tiller initiation.

Other factors that potentially contribute to Themeda tussock decline with increasing time-since-fire also reflect the effects that standing dead and litter material have on microclimate at the tussock bases. Two factors appear to warrant further consideration, namely: (i) the effects of red:far red light (i.e. light quality) (Deregibus et al., 1985) and, (ii) below- and above-ground temperatures (Old, 1969; Knapp, 1984). Both factors have been implicated in the abilities of other tussock grasses to initiate new tillers, with modifications in light quality by a dense grassland canopy being particularly detrimental to tiller populations of some other C4 grasses (Deregibus et al., 1985).

After a long fire-free period (12 yr), a single fire did not, in the short-term, return the grassland's tussock structure to a state more characteristic of a site with a shorter inter-fire interval (i.e. 4 yr). There were fewer tillers and tussocks per 0.25 m<sup>2</sup> in the long unburnt site six months after fire relative to the shorter fire-interval site and, in general, the tussock structure resembled that in the pre-fire grassland. The rate of Themeda canopy recovery was also slower in the long unburnt area. This has also been observed in a nearby grassland when fire was reintroduced after 17 yr (Lunt and Morgan, 1998). Slow vegetative recovery probably results because pre-fire tiller health was poor, with many aerial tillers being killed by fire, and hence, the subsequent regrowth is from the relatively few, newly initiated tillers found at the soil surface. Regrowth from tillers in the more frequently burnt areas, however, is more likely to be from the recovery of existing tillers, protected by the densely crowded meristems in the basal tuft (Morgan, 1998b). Whether Themeda tussock recovery in the long unburnt area continues in the subsequent post-fire yr, enabling the grassland to more closely resemble the frequently burnt area, is unknown. At the nearby Laverton North Grassland Reserve, however, areas burnt after 17 yr of fire exclusion appear to retain their differences (i.e. low tussock density, less canopy cover) at 3 yr after burning compared to adjacent areas burnt more frequently (Morgan, pers. observation).

The decline in Themeda health with long time-since-fire intervals has two major implications for conservation management at Derrimut. Firstly, changes in

grassland structure may affect the habitat suitability of the site for the endangered Delma impar (Striped Legless Lizard), a species largely dependent on the western volcanic plains grassland community. The animal's habitat requirements have not been conclusively determined (e.g. Coulson, 1990; Moro, 1990) but are presumed to revolve around the dense Themeda cover that develops in the yr after fire. Further research is clearly needed to identify the structural requirements most favoured by D. impar, perhaps using a technique similar to the point quadrat method used here to quantify grassland structure. However, it is apparent from this study that excluding fire for long periods is likely to cause sward deterioration and hence, potential habitat loss for this species in the long-term.

Secondly, Themeda sward health may play a role in resisting invasion into the grassland by the aggressive alien perennial grass Nassella neesiana (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). Nassella neesiana is perhaps the most serious environmental weed in remnant native grasslands in southern Victoria (McDougall and Kirkpatrick, 1994; McLaren et al., 1998) and poses a major threat to the conservation of this endangered ecosystem. When Themeda swards are productive and dense (>50% live cover) and tussock densities are high, invasion appears to be inhibited relative to areas where the Themeda sward cover is low and/or unhealthy (Lunt and Morgan, submitted). Leaving grassland areas unburnt for long periods is likely to increase the potential for, and rate of, invasion by N. neesiana because of the decline in vigour and competitive ability of Themeda. Maintenance of a healthy sward of Themeda may prove to be an extremely cost-effective method of slowing (but not preventing) invasion by N. neesiana at Derrimut.

In summary, the productive, ungrazed grassland at Derrimut requires frequent biomass removal via fire if the structural dominant (T. triandra) is to remain in a vigourous state. Short inter-fire intervals (i.e. <5 yr intervals) will allow Themeda to maintain its competitiveness and the habitat values it provides for endangered vertebrates in the long-term. Burning will also benefit an inter-tussock native flora that can be rapidly eliminated from grasslands due to severe competition from Themeda in the absence of disturbance. Frequent ecological burning is therefore likely to be a far more cost-effective conservation management option at Derrimut than the current practice of intermittent, and largely unplanned, burning. When the time between ecological burns exceeds 5–6 yr, however, substantial costs are likely to be incurred to (a) restore degenerate Themeda swards again to a healthy condition and, (b) control aggressive perennial weeds that flourish with long inter-fire intervals. Such activities are non-sustainable in the long-term and importantly, they are almost entirely avoidable in the short-term.

1	*Proceedings — Fire Effects on Rare and Endangered Species and Habitats Conference, Nov. 13-16, 1995. Coeur d'Alene, Idaho. © IAWF, 1997. Printed in U.S.A.*
2	
3	163
4	
5	# **Conservation of Endangered Plants in Urban Fire-Prone Habitats**
6	
7	**Tony D. Auld and Judith Scott** 
8	
9	*New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville N.S.W. 2220, Australia Tel. +61 02 9585 6497; Fax +61 02 9585 6495; E-mail tauld@pws.nsw.gov.au*
10	
11	**Abstract.** A number of endangered plant species occur in National Parks and associated bushland that are adjacent to urban areas in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia. Within these areas fire is a repeated and frequent disturbance event that potentially threatens not only the endangered flora but life and property as well. These threats were well illustrated by the impact of the fires that occurred in January 1994 in Sydney.
12	
13	For the management of such fire-prone areas there is a need to identify those fire regimes likely to drive the endangered flora to extinction. Management of fire-sensitive, threatened *Darwinia* (Myrtaceae) and *Grevillea* (Proteaceae) species illustrates how conservation goals can be applied along with protection of life and property. A regime of frequent fire will lead to local population declines and extinction in both *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species. Consequently, frequent burning on a regular basis for hazard reduction to protect property assets is inappropriate for the conservation of these species. *Darwinia* species also require fires that cause significant soil heating (high consumption of fine fuel) to break seed dormancy in soil stored seed, while *Grevillea* species require fires of a large spatial extent to minimise the impact of mammalian seed predators on seed outputs from the first few seed-crops produced by plants after a fire.
14	
15	**Keywords:** Fire regime; Threatened species; *Darwinia*; *Grevillea*
16	
17	#### **Introduction**
18	
19	In the Sydney Region of southeastern Australia, much of the vegetation is highly flammable and fires are a common and frequent event. For example, during January of 1994, some 90% and 65% respectively of the two major, large urban reserves (Royal and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Parks) were burnt. In this rich and diverse floristic area, around 2000 plant species regularly experience fire. As a consequence, the management of fire is one of the principal challenges facing managers of natural ecosystems in the Sydney Region. Managers must attempt to protect life and property from the dangers posed by fire in urban bushland as well as conserving this biodiversity.
20	
21	Given the high potential for extreme fire events, where effective control of wildfire is not always possible (as happened in January 1994), there is increasing pressure for widespread fuel reduction burning in urban bushland adjacent to human assets such as houses. Such areas contain a number of endangered, vulnerable or rare plant species that are of high conservation significance, as well as more common species, all of which will have particular fire requirements which may or may not be compatible with burning for fuel reduction purposes. Hence, there is a potential for a conflict over protection versus conservation priorities (Bradstock, Keith & Auld 1995, Bradstock & Scott 1995). To attempt to resolve such conflicts we must have a sound knowledge of the effects of different fire regimes on plant and animal species and as land managers apply an informed choice of appropriate fire regimes to ensure the maintenance of populations of plants and animals.
22	
23	This paper presents data on the effect of different components of the fire regime on several threatened plant species in order to provide land managers with potential conservation prescriptions for threatened plant species. In particular, we identify those fire regimes that may cause populations to decline. Such prescriptions can then be incorporated into planning and the implementation of a fuel reduction program, so that conservation issues are not ignored and fire regimes which threaten plant conservation are avoided.
24	
25	#### **Study Area**
26	
27	The Sydney area in south-eastern Australia is a large urban area fringed with large bushland reserves and containing many smaller reserves (Figure 1). Within this area, the vegetation is dominated by sclerophyll heathlands, woodlands and forests, situated on infertile sandy soils derived from Hawkesbury sandstone (Beadle 1981), in a landscape of dissected sandstone plateaux. Rainfall is around 1200mm per annum with a peak in late summer. Average monthly maximum/minimum temperatures for
28	
29	
30	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
31	
32	164 Auld, T. D. and Scott, J.
33	
34	Legend: Cleared areas; Vegetated areas; National Parks; scale 0-25 km. ○ *Grevillea caleyi*; ● *Grevillea longifolia*; ○ *Grevillea shiressii*; ■ *Darwinia biflora*; □ *Darwinia diminuta*; ▲ *Darwinia glaucophylla*; △ *Darwinia procera*.
35	
36	**Figure 1.** The Sydney urban area and adjacent bushland reserves showing the distribution of *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* study species.
37	
38	Sydney are 26/18°C in summer and 16/8°C in winter. A broad range of fire regimes are possible in the Sydney Region. High intensity wildfires occur in the order of once every 5-10 years, while deliberate prescriptions of low intensity fires are commonly used for fuel reduction. Arson is a major source of wildfire ignitions.
39	
40	#### **The Fire Regime**
41	
42	For the long term survival of plants and animals we need to know how they are affected by the fire regime, ie. (frequency, intensity, season, spatial extent). Here we concentrate on fire-sensitive plants.
43	
44	#### *Fire frequency*
45	
46	All fires burn areas of vegetation that have been burnt some time before. Consequently, the vegetation is really a mosaic of fire histories, with some parts having had more fires than others over a given time period. We need to try and understand how important this unequal patchiness of fires through time is for the survival of plants.
47	
48	Plants that are killed by fire rely on seed germination after fires to survive at a particular location. For these fire-sensitive plants, there must be sufficient time between successive fires for seedlings to mature and produce more seeds and hence, add seeds to the seedbank. In the Sydney area, this time will vary between species and loca
49	
50	
51	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
52	
53	- Conservation of Endangered Plants in Urban Fire-Prone Habitats - 165
54	
55	tions (Benson 1985), from species that flower within 1-2 years after fire (*Actinotus helianthi, Acacia suaveolens*) to those that may take 4-8 years to reach maturity (*Banksia ericifolia*). If another fire should occur before these plants have matured, dramatic changes in the vegetation may occur. Fire-sensitive plants with seed stored in woody capsules usually release all their seeds after a fire and no residual seeds remain in cones. These plants are the group of species most susceptible to two fires in short succession. Plants that have seeds stored in the soil usually have some residual seedbank remaining in the soil following post-fire germination. For these species, a second fire before seedlings mature may severely reduce population numbers but it may not eliminate species locally. However, in some places, after some fires, the entire soil seedbank may be exhausted, eg. Restionaceae and Epacridaceae (Meney et al. 1994), Grevillea (Auld unpubl.) and local extinction will occur if two fires occur close enough together to kill seedlings from the first fire before they are mature. Ideally, as land managers with concerns for the conservation of biodiversity, we should allow the interval between fires to be long enough not only simply for plant species to mature, but at a minimum, several fruiting seasons beyond this so that a sufficiently large seedbank can be established before the next fire occurs.
56	
57	#### *Fire Intensity*
58	
59	How hot a fire is will depend on how much combustible fuel is available, how dry this fuel is, the topography of the area and the weather conditions, such as humidity and windspeed. When an area is burnt, the important thing for plants and animals is how much heat is produced, and in many areas around Sydney, this usually varies markedly even on a very small scale (i.e., over tens of meters). How much heat a fire produces can affect the survival of plants. In intense fires there is likely to be higher levels of resprouting plants killed, and longer periods needed before the next fire for recovery, than in mild fires. For plants, the more heat produced by a fire, the greater are the opportunities for seedling recruitment and the greater the magnitude of seedlings that are recruited (Auld & O'Connell 1991). Many plant species have seeds which lie dormant in the soil and for a number of these the amount of soil heating that occurs during the passage of a fire will govern the degree of germination after the fire. This heat response is widespread in many plant families, particularly legumes, in fire-prone communities throughout the world (Martin et al. 1975, Jeffery et al. 1988, Auld & O'Connell 1991, Keeley 1991). Bradstock and Auld (1995) have shown that in Hawkesbury sandstone soil around Sydney, it is the amount of fine fuel that is consumed during a fire that governs the degree of soil heating.
60	
61	#### *Fire season*
62	
63	Given the prevalence of arson and widespread hazard reduction burning for the protection of life and property, fires can now be expected to occur at just about any time of the year in the Sydney Region. The question is, for the long-term survival of plants does it matter when the vegetation is burnt? In Sydney, Bradstock and Bedward (1992) have suggested that seedling survival after fire is largely independent of season of burn because rainfall is very variable. Although there is a trend for wetter periods in late summer/autumn and drier periods in spring this pattern is not strong enough to allow accurate predictions about the impact of season of burn on seedling survival post-fire. Perhaps the most critical role season of burning may play is in influencing fire intensity. Fires in the hot dry summer months when fuel moisture is low will generally be of higher intensities than burns in winter when the vegetation is moister, an ambient temperatures are lower.
64	
65	#### *Fire Spatial Extent*
66	
67	What is the impact of the spatial extent of fires on plants? In Sydney, fires come in all shapes and sizes. Some burn very extensive areas, while others may only burn a hectare or so. Within the boundaries of a burnt area, fires may be widespread and burn most of the vegetation or leave large parts of the vegetation unburnt or simply lightly scorched. All fires will be different, depending on the terrain, rate of fire spread, amount of fuel available and its moisture content and weather conditions and natural or man-made fire breaks. This results in a patchiness of fires in area and intensity.
68	
69	For plants, the spatial extent of fires may be important where burns occur on a very small scale (a few hectares). In such cases, native animals from surrounding unburnt vegetation may graze heavily on the new green shoots that appear after fire and hence, cause a decline in some plant species. These native animals may also consume many of the seeds that are produced in the first few years after fire for those fire-sensitive plants that are trying to replenish their soil seedbanks. This will slow the rate of recovery of such plants.
70

94	#### **The Effects of the Fire Regime on Threatened Plant Species**
95	
96	For all study species, demographic data were collated on threatened *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species (Scott 1986, Auld et al. 1991, Auld et al. 1993, Auld and Tozer 1995, Scott et al. 1995) and the impacts of components of the fire regime were assessed. A summary of the significant demographic characteristics of our threatened study species is presented in Table 1.
97	
98	#### *Darwinia* spp. (Myrtaceae)
99	
100	As the *Darwinia* spp. studied are all killed by fire, a fire-free period is needed after any one fire to allow seedlings to mature and replenish the soil seedbank. Plants can produce a few fruits two years after fire. As plants grow, fecundity increases and for all *Darwinia* species, soil seedbanks should increase rapidly 5-10 years after a fire. Most of the annually produced seed-crop is released in a viable, dormant state and would be incorporated into this seedbank, although there is some yearly variation in the proportion of non dormant seeds produced (eg. *D. glaucophylla,* Table 1).
101	
102	For *D. biflora,* some 75% of the dormant seed released in any one annual seed-crop becomes non dormant and has germinated by 24 months after release, i.e., most seeds from any one seed-crop are short-lived in the soil. The seedbank should buildup in the soil rapidly after a site is burnt, but the seedbank will also decline rapidly should adult plants senesce. The low level of seed longevity in the soil in *D. biflora* (Table 1) suggests that both adult survival and the level of adult fecundity are the critical factors that govern persistence of the soil seedbank. As seeds decay rapidly in the soil, adult plants must regularly produce seeds to maintain a soil seedbank. The longevity of annual seed inputs to the soil seedbank is currently unknown for the other *Darwinia* spp. However, for *D. diminuta, D. glaucophylla* and *D. procera* the seedbank size is likely to be much larger than in *D. biflora,*  given the higher fecundity levels in these species (Figure 2).
103	
104	The fate of those seeds in the soil which lose their dormancy and germinate is unknown. It seems likely that

136	#### *Grevillea* spp. (Proteaceae)
137	
138	All *Grevillea* species studied were killed by fire and relied on seed germination after a fire to maintain populations. For all species, the magnitude of the soil seedbank will be largely controlled by the levels of adult fecundity, mammal seed predation and adult mortality.
139	
140	In *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia,* seedlings do not flower and produce seeds before 2.5-5 years of age. Fecundity is low in *G. caleyi* with only about 3% of flowers resulting in mature seed (Scott 1986). The level of fecundity in both *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia* increases until around 10 years of age in response to plant growth (Figure 3). No fecundity estimates have been made for *G. shiressii.* Seeds had a high level of viability and were largely released in a dormant state in *G. caleyi* and *G. shiressii.* In *G. longifolia,* a large fraction of seeds were released in a non dormant state (Table 1), although this is variable across populations and years. Predispersal seed predation is known to be high in *G. caleyi* and *G. shiressii* with significant losses to the weevil *Cydmaea dorsalis* Lea (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) in *G. caleyi* and to the wasp *Eurytoma* sp. (Hymenoptera: Eurytomidae) in *G. shiressii.* In *G. caleyi* and *G. longifolia,* seed dispersal is minimal. At maturity the fruits dehisce, dropping the seed to the ground beneath the parent plant. The seeds lack any lipid body attachment that would make them attractive to ants (Auld 1995). In contrast, *G. shiressii* seeds have a lipid body attachment and some 28% of seed are dispersed by ants. In all three threatened *Grevillea* spp. and other more common *Grevillea* spp., post-dispersal seed predation is very high (Auld 1995, Auld & Denham in prep.). 170	#### **Implications for Fire Management**
171	
172	What are the implications for the management of these obligate seeding species? The most critical aspect of fire management for obligate seeders is the impact of frequent fires on these populations. Population declines or local extinctions are predicted after 2-3 fires occurring in close succession and hence, minimum fire-free intervals are needed to maintain the species. The fire free-intervals will vary depending on the rate of replenishment of the soil seedbank after any one fire and the proportion of seeds that emerge from the seedbank after a fire (ie, the degree to which the seedbank is depleted after a fire). Estimates of the minimum fire free intervals needed to maintain populations of threatened *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species vary from 5-10 to 8-12 years (Table 2). It is not only important to maintain these threatened species, but also the species with which they co-habit. These suggested minimum fire-free intervals do not contradict with suggested minimum fire-free intervals for other plants species that co-habit with threatened *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* species (Bradstock and Auld 1987). Consequently, for the long-term survival of threatened species of *Darwinia* and *Grevillea* and their associated vegetation communities, under a regime of repeated fires, care should be taken to accurately record the fire histories of all remaining populations. This will allow sites potentially threatened by high fire frequency to be identified.
173	
174	In *Darwinia* species, where heat is the fire-related cue that breaks seed dormancy, some residual seedbank should be present after any single fire. The amount and location of this seed will depend on the level of soil heating during the passage of a fire (Bradstock and Auld 1995). In *Grevillea,* the fire-related dormancy breaking cue is unknown, although it is not simply heat (Auld and Tozer 1995). In *Grevillea,* a high proportion of seeds within the soil seedbank may emerge after any one fire and in some
