# **INTRODUCTION**

The natural fire regimes of the treeless high mountain vegetation of Australia are difficult to quantify, and the role of fire in the dynamics of alpine and subalpine vegetation in Australia is largely unknown. At the landscape scale (that of square kilometres or more), fire appears to be relatively rare in these environments (Kirkpatrick & Dickinson 1984; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Wimbush & Forrester 1988; Williams & Costin 1994). Given that few fires have occurred in alpine and subalpine vegetation, knowledge of post-fire ecology, especially initial impacts and early responses, in alpine and treeless subalpine vegetation is also scant.

Aboriginal people utilized the high country, but little is known about their use of fire there. Good evidence exists for fire-stick farming in lowlands surrounding high mountains, but there is little evidence for the extensive use of fire, or even the need to use fire extensively, in the treeless vegetation (Flood 1980). Prior to European settlement, landscape-scale fires are likely to have occurred in high mountain treeless vegetation in mainland Australia only once or twice per century (Leigh *et al*. 1987). European settlement in and around the high country commenced in the mid-19th century. Prescribed burning was used by pastoralists in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to improve the quality of green pick, and miners used fire to clear undergrowth to expose geological features (Costin

# Early post-fire regeneration in subalpine heathland and grassland in the Victorian Alpine National Park, south-eastern Australia

C-H. A. WAHREN,1† W. A. PAPST2‡ AND R. J. WILLIAMS<sup>3</sup> \*

1 *Department of Agricultural Sciences, La Trobe University, Victoria,* <sup>2</sup> *Centre for Land Protection Research, Bendigo, Victoria and* <sup>3</sup> *CSIRO Sustainable Ecosystems, PMB 44, Winnellie Northern Territory 0822, Australia (Email: dick.williams@terc.csiro.au)*

**Abstract** Landscape fire (at the scale of square kilometres or more) is relatively rare in the alpine and subalpine environments of Australia. In early 1998, a major fire (the 'Caledonia Fire'), burnt approximately 35 000 ha, of which approximately 3000 hectares was subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland within the Victorian Alpine National Park. This fire was one of only three landscape-scale fires that have occurred anywhere in the treeless vegetation of the Victorian Alps in the past 100 years, the others being in 1939 and 1985. Monitoring of regeneration in subalpine vegetation commenced 3 weeks postfire. Sites were established in burnt grassland at Holmes Plain (1400 m a.s.l.) and burnt grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain (1480 m a.s.l.), and in unburnt grassland at both sites. In burnt grassland and heathland, the fire consumed much of the vegetation, leaving extensive areas of bare ground. The cover of dense vegetation declined from > 70% prefire, to approximately 15% immediately postfire. Bare ground at the Holmes and Wellington Plains sites ranged from 70% to 85% immediately postfire. By May 2000, approximately 2.5 years postfire, dense vegetation cover in grassland had increased to approximately 20%, and bare ground had decreased to an average of approximately 30%. In unburnt grassland, dense vegetation cover was generally > 95%, and the amount of bare ground less than 5%. The tussock-forming snow grasses resprouted vigorously following fire, and had flowered prolifically after 1 year. In heathland, most of the shrubs were incinerated, leaving close to 100% bare soil. Since then, a number of grasses and some dominant shrubs have resprouted vigorously, with some seedling regeneration. By May 2000, in heathland, bare soil was still > 50% and dense vegetation < 20%. Such ground cover conditions during this early postfire period were well below prefire levels, and well below the levels necessary to protect alpine soils from erosion. The Caledonia Fire has provided a rare opportunity to study ecological processes associated with postfire regeneration in treeless subalpine landscapes.

**Key words**: alpine, bare ground, biomass, Caledonia Fire, catchment protection, disturbance, fire regime, litter, vegetation cover.

Accepted for publication May 2001.

<sup>\*</sup>Corresponding author.

Present address: Boreal Ecology Cooperative Research Unit, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Alaska USA.

Present address: Department of Agricultural Sciences, La Trobe University, Victoria, Australia.

{1}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

1954; Carr & Turner 1959a; Lawrence 1999). These practices all increased the frequency of fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation (Pryor 1939; Stretton 1946; Raeder-Roitzsch & Phillips 1958; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Banks 1989; Kershaw & Strickland 1989; Lawrence 1999). On mainland Australia, prescribed fire in treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation was banned in the 1940s and 1950s, as its use was linked clearly to land degradation in the high mountain catchments (Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin *et al*. 1959; Williams & Costin 1994).

In Victoria, there are few detailed data on the occurrence of fires and their effects on alpine and subalpine plant communities. Extensive fires in treeless vegetation are known to have occurred on two occasions in the 20th century. According to Carr & Turner (1959a) '. . . small fires spread onto the high plains from the neighbouring slopes prior to 1939, such as in 1926, but these fires were of minor importance'. In contrast, the State-wide fires of 1939 burnt approximately 80% of the snow gum country on the Bogong High Plains above approximately 1500 m a.s.l. (Carr & Turner 1959a). Although these fires burnt much treeless subalpine and alpine vegetation, that is, heathland, grassland, and wetland (Carr & Turner 1959a), we do not know the precise extent or severity of these fires. In 1985, a fire at Mount Buffalo burnt approximately 11 000 ha of lowland and forested foothill vegetation, and approximately 150 ha of treeless subalpine heathland, grassland and wetland (Wahren *et al*. 1999). The subject of the present paper is an extensive fire that occurred in the south-eastern parts of the Victorian Alpine National Park in January 1998: the 'Caledonia Fire'.

Subsequent to the last glaciation, Australian alpine environments have evolved in response to relatively small-scale disturbances (1 m<sup>2</sup> –1 ha) such as localized frost heave, wind blasting and insect herbivory. Larger scale disturbances such as fire and extensive grazing by large vertebrate herbivores over square kilometres of country are rare or non-existent (Williams 1990; Williams & Costin 1994). Under such a native regime of small-scale disturbances, Australian alpine environments are characterized by a high cover of vegetation (normally close to 100%) and relatively little exposed bare soil (< 1–2%; Australian Academy of Science 1957; Costin 1958; Williams & Costin 1994). The removal of vegetation and litter by fire, and the consequent exposure of bare soil, has major implications in Australian alpine landscapes, because exposure of alpine soils is undesirable for soil conservation purposes, and subsequent regeneration to adequate soil cover is slow (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).

In the present paper, we summarize the early postfire changes in vegetation and ground cover conditions that have occurred in grassland and heathland on Holmes and Wellington Plains, two of the larger high plains burnt in the Caledonia Fire (Fig. 1). We focus on the first 2 years post-fire because there have been no detailed, quantitative studies of early post-fire responses in Australian alpine landscapes following fires of such magnitude. The specific aim is to document the changes in vegetation cover, the amount of bare ground, and changes to gaps that have occurred in grassland and heathland over the first 2 years post-fire. Both communities are extensive in treeless high mountain environments in Australia. Within each, the amount of bare ground and both the quality and quantity of vegetation cover, and the nature of gaps created by the death of grass tussocks or shrubs, are critical determinants of both vegetation change and landscape condition in Australian high mountain landscapes (Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994).

#### **Fire and study sites**

The Caledonia Fire started on 31 December 1997, from an abandoned campfire on the Caledonia River, in mixed lowland eucalypt forest. 1 January 1998 was a day of extreme fire weather: the predicted forest fire danger index (Luke & McArthur 1978) for the nearby town of Heyfield was 50 (Tolhurst 1998). Fire weather and drought conditions at this time were broadly similar to those of other years in the past century when widespread fires occurred in Victoria: 1983, 1967, 1964, 1939 and 1926 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000). The fire burnt approximately 35 000 ha of the Carey Forest, of which approximately 22 000 ha was within the Alpine National Park, and approximately 3000 ha was treeless subalpine vegetation.

The landscape above approximately 1400 m is a mosaic of high ridges, wooded slopes, rolling grassy plains and wetlands. The treeless plains and surrounding snow gum (*Eucalyptus pauciflora*) woodlands have been grazed during summer and autumn by free ranging cattle since the late 19th century and cattle were present at the time of the fire. Sporadic grazing continued for 3 months post-fire, but grazing was excluded from the fire-affected area for the 1998–1999 and 1999–2000 seasons.

The fires were intense crown fires in both the eucalypt forests of the foothills and the subalpine snow gum woodlands. In the treeless vegetation, fire intensity was unknown, but field observations indicated that the fire at Wellington Plain was more intense and burnt more of the vegetation than at Holmes Plain. At Holmes and Wellington Plains, > 90% of the grassland, heathland and snow gum woodlands were burnt, and the subalpine bogs were also extensively burnt. This represents the most extensive fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation since 1939 (McCarthy & Tolhurst 2000).

{2}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

# **METHODS**

#### **Monitoring sites**

At the end of January 1998, 3 weeks after the fire, monitoring sites were established at Holmes Plain (146°45-14--E, 37°24-32--S; 1400 m a.s.l.) and Wellington Plain (146°49-54--E, 37°29-46--S; 1480 m a.s.l.). These plains were selected because they were representative of the extensive subalpine high plains in this region of the Victorian Alps (Walsh *et al*. 1984, 1986) and, in the case of Holmes Plain, because two sites had been established in grassland in 1991 as part of a general monitoring program in the high country. At both sites, the soil was alpine humus soil, a wellstructured organic loam that is acid, nutrient poor, and is typical of most alpine and subalpine grasslands and heathlands in mainland Australia (Williams & Costin 1994). One of these sites was burnt, the other was outside the fire perimeter; both sites were used for the present study. Extra sites were established in burnt heathland and grassland at both Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in an unburnt area of grassland at Wellington Plain, close to the burnt grassland. This unburnt grassland was within the fire perimeter. Using this network of sites, the changes in the burnt grassland over time could be compared with those in longunburnt grassland. Unfortunately, there were no suitable unburnt heathland sites.

# **Estimation of ground cover and biomass**

Point quadrats, sampled along permanent transects (Kent & Coker 1992), were used to record species composition and ground cover conditions. Transects were 10 m long with points 4 mm in diameter, and 20 cm apart (50 points per transect). This method has been widely used for many decades to estimate the cover of individual species and life forms (grasses, forbs and shrubs) in treeless vegetation in Australia (Carr & Turner 1959b; Wimbush & Costin 1979a,b,c; Wahren *et al*. 1994). Ground cover at each point was rated in terms of three cover classes (Wahren *et al*. 1994). Cover class 1 (CC1) is fixed litter or dense live vegetation, cover class (CC2) provides intermediate vegetation cover but the litter is loose, and cover class (CC3) consists of bare ground or sparse vegetation and/or thin (< 5 mm thick) loose litter. Live vegetation and litter were measured together in all cover classes, as both are important for soil protection in Australian alpine environments (Wahren *et al*. 1994).

In the Holmes Plain grassland, there were 40 transects (including 13 from 1991) distributed over an area of approximately 40 ha of burnt grassland. There were an additional 10 transects (six from 1991) in the unburnt grassland, over an area of approximately 2 ha; burnt and unburnt grassland sites were approximately 1 km apart. At Wellington Plain, there were 40 transects established in burnt heathland over an area of approximately 40 ha, and 10 transects in burnt grassland over an area of 2 ha. Subsequent to January 1998, the vegetation was remeasured along the transects in May 1998, January, May and December 1999, and late April/early May 2000. In December 1999, four transects were set up in a patch of unburnt grassland at Wellington Plain, 200 m from the burnt grassland; these were remeasured in May 2000.

Above-ground biomass was sampled in March–May 2000, using direct harvest from 10 0.25-m<sup>2</sup> quadrats distributed at random in both burnt and unburnt grassland of Holmes and Wellington Plains. Samples were separated in the field into standing vegetation and litter components. Biomass samples were not collected from heathland because of the likely damage to regenerating areas where there was at least 50% bare ground and small shrub seedlings.

#### **Assessment of grass tussock basal area, intertussock gaps and prefire shrub cover**

In addition to changes in bare ground and vegetation cover, we documented changes in the size and type of gap, both interdominant and within-canopy, in grassland and heathland. Such gaps are important determinants of ecological processes in these communities (Williams & Ashton 1988; Williams 1992). The area occupied by intertussock gaps and *Poa* tussock bases was estimated by line intercepts (Bonham 1989). Intercepted basal tussock length was measured by using a metal pin, 4 mm in diameter, placed vertically against the edge of the tussock. Ten randomly distributed 10-m long transects were sampled in both burnt and unburnt grassland at Holmes Plain, and in burnt grassland at Wellington Plain. As there were no prefire data of shrub cover in open heathland, this was estimated at Holmes Plain by using line intercepts to determine the diameter of burnt shrubs, based on the extent of burnt branches. This method could not be applied at Wellington Plain because the fire had incinerated most shrubs, leaving few or no stems.

# **Data analysis**

Point quadrat data were explored using box and normal probability plots (Sokal & Rohlf 1995), which showed that all data met the assumptions for ANOVA. As the vegetation was sampled at the same sets of transects over time, we used repeated measures ANOVA (von Ende 1993). Mean intertussock gap size and mean tussock basal size, in burnt and unburnt grassland, were

{3}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

analysed by one-way ANOVA, whereas the biomass data were analysed by two-way (site fire) ANOVA. All analyses were undertaken using SYSTAT 8.0 (SPSS, Chicago).

#### **RESULTS**

## **Immediate fire impact**

The Caledonia Fire affected most vegetation and all plant communities of both Holmes and Wellington Plains. The main impact was removal of vegetative cover and litter, resulting in high levels of bare ground and little vegetation cover. In burnt grassland at Holmes Plain, the average amount of CC1 was 17%, and the average amount of CC3 was 76%. This was a substantial decrease in the quality of cover at Holmes Plain compared with the prefire state (Fig. 2a). In burnt grassland at Wellington Plain, the respective figures were 11 and 85% (Fig. 2b). In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, all shrubs were incinerated, resulting in virtually no vegetation (CC1 = 3%) and an almost complete cover of bare ground (CC3 = 96%; Fig. 2b).

# **Post-fire regeneration**

#### *Changes in vegetation cover and biomass*

In burnt grassland, both at Holmes and Wellington Plains, and in burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, CC1 increased significantly, and CC3 decreased significantly over the 2.5-year study period, with most of the changes occurring in the first 18 months post-fire. There was a significant change in both CC1 and CC3 between February 1998 and May 1999, but between May 1999 and May 2000, there was little or no significant change in the average value of either cover class across sites (Fig. 2a). Similarly, there were significant changes in the cover classes in both grassland and heathland at Wellington Plain between January 1998 and May 1999, but relatively little change between May 1999 and May 2000 (Fig. 2b). By May 2000, the average CC3 in burnt grassland was 35% at Holmes Plain (Fig. 2a) and 25% at Wellington Plain (Fig. 2b). The respective figures for CC1 were 23 and 36%. In burnt heathland at Wellington Plain, average CC3 in May 2000 was 53%, and average CC1 was 16% (Fig. 2b).

The post-fire increase in vegetation cover at both Holmes and Wellington Plains was primarily due to the rapid resprouting of snow grass tussocks and forbs (Figs 3a,4). The cover of *Poa* increased rapidly postfire in both grassland and heathland. At Holmes Plain it was 84% by January 1999 (Fig. 3a); at Wellington

Plain it was approximately 65% in grassland by May 1999, and 55% in heathland (Fig. 4a,b). *Poa* cover remained at or near these levels at both sites until May 2000. This cover was almost completely due to surviving tussocks resprouting post-fire, rather than seedling establishment and growth. The rapid resprouting of the snow grasses was accompanied by pyrogenic flowering, which commenced in the year following the fire and occurred in virtually all tussocks. Forbs also re-established rapidly from perennating subterranean organs or seedlings. Forb cover was approximately 40% by January 1999 at both grassland sites, and by December 1999 at the heathland site (Figs 3a,4). Most forb cover was provided by *Asperula gunnii, Craspedia* spp. and *Leptorhynchos squamatus*. In contrast to the rapid regeneration of snow grasses and forbs, shrubs in the heathland of Wellington Plain were slow to regenerate (Fig. 4b). Shrub cover increased at approximately 7% per annum, such that by May 2000, shrub cover was 17%. Although the prefire shrub cover at this site is unknown, it is likely to have been at least 50%, as the area had been mapped as closed heathland by Walsh *et al*. (1984). Shrubs, including the dominants, whether seedlings or resprouts, had not flowered after 2.5 years.

The cover classes at the various prefire or unburnt grassland sites showed some intersite variation across the landscape and over time. In 1991 at Holmes Plain, at one site that was subsequently burnt in 1998, CC1 was 49% and CC3 was 21% (Fig. 2a). At the first site, total live vegetation cover was 80%, of which *Poa* provided three-quarters of the cover and forbs approximately one-quarter. The intertussock gaps at this site were generally occupied by forbs only, with little or no live grass foliage overlapping the gap, and only sparse litter within the gap. At the second site, unburnt by the Caledonia Fire, the respective CC1 and CC3 values in 1991 were 69 and 3%, and 73 and 5% in February

The death of these shrubs has effectively altered the structure of this community on Holmes Plain from heathland to grassland. At Wellington Plain, where most shrubs were incinerated, the dominant shrubs, although resprouters, were still in the early stages of regeneration and yet to develop a full canopy. As for *Grevillea* at Holmes Plain, the litter associated with the shrubs at Wellington Plain was completely burnt.

# **DISCUSSION**

#### **Fire regimes in alpine and subalpine environments in Australia**

The available historical, meteorological and biological evidence points strongly to landscape-scale fire being a relatively rare event in Australian alpine and subalpine vegetation. McCarthy and Tolhurst (2000) estimated that the fire-weather conditions associated with the Caledonia Fire have occurred five times in the past century. Assuming a relative lack of ignition sources in treeless high mountain vegetation compared with

**Fig. 4.** Cover of main growth forms on Wellington Plains 1998–2000. (a) burnt grassland (b) burnt heathland. *y* axis = % Cover ( SEM; *n* = 10). (), *Poa*; (), forbs; (), shrubs.

{7}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

forest vegetation, they concluded that a fire frequency of once or twice per century was 'a reasonable prediction'. In subalpine areas in the ACT and NSW, the data of Pryor (1939) and Raeder-Roitzsch and Phillips (1958) are consistent with this conclusion.

This relatively low frequency of fire in Australian alpine landscapes is a function of the generally low to moderate fire weather conditions that occur at high altitude compared with landscapes at lower altitudes (Gill & Moore 1990). Fire in alpine and subalpine vegetation occurs only in exceptional circumstances, such as when drought is coupled with extreme fire-weather conditions. The fire discussed here has therefore provided a rare opportunity for detailed monitoring, in both the immediate post-fire period and the longer term, of the ecological processes governing post-fire vegetation change in high mountain treeless vegetation.

# **Post-fire patterns of regeneration**

The most conspicuous response to fire was the rapid resprouting of most species. The vast majority of the alpine vascular flora has the capacity to resprout, from rhizomes or rootstock, and other perennating buds are generally protected by foliage and occur close to the ground (Williams & Costin 1994). This early onset of regeneration following fire is common in many ecosystems, and is often a function of increased soil nutrients in combination with a more open habitat and reduced competition (Gill 1981; Clarkson 1997; DeBano *et al*. 1998). In the Alps, such strong vegetative regeneration post-fire, however, is most likely an adaptation to the exigencies of the alpine climate rather than an adaptation to fire per se.

In the grasslands and heathlands, there was massed pyrogenic flowering of snow grasses, a phenomenon that is relatively common in the first year or two postfire in alpine and subalpine grasses (Leigh *et al*. 1987; Yeates & Lee 1997). In the burnt grasslands and heathlands, such flowering will naturally provide a significant input to the soil seed-bank.

Based on 1991 figures, the cover of snow grasses and forbs had returned to approximately prefire levels by May 1999 (17 months post-fire). These responses occurred on both Holmes and Wellington Plain. This initial burst of regeneration was accompanied by a relatively rapid initial decline in the amount bare ground and/or thin loose litter with little vegetation cover (CC3) compared with the high values immediately post-fire.

Despite this rapid resprouting, and the return of total grass and forb cover to prefire levels within 2.5 years, the amount of CC3 (25–53%) was well above, whereas the amount of dense vegetation cover (CC1, 16–36%) was well below, levels typical for grassland and heathland in an unburnt state. At the majority of unburnt sites currently being monitored in the study area, the Holmes and Wellington Plains sites, and at independent sites at Wellington Plain and Mount Reynard (A. Tolsma, University of Melbourne School of Forestry, unpubl. data), vegetation cover was in excess of 95%, and bare ground was < 3%. Such values are typical of long unburnt, ungrazed alpine and subalpine vegetation elsewhere in Australia, where bare ground is generally less than 1–2%, and vegetation cover is almost complete (Costin *et al*. 1960; Wahren *et al*. 1994; Williams & Costin 1994; Williams *et al*. 1997; Wahren & Papst 2000).

While tussocks and shrubs establish and mature, the burnt grasslands and heathlands of these subalpine plains will remain vulnerable and sensitive to physical disturbances, such as frost heave, and any trampling by livestock. Post-fire regeneration studies from numerous alpine, subalpine or tundra sites around the world (Wimbush & Costin 1979a,b,c; Leigh *et al*. 1987; Racine *et al*. 1987; Gitay *et al*. 1992; Landhausser & Wein 1993; Wahren *et al*. 1994; Maumary *et al*. 1995; Williams *et al*. 1997; Yeates & Lee 1997; Vavrek *et al*. 1999) indicate that recovery to adequate levels of vegetation to protect the soil from subsequent disturbances is likely to take a decade or more. Given such high levels of bare or sparsely covered ground and low levels of vegetation cover in burnt sites, and the general slowness of vegetation regeneration following largescale disturbances in Australian alpine environments, we conclude that the vegetation at Holmes and Wellington Plains has not recovered to prefire levels. Thus, there has been only limited post-fire regeneration, and, 2.5 years after the Caledonia Fire, the potential for soil erosion still exists in the burnt, treeless vegetation.

# *Patterns in grasslands*

The biomass (including litter) of burnt grassland 2.5 years post-fire was significantly less than that of unburnt grassland, and less than that considered necessary for adequate protection of alpine soils (10 t ha–1; Costin *et al*. 1960). The litter component of biomass in burnt areas was negligible, whereas in the unburnt grassland, litter constituted almost half the biomass. Litter performs a crucial role in alpine environments, because it blankets the soils against extremes of temperature, and is a major source of organic matter that is an important determinant of soil chemical and physical health (Baldock & Nelson 2000). Such litter, much of which occurs in intertussock gaps, was totally consumed by the fire.

In grasslands, fire not only consumed litter, but resulted in a significant decline in the basal cover of snow grass tussocks and an increase in the size of intertussock gaps. By May 2000, the vegetation of these gaps was relatively sparse, with little dense cover. Thus, by 

{8}<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

increasing the size of the gaps, and consuming the litter within the gaps, fire has increased the potential area of sparse ground cover and therefore the potential for soil erosion. As regeneration in alpine communities is generally slow, the return of the litter component and the centripetal in-filling of gaps in the grasslands will take several more years.

# *Patterns in heathlands*

Most shrubs were incinerated, as was the thick litter beneath the shrub canopy, causing almost 100% bare ground. Resprouting in the shrubs was slower than that of the herbaceous species. *Grevillea australis*, a shrub that is a known obligate seeder (Williams & Ashton 1988), was killed by 100% leaf scorch. Despite the decrease in the amount of bare ground in heathland post-fire, by May 2000 it was still high (mean 53%, pooling sites).

Whether or not a return to prefire state occurs will depend mainly on species, mode of regeneration and subsequent disturbance regime (e.g. Gill 1981; DeBano *et al*. 1998). Where *Grevillea* seedlings established, they were still < 10 cm tall 2.5 years post-fire, and development to mature shrubs will take a decade or more (Williams & Ashton 1987, 1988). Other postfire regeneration studies in heathland elsewhere in the Victorian Alps, such as at Mount Fainter and Mount Buffalo (Wahren *et al*. 1999), have shown that recovery of heathland to prefire levels of vegetation cover (including litter) and bare ground is likely to take 10–15 years. As for the grasslands, then, the heathlands will therefore remain sensitive to physical disturbance while plants re-establish and mature.

# **Conclusion**

The primary impact of fire in the subalpine landscapes on Holmes and Wellington Plain was, like any fire, the almost total removal of vegetation cover and litter and extensive exposure of bare ground. Such low levels of vegetation cover are highly unusual in virtually all unburnt Australian alpine and subalpine grassland and heathland communities. Although resprouting of herbaceous species following the fire was initially rapid in both grassland and heathland, the amount of vegetation cover in both communities 2.5 years post-fire was still insufficient to protect the soils. Soil and catchment protection is a major land use in the Australian Alps. As has been documented for other subalpine and alpine heathlands and grasslands subject to fire, the development of levels of vegetation and litter that will adequately protect the soil, and hence the catchments, will take a decade or more. The rarity of landscape-scale fire, and the slowness of regeneration post-fire, in treeless vegetation of the Australian Alps is such that the

lands affected by the Caledonia Fire warrant intensive long-term studies. Such studies are the principal means of gaining an understanding of both species and plant community responses following major but rare disturbances such as a landscape-scale fire.

Miller [\(russell.miller@dbca.wa.gov.au\)](mailto:russell.miller@dbca.wa.gov.au) 14 15 **Received:** 19 May 2024 | **Revised:** 17 December 2024 | **Accepted:** 19 December 2024 16 17 **Funding:** This work was supported by an Australian Research Council Linkage grant (LP160100996) to NJE, JBF, and BPM. 18 19 **Keywords:** fire interval | fire management | generalised additive modelling | immaturity risk | juvenile period | seedling regeneration | southwestern Australia 20 21 #### **ABSTRACT** 22 23 The time interval between fires is a critical component of the fire regime that affects plant species persistence in fire-prone ecosystems. Fire intervals that are too short or too long may not support regeneration from seed banks or resprouting. Fire intervals that support adequate regeneration may also vary with other factors such as climate, herbivory, and population structure. Using field data on flowering and canopy seed banks, we modelled post-fire reproduction for woody fire-killed (obligate seeding) and resprouting species under varying rainfall and herbivory along a 35-year fire age chronosequence in Banksia woodlands in southwestern Australia. We found that fire-killed species attained reproductive maturity rapidly after fire with predicted juvenile periods (time to 50% flowering) of 1.5–2.3years for shrubs and 4 years for trees. Resprouting species had similar juvenile periods to fire-killed species (1–3.5 years for resprouting shrubs, 4.4 years for resprouting trees). Reproduction varied with rainfall and herbivory with juvenile periods at least doubling under low rainfall or high herbivory for some species. Serotinous species produced cones (woody fruits containing seeds) shortly after flowering commenced, with some evidence of seed bank decline in the oldest sites. While reproduction was clearly correlated with time since fire, plant size was a much stronger predictor. Some species form multi-cohort populations which can introduce large variation into post-fire reproductive trajectories, and this should be considered when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence. This study provides critical information to assess fire interval-related threats for Banksia woodlands and suggests that woody species of these woodlands are generally tolerant of a wide range of fire intervals. Only the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species (*Banksia prionotes*, Proteaceae) may require fire intervals >10 years to reduce immaturity risk under the least favourable growing conditions, and this species often occurs in discrete patches in the landscape such that fire management can be tailored accordingly. 24 25 #### **1   |   Introduction** 26 27 Fire is a dominant ecological disturbance that has long shaped terrestrial ecosystems and driven plant species evolution globally (Bond, Woodward, and Midgley [2005](#page-17-0); He and Lamont [2018;](#page-19-0) Keeley et al. [2011;](#page-19-1) Lamont [2022](#page-19-2)). Over evolutionary time periods, fire regimes (fire interval, severity, season and type at a point, which form spatial patterns at landscape scales) *sensu* (Gill [1981\)](#page-18-0) have driven the development of a diversity of plant traits and life history strategies that allow populations to persist 28 29 This is an open access article under the terms of the [Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/) License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. 30 31 © 2025 The Author(s). *Austral Ecology* published by John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd on behalf of Ecological Society of Australia. 32 33 {1} 34 35 in fire-prone landscapes (Harrison et al. [2021;](#page-19-3) Schwilk and Ackerly [2001](#page-20-0)). However, with ongoing climate change, fire is projected to occur with greater frequency and intensity in many regions (Jones et al. [2022](#page-19-4)), thereby imposing altered fire regimes on biota which may threaten their persistence (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2015](#page-18-1); Le Breton et al. [2022](#page-19-5)). Fire intervals, in particular, are considered to have a strong influence on species persistence, especially in ecosystems characterised by high severity or stand-replacing fire regimes (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2015;](#page-18-1) Gallagher et al. [2021\)](#page-18-2). Land management agencies tasked with conserving fire-prone ecosystems often include minimum fire-free intervals in their planning to maximise species persistence (Bradstock and Kenny [2003;](#page-17-2) Burrows and McCaw [2013](#page-17-3)). 36 37 Plant species which inhabit fire-prone environments are generally characterised as one of two major fire response types: (1) fire-killed (or obligate seeders), which are killed by complete canopy scorch and rely on soil or canopy-stored seeds for post-fire recovery; and (2) resprouters, which primarily survive fire and regrow from buds protected from the heat of fire, but can often also recruit new individuals from seed (Clarke et al. [2015;](#page-18-3) Pausas and Keeley [2014](#page-19-6)). Plants of both types face two key threats in relation to fire interval: immaturity risk and senescence risk. Immaturity risk occurs when intervals between lethal fires are shorter than the time required to reach reproductive maturity, establish a seed bank and/or develop resprouting capacity (Keeley, Ne'eman, and Fotheringham [1999\)](#page-19-7), whereas senescence risk occurs when fire intervals exceed the lifespan of mature plants and their seed bank or stock of live buds (Enright et al. [2011](#page-18-4); Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013\)](#page-18-5). Tolerable fire intervals, defined by minimum and maximum inter-fire periods that avoid species loss through immaturity and senescence risk respectively, are widely used in planning fire management with conservation objectives (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6). Immaturity risk and shortened fire intervals arguably pose the greatest risk to species persistence, with fire-killed species particularly vulnerable to decline or local extinction if they are slow maturing and require an ample fire-free period to flower and produce seeds (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2014\)](#page-18-7). Resprouters, while generally considered to be more resilient to short fire intervals, may be vulnerable to unusually short intervals due to the depletion of resources required for resprouting and reduced recruitment probability from seed (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7), [2011;](#page-18-4) Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016\)](#page-18-8). 38 39 Defining potential immaturity or senescence risks in a population or species is often achieved using demographic or reproductive information such as the timing of post-fire reproductive maturity, long-term trajectories of reproductive output and adult lifespans (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996;](#page-18-9) Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013](#page-18-5); Kraaij et al. [2013](#page-19-8)). The juvenile period approach for quantifying post-fire reproductive maturity and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals originates from a concept by Gill and Nicholls ([1989\)](#page-18-10) and has been applied to a variety of woody plant species in Australia and South Africa (Gill and McMahon [1986](#page-18-11); Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Harvey et al. [2017;](#page-19-9) Kraaij et al. [2013;](#page-19-8) McCaw [2008;](#page-19-10) Muir, Vesk, and Hepworth [2014](#page-19-11)). The juvenile period can be defined in a number of ways, including the time to first flowering or fruiting after fire in the most 40 41 precocious individual, or the time to flowering or fruiting in a certain portion of the population, often 50% (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Kraaij et al. [2013\)](#page-19-8). While the first signs of reproduction may indicate the minimum time to maturity, several years of flowering and subsequent successful seed set may be required to accumulate a seed bank large enough for population replacement after fire, particularly for fire-killed species (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003\)](#page-17-5). A suggested rule of thumb, therefore, is that a fire interval equal to two times (or three times for particularly sensitive species) the juvenile period is the minimum period required for population persistence under average growing conditions (e.g., average post-fire rainfall) (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003;](#page-17-5) Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)). A rule of thumb applied in South African shrublands is that at least half a population must have flowered at least three times (Kraaij et al. [2013\)](#page-19-8). The juvenile period approach is specifically designed for fire-killed species where there is no persistence via resprouting, all individuals are normally killed by fire (i.e., fire is not patchy), there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment and seed banks are exhausted by fire (i.e., no residual seed bank) (Bell [2001\)](#page-17-6). While this approach is supported by a few single- or multi-species studies on post-fire maturation rates (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003](#page-17-5); Treurnicht et al. [2016\)](#page-20-1), it was only originally intended to provide guidance until more detailed assessments were available (Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)), and there has been little critical evaluation of whether the 2×rule of thumb is appropriate across a wide range of species. 42 43 Maximum tolerable fire intervals are not commonly defined, but can be identified from adult longevity (e.g., evidence of senescence) or a decline in reproductive output in the long absence of fire, where there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment to maintain populations in the absence of fire (Bond [1980](#page-17-7); Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013](#page-18-5)). Maximum tolerable intervals for resprouters probably even precede adult senescence as the stock of live buds required for resprouting declines with plant age such that plants approaching the end of their lifespan have decreasing probability of survival through fire (Enright et al. [2011\)](#page-18-4). 44 45 Variation in post-fire juvenile periods at least partly depends on the mode of plant regeneration (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Harvey et al. [2017](#page-19-9)). The juvenile period for plants regenerating from seed after fire (termed the primary juvenile period) tends to be longer than that for plants resprouting or recovering vegetatively after fire (termed the secondary juvenile period) (Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-17-2); Zammit and Westoby [1987\)](#page-20-2). Given that fire-killed species typically recover entirely from seed, only the primary juvenile period is relevant, whereas postfire populations of resprouting species may contain a mix of resprouting individuals and post-fire seedlings so that both primary and secondary juvenile periods can be defined. In practice, reported juvenile periods for resprouting species are generally a composite value of both primary and secondary juvenile periods, but since new recruits are often infrequent, such estimates are best regarded as estimates of the secondary juvenile period (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-18-12)). Estimates of the primary juvenile period for resprouter species are rare due to sample size constraints associated with low rates of recruitment, and the usually much longer times to first reproduction (Keeley, Fotheringham, and Baer-Keeley [2006;](#page-19-12) Zammit and Westoby [1987](#page-20-2)). While the juvenile period approach largely focusses on fire-killed species, as 46 47 {2} 48 49 these are considered to be most sensitive to fire interval impacts (Bowman et al. [2014](#page-17-1); Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7); Harvey et al. [2017\)](#page-19-9), successful reproduction and seedling recruitment are also required for the long-term persistence of resprouting species (Enright et al. [2014\)](#page-18-7). 50 51 Despite global applicability of the juvenile period approach for assessing immaturity risk and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals, including widespread use in some regions, including southern Australia and South Africa, there has been limited evaluation of the relationship between the onset of flowering and seed bank accumulation for different species, or of the consequences of variation in environmental conditions or population size structure for sensitivities to shortened fire intervals (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) McCaw [2008;](#page-19-10) Treurnicht et al. [2016](#page-20-1); von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [2018](#page-20-3); Wooller, Wooller, and Brown [2002\)](#page-20-4). Variation in climate, herbivory and other environmental factors which affect plant growth and population structure can alter reproductive trajectories such that a single species-level juvenile period value may over- or under-estimate the fire-free period required for different populations (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Kraaij et al. [2013;](#page-19-8) McCaw [2008](#page-19-10); Morgan, McCarthy, and Willocks [2021](#page-19-13)). Longer juvenile periods are often associated with low-productivity environments, including sites with low average rainfall, or low rainfall in the few years following fire (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) McCaw [2008\)](#page-19-10). Low environmental productivity can act to delay maturation, reduce growth, flowering and seed set, and increase the seedbank required for replacement after subsequent fires (Enright et al. [2015\)](#page-18-1). High herbivore pressure may also delay or reduce flowering and seed production by reducing the size of plants and altering the resources available for reproduction, although these effects are less well documented (Brown, Paczkowska, and Gibson [2016\)](#page-17-8). While variation in reproductive attributes across sites or years will always be a confounding factor in defining tolerable fire intervals, understanding the causal relationships behind variation in reproductive trajectories is particularly important for the management of contemporary landscapes with warming and drying climates alongside ongoing fragmentation and other human disturbances. 52 53 In this study, we used field data to model post-fire reproductive trajectories across varying environmental conditions for six woody plant species in fire-prone Banksia woodlands of southwestern Australia. Increasing understanding of fire intervalrelated population dynamics offers the opportunity to manage fire regimes for species conservation. We employed a space-fortime sampling approach to quantify reproduction (flowering rate, flower counts, and cone counts per plant) in co-occurring fire-killed and resprouting species along a post-fire chronosequence of 1–35 years since the last fire and across sites with varying rainfall and herbivory. Vegetation in this region regularly experiences fire, and native species exhibit a variety of firerelated traits and adaptation syndromes which we anticipate would be reflected in varying post-fire reproductive trajectories. Objectives for risk reduction through prescribed burning (managed fire intervals) indicate fire intervals of 13–33 years (Ritchie et al. [2021](#page-19-14)). Recent data show post-fire ages ranging from 1 to 56 years since the last fire, with some areas potentially older (Tangney et al. [2022\)](#page-20-5). During the period 1970–2009, median fire intervals (prescribed burns and wildfires combined) across the northern (drier) part of our study area was 9 years with an average of 37% of area burnt attributed to wildfires (Wilson et al. [2014](#page-20-6)). 54 55 We aim to quantify post-fire juvenile periods (defined here as time to 50% flowering), estimate minimum tolerable fire intervals based on the '2 × juvenile period' rule of thumb guideline, explore whether this rule of thumb reflects sufficient flowering and canopy seed bank accumulation and quantify reproduction in the long absence of fire. We also aim to quantify reproductive patterns under varying rainfall and herbivory conditions and how this affects minimum tolerable fire interval estimates. Populations of fire-killed and resprouting species may also be multi-cohort (Hobbs and Atkins [1990\)](#page-19-15) which can complicate reproductive dynamics; therefore, we also aim to evaluate models of reproduction relative to plant size (as a surrogate for age or cohort) to investigate the causal relationship between size and reproduction and test the strength of time since fire as a predictor of reproduction commonly used to inform fire management. 56 57 #### **2   |   Methods** 58 59 ## **2.1   |   Study Area** 60 61 This study was conducted in urban and peri-urban reserves in the Swan Coastal Plain bioregion of southwestern Australia. Low open Banksia woodlands are the dominant vegetation type in this region, with an estimated 50%–60% of their original extent having been cleared in recent decades for the rapid urbanisation of Western Australia's capital city of Perth (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14). Most remaining vegetation is restricted to a few large conservation areas on the city margins, and small urban and peri-urban reserves, but even in these areas, there is projected ongoing species loss associated with time-delayed effects of habitat loss and fragmentation (Fowler et al. [2023](#page-18-13)). In 2016, Banksia woodlands were recognised as a Threatened Ecological Community under Australia's national environmental law, and smaller portions have conservation listings at the state level (Commonwealth of Australia [2016;](#page-18-14) Ramalho et al. [2014](#page-19-16); Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14). 62 63 Banksia woodlands are characterised by a low (4–8m height), open canopy of *Banksia* (Proteaceae) trees (predominantly the resprouters *B. attenuata* and *B. menziesii*, and fire-killed *B. prionotes*) and a species-rich understorey dominated by sclerophyllous shrubs in the plant families Dilleniaceae, Ericaceae, Fabaceae, Myrtaceae and Proteaceae (Dodd and Griffin [1989;](#page-18-15) Ritchie et al. [2021](#page-19-14)). The nutrient-poor, deep sandy soils of the Swan Coastal Plain are comprised largely of two major Pleistocene dune complexes (Bassendean and Spearwood), distinguished by their age of origin (Spearwood sands: 120k—500ka old, Bassendean sands: ~2ma old) and nutrient content (particularly nitrogen and phosphorus, declining with age) (Turner, Hayes, and Laliberté [2018](#page-20-7)). The region has a Mediterranean-type climate, with cool, wet winters and hot, dry summers, making vegetation highly fire-prone during the dry season (austral summer and autumn; December–May). Average annual precipitation ranges from approximately 800mm in the south to 550mm in the north, 80% of which falls between May and October (Tangney et al. [2022\)](#page-20-5) (Figure [S1\)](#page-20-8). 64 65 {3} 66 67 Fire is a regular occurrence on the Swan Coastal Plain, including low-moderate severity prescribed burning for risk reduction and conservation purposes during autumn and spring periods, and high severity wildfires mostly from human-caused ignitions during the hot, dry summer period (Densmore and Clingan [2019;](#page-18-16) Enright and Fontaine [2014;](#page-18-17) Howard et al. [2020](#page-19-17); Plucinski [2014\)](#page-19-18). The proximity of urban and peri-urban Banksia woodlands to human homes and infrastructure has placed substantial attention and importance on fire management in this ecosystem. While there are no direct estimates of historical or long-term fire intervals in Banksia woodlands that might suggest lower or upper limits to their adaptations, they share attributes (e.g., key plant functional types, surface and elevated fuel types) with surrounding vegetation types, including shrublands to the north and eucalypt forests to the east and south, where typical fire intervals have been estimated at 10–40+ years (shrublands) and 5–20 years (low severity, forest) or 20–100 years (high severity, forest) (Burrows, Ward, and Robinson [1995](#page-17-9); Enright et al. [2012;](#page-18-18) Enright and Thomas [2008](#page-18-19); Murphy et al. [2013\)](#page-19-19). Indigenous use of fire was widespread in the region prior to European colonisation but specific information regarding burning in Banksia woodlands is not clear (Lullfitz et al. [2020;](#page-19-20) Rodrigues et al. [2022](#page-20-9)). 68 69 ## **2.2   |   Study Species** 70 71 To explore fire interval effects on reproduction, we chose six woody plant species with a range of growth forms, fire response traits and seed bank storage modes across four common plant families (Table [1](#page-3-0)). All species are native, common and widespread in Banksia woodlands and considered indicators of the vegetation type; although varying in their abundance and distribution within the landscape (Gibson et al. [1994](#page-18-20)). Serotinous (canopy seed bank) species typically accumulate woody fruits containing seeds (hereafter cones) in the canopy over multiple years, therefore allowing assessment 72 73 of cumulative reproductive output. In the study area, the two selected *Banksia* species are known to be weakly serotinous, with most seeds released from woody fruits (hereafter cones) within 1–2 years of cone maturity (Cowling and Lamont [1985](#page-18-21)). The dioecious shrub species *Allocasuarina humilis* is moderately serotinous with female plants retaining seeds in cones for up to 5 years (personal obs.). By pairing serotinous species with species with other seed storage modes, here specifically soil seed banks, we aim to gain an insight into the response of the broader plant community. 74 75 ## **2.3   |   Site Selection** 76 77 To assess varying fire intervals, we employed a space-for-time approach and selected sites with a broad range of recent fire histories (time since fire, TSF). We first interrogated fire history data for remnant vegetation in urban and peri-urban reserves across the study region to identify a set of candidate sites with a wide range of fire ages, suitable access (with permission from land managers) and appropriate vegetation type (i.e., not wetland, riparian, or limestone vegetation). Year of last fire for each site was determined from spatial data layers maintained by the Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA-060, ); historical satellite and aerial imagery (Landgate, [https://map](https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html)[viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html](https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html)); and local government records. Given limitations in fire history records and satellite and aerial imagery, we were unable to confirm exact ages for some sites beyond 35 years (occurring before approximately 1986). Sites with no assignable post-fire age are referred to here as long unburnt (LUB), and for analysis are given a notional age of 35 years. 78 79 We visited candidate sites to confirm the above criteria as well as the presence of the study species and the absence of 80 81 **TABLE 1**    |    Key life history traits and the number of sites (N sites) for the six study species. 82 83

This produced a total of 34 sites across a fire interval chronosequence from 1 to 35years (or more), with each site containing one to five study species. The number of sites surveyed for each species ranged from 11 to 17, all spanning a similar post-fire chronosequence (Table [1\)](#page-3-0). Some sites were surveyed over two successive years, creating two nonindependent TSF samples. 90 91 Sites were mostly (91%) located on Spearwood sands across a 100 km north–south extent of the Swan Coastal Plain (Figure [1](#page-4-0)). Mean annual rainfall ranged from 698 mm in the north (Muchea, 1971–2000) to 843 mm in the south (Halls Head, 1971–2000; Australian Bureau of Meteorology [2020](#page-17-10)) (Figure [S1\)](#page-20-8). All species except *B. prionotes* were sampled across the full extent of this rainfall gradient. *Banksia prionotes* was only found across a very narrow (negligible) range (30 mm mean annual rainfall difference) in the sampled study area, but occur more broadly in the region, as do the other study species. The presence (*n* = 19) or absence (*n* = 15) of kangaroos (western grey kangaroo, *Macropus fuliginosus*) as major herbivores was assessed at each site based on sightings of individuals or their scats as well as local knowledge and records (City of Joondalup [2015](#page-17-11); City of Nedlands [2014;](#page-17-12) Ecoscape (Australia Pty Ltd) [2008;](#page-18-22) Government of Western Australia [2000;](#page-19-21) Natural Area Consulting [2012](#page-19-22)). Where present in urban reserves, kangaroos (or signs of their presence) are easily observed, and populations often achieve high density. There was no discernible change in kangaroo abundance over the study period. 92 93 #### **2.4   |   Field Surveys** 94 95 At each site, data were collected on reproductive and size attributes for live individuals. Seedlings less than 1–2 years old in sites older than 4years since fire (inter-fire seedlings) were excluded as these individuals can have a low survival rate and therefore have little consequence for the reproductive status of populations. Data on the abundance of inter-fire seedlings from the same sites are presented in Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [\(2024](#page-19-23)). Seedlings were distinguished by the presence of cotyledons, lack of signs of current or past reproduction, and were generally <10–20 cm tall for shrub species or <30 cm tall for tree species. Estimates of seedling age were confirmed by observations of seedlings of known age in post-fire sites. 96 97 Data were mostly collected within plots positioned to include as many of the target species as possible and ranging in size from 25 to 150 m2 as necessary to suit different species and plant densities, and to ensure sampling of at least 30 individuals. Plant densities were calculated from the number of individuals in each plot and scaled to the number of plants per hectare. Smaller plots were used for shrub species (density range 0.1–4.6 plants m−2), and larger plots for tree species (0.03–1.58 plants m−2). At least two plots were established at each site, but where plant density was particularly low, measurements were taken based on a nearest-neighbour search until a minimum of 30 plants were recorded. For some plotbased surveys, additional nearest plants outside of plots were measured to fulfil sample size criterion. Field surveys were undertaken from 2016 to 2018 during peak flowering times for each species (Table [1\)](#page-3-0). 98 99 Measurements recorded for each individual included: (1) number of flowers (or inflorescences; all species), (2) number of mature cones with unopened follicles (canopy seed bank species only) and (3) size (all species). *Allocasuarina humilis* is a dioecious species and we identified and recorded attributes of male and female plants separately (only female plants produce cones). The number of cones recorded represents the cumulative canopy seed bank from all previous reproductive seasons excluding seed loss from seed predation, disease and spontaneous follicle opening, among other factors. Size was recorded as aboveground plant height (*Gompholobium tomentosum* and *Acacia pulchella*), canopy volume (*Hibbertia hypericoides* and *Allocasuarina humilis*) or stem diameter at breast height (DBH, 1.37m above the ground; *Banksia attenuata, B. prionotes*). Population-level attributes were calculated from all individuals surveyed, including resprouting and young (nonreproductive) plants, where present. We employed a model selection approach whereby we constructed a set of plausible models from subsets of the a priori predictors and compared these using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc) and AICc model weights (ωAICc) which represent the probability or weight of evidence for each model (Burnham, Anderson, and Huyvaert [2011](#page-17-13); Hurvich and Tsai [1989\)](#page-19-25). Models with ΔAICc <5 generally represented a cumulative ωAICc of ≥0.95 and therefore are presented here as part of the 95% confidence set, following Symonds and Moussalli ([2011\)](#page-20-11). Models with ΔAICc<2 are considered to have substantial support (Burnham and Anderson [2002\)](#page-17-14). We conducted this analysis in *R* (version 4.0.3) (R Core Team [2020\)](#page-19-26) using the *FSSgam* package (Fisher et al. [2018\)](#page-18-23) which enables an all subsets approach and uses the *gam()* function from the *mgcv* package (Wood [2017\)](#page-20-12). 112 113 Flowering rate, presented as proportions, was modelled using a binomial error distribution (logit link function) with data weighted by the number of individuals recorded per site. Mean number of flowers and cones per plant were modelled using a tweedie error distribution (log link function) to account for many zero values (i.e., non-flowering/non-fruiting individuals). TSF was logtransformed for analysis as responses are expected to change most rapidly in the first few years after fire, and to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range. TSF was included as a continuous smoother in the model set to allow for non-linear relationships with time. In all models, the smoothing parameter was limited to a simple spline (k=3) to avoid overfitting. Mean annual rainfall was included as a linear predictor in all models, and any effects were presented as predictions at the 10th and 90th percentile of mean annual rainfall across the TSF chronosequence, representing post-fire reproductive trajectories for 'low' (~720mm) and 'high' (~790mm) rainfall sites, respectively. 114 115 Herbivory was included as a two-level factor variable (absence or presence of kangaroo herbivores) in model sets for shrub species only (i.e., excluding *B. attenuata* and *B. prionotes*) as we lacked a strong a priori expectation of the effects of herbivory from kangaroos (generally <2m tall) on tree species that are typically >4m 116 117 tall at maturity. A two-way interaction between log-transformed TSF and herbivory was included in the model set for *G. tomentosum* only to explore if effects of herbivory varied by TSF. Replication of different herbivory levels across the range of log-transformed TSF was not considered to be adequate for the other shrub species and therefore was only included as an additive effect in other model sets. An identifier for the year of survey was included as a random smoother in all models for species where measurements were recorded in two successive years to account for repeat measures and any annual variation in environmental conditions (e.g., rainfall) other than an increase in TSF by 1year. 118 119 Modelling of flowering rate and flower counts was conducted separately for male and female plants of the dioecious species *A. humilis*. Top-ranking model comparisons are presented for models on female data only. Only female plants produce cones and seeds and so modelling of cone counts was necessarily restricted to female plant data. Juvenile period was calculated from the flowering rate of female plants. The sex ratio was, on average, 45% females and 55% males across all populations (excluding non-reproductive individuals), or 49% females and 51% males after the post-fire maturation period (i.e., after 4years) (Figure [S2\)](#page-20-8). 120 121 #### **2.5.2**|**Time Since Fire as a Predictor of Reproduction** 122 123 To assess the strength of TSF as a predictor of reproduction, we compared GAMMs with single predictors of either TSF or plant size (height, canopy volume or effective DBH) for each of the three reproductive attributes measured. Models using plant size as the predictor represent the mechanistic relationship between TSF and reproduction, where the growth of plants following fire enables greater access to resources and an increase in reproductive output. For single-cohort populations (i.e., fire-killed species), we would expect that models using single predictors of TSF and plant size would explain similar amounts of variation (i.e., *R*2 ) and have a similar weight of evidence (i.e., AICc and ωAICc). However, for multi-cohort populations (usually resprouters, but also possible for some fire-killed species), we would expect that models using size would explain much more variation and have a much greater weight of evidence than models using TSF. 124 125 GAMMs were constructed as outlined above, where models of TSF or size alone were compared using *FSSgam*. Size measurements (height, canopy volume, effective DBH) were log-transformed to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range and improve model fit. For the dioecious species (*A. humilis*), modelling was conducted separately for male and female plants, with top-ranking model comparisons presented for female data only. 126 127 #### **3   |   Results** 128 129 ## **3.1   |   Flowering Rates and Juvenile Periods** 130 131 TSF consistently appeared in top-ranked models of flowering rates for all species (Table [2](#page-6-0)). Flowering rate generally increased rapidly in the first few years after fire and stabilised thereafter (Figure [2](#page-6-1)). *Acacia pulchella* was the only species with an apparent decline in flowering rate in longer unburnt sites; in sites older than 30years, predicted flowering rate fell below 50%, however, 132 133 *V* = 4 3 × *𝜋* × *H* 2 × *W*1 2 × *W*2 2 134 135 {6} 136 137 confidence interval bands are wide at sites older than 20years and so this result is interpreted with caution (Figure [2A\)](#page-6-1). Predicted times to 50% flowering ranged from 1 to 4.4years, corresponding to minimum tolerable fire intervals (2×juvenile period rule of thumb) of 2 to 8.8years (Table [3\)](#page-7-0). Mean predicted juvenile period for fire-killed species (2.6±0.7years [SE]) was similar to that for resprouting species (3.0±1.0years; Table [3\)](#page-7-0). For all species other than the two resprouting shrubs, there was considerable site-tosite variation in flowering rate at any given TSF, as reflected in 95% confidence intervals (Figure [2A,C,D](#page-6-1)). For these species, 12% of sites older than predicted juvenile periods had <50% of plants flowering. 138 139 **TABLE 2**    |    Top-ranking generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) for predicting flowering rates for the six study species. 140 141

Models suggested that mean flower count increased steadily with increasing TSF for most species except *A. pulchella* (Figure [4\)](#page-9-0). *Acacia pulchella* instead showed a rapid increase in flowering until around 5–8years post-fire, followed by a slight decline thereafter (Figure [4A](#page-9-0)). Similarly, female plants of *A. humilis* showed an increase in flowering until around 10–15years post-fire, followed by a slight decline thereafter (Figure [4B\)](#page-9-0). Male plants of *A. humilis* showed a steady increase in flowering with increasing TSF. The peak mean flower count occurred beyond the predicted minimum tolerable fire interval for all species (Figure [4\)](#page-9-0). At this predicted minimum tolerable fire interval, populations of all species had reached 22%–84% of their peak flower count (Table [3\)](#page-7-0). 188 189 Mean annual rainfall appeared in the top-ranked models of mean flower count for the two fire-killed shrub species (*G. tomentosum* and *A. pulchella*) (Table [5\)](#page-8-2). Models predicted that mean flower count was 61% lower in low rainfall sites (10th 190 191 percentile) compared to high rainfall sites (90th percentile) for these two species across all ages (Figure [5](#page-10-0)). Populations of *B. attenuata* had produced cones even in the youngest sites sampled (1–2 years post-fire), and mean cone count increased steadily with increasing TSF (Figure [6](#page-10-1)).
