{0} ## **RESEARCH ARTICLE [OPEN ACCESS](https://doi.org/10.1111/aec.70023)** # **Using Patterns of Post-Fire Plant Reproduction to Inform Minimum Fire Intervals for Conservation Management in a Fire-Prone Woodland** Russell G. Mille[r1,2](#page-0-0) | Neal J. Enrigh[t1](#page-0-0) | David J. Merritt[2,3](#page-0-1) | Ben P. Miller[2,3](#page-0-1) | Joseph B. Fontain[e1](#page-0-0) 1School of Environmental and Conservation Sciences, Murdoch University, Murdoch, Western Australia, Australia | 2Biodiversity and Conservation Science, Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions, Kings Park, Western Australia, Australia | 3School of Biological Sciences, University of Western Australia, Crawley, Western Australia, Australia **Correspondence:** Russell G. Miller [\(russell.miller@dbca.wa.gov.au\)](mailto:russell.miller@dbca.wa.gov.au) **Received:** 19 May 2024 | **Revised:** 17 December 2024 | **Accepted:** 19 December 2024 **Funding:** This work was supported by an Australian Research Council Linkage grant (LP160100996) to NJE, JBF, and BPM. **Keywords:** fire interval | fire management | generalised additive modelling | immaturity risk | juvenile period | seedling regeneration | southwestern Australia #### **ABSTRACT** The time interval between fires is a critical component of the fire regime that affects plant species persistence in fire-prone ecosystems. Fire intervals that are too short or too long may not support regeneration from seed banks or resprouting. Fire intervals that support adequate regeneration may also vary with other factors such as climate, herbivory, and population structure. Using field data on flowering and canopy seed banks, we modelled post-fire reproduction for woody fire-killed (obligate seeding) and resprouting species under varying rainfall and herbivory along a 35-year fire age chronosequence in Banksia woodlands in southwestern Australia. We found that fire-killed species attained reproductive maturity rapidly after fire with predicted juvenile periods (time to 50% flowering) of 1.5–2.3years for shrubs and 4 years for trees. Resprouting species had similar juvenile periods to fire-killed species (1–3.5 years for resprouting shrubs, 4.4 years for resprouting trees). Reproduction varied with rainfall and herbivory with juvenile periods at least doubling under low rainfall or high herbivory for some species. Serotinous species produced cones (woody fruits containing seeds) shortly after flowering commenced, with some evidence of seed bank decline in the oldest sites. While reproduction was clearly correlated with time since fire, plant size was a much stronger predictor. Some species form multi-cohort populations which can introduce large variation into post-fire reproductive trajectories, and this should be considered when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence. This study provides critical information to assess fire interval-related threats for Banksia woodlands and suggests that woody species of these woodlands are generally tolerant of a wide range of fire intervals. Only the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species (*Banksia prionotes*, Proteaceae) may require fire intervals >10 years to reduce immaturity risk under the least favourable growing conditions, and this species often occurs in discrete patches in the landscape such that fire management can be tailored accordingly. #### **1   |   Introduction** Fire is a dominant ecological disturbance that has long shaped terrestrial ecosystems and driven plant species evolution globally (Bond, Woodward, and Midgley [2005](#page-17-0); He and Lamont [2018;](#page-19-0) Keeley et al. [2011;](#page-19-1) Lamont [2022](#page-19-2)). Over evolutionary time periods, fire regimes (fire interval, severity, season and type at a point, which form spatial patterns at landscape scales) *sensu* (Gill [1981\)](#page-18-0) have driven the development of a diversity of plant traits and life history strategies that allow populations to persist This is an open access article under the terms of the [Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/) License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited and is not used for commercial purposes. © 2025 The Author(s). *Austral Ecology* published by John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd on behalf of Ecological Society of Australia. {1} in fire-prone landscapes (Harrison et al. [2021;](#page-19-3) Schwilk and Ackerly [2001](#page-20-0)). However, with ongoing climate change, fire is projected to occur with greater frequency and intensity in many regions (Jones et al. [2022](#page-19-4)), thereby imposing altered fire regimes on biota which may threaten their persistence (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2015](#page-18-1); Le Breton et al. [2022](#page-19-5)). Fire intervals, in particular, are considered to have a strong influence on species persistence, especially in ecosystems characterised by high severity or stand-replacing fire regimes (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2015;](#page-18-1) Gallagher et al. [2021\)](#page-18-2). Land management agencies tasked with conserving fire-prone ecosystems often include minimum fire-free intervals in their planning to maximise species persistence (Bradstock and Kenny [2003;](#page-17-2) Burrows and McCaw [2013](#page-17-3)). Plant species which inhabit fire-prone environments are generally characterised as one of two major fire response types: (1) fire-killed (or obligate seeders), which are killed by complete canopy scorch and rely on soil or canopy-stored seeds for post-fire recovery; and (2) resprouters, which primarily survive fire and regrow from buds protected from the heat of fire, but can often also recruit new individuals from seed (Clarke et al. [2015;](#page-18-3) Pausas and Keeley [2014](#page-19-6)). Plants of both types face two key threats in relation to fire interval: immaturity risk and senescence risk. Immaturity risk occurs when intervals between lethal fires are shorter than the time required to reach reproductive maturity, establish a seed bank and/or develop resprouting capacity (Keeley, Ne'eman, and Fotheringham [1999\)](#page-19-7), whereas senescence risk occurs when fire intervals exceed the lifespan of mature plants and their seed bank or stock of live buds (Enright et al. [2011](#page-18-4); Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013\)](#page-18-5). Tolerable fire intervals, defined by minimum and maximum inter-fire periods that avoid species loss through immaturity and senescence risk respectively, are widely used in planning fire management with conservation objectives (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6). Immaturity risk and shortened fire intervals arguably pose the greatest risk to species persistence, with fire-killed species particularly vulnerable to decline or local extinction if they are slow maturing and require an ample fire-free period to flower and produce seeds (Bowman et al. [2014;](#page-17-1) Enright et al. [2014\)](#page-18-7). Resprouters, while generally considered to be more resilient to short fire intervals, may be vulnerable to unusually short intervals due to the depletion of resources required for resprouting and reduced recruitment probability from seed (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7), [2011;](#page-18-4) Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016\)](#page-18-8). Defining potential immaturity or senescence risks in a population or species is often achieved using demographic or reproductive information such as the timing of post-fire reproductive maturity, long-term trajectories of reproductive output and adult lifespans (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996;](#page-18-9) Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013](#page-18-5); Kraaij et al. [2013](#page-19-8)). The juvenile period approach for quantifying post-fire reproductive maturity and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals originates from a concept by Gill and Nicholls ([1989\)](#page-18-10) and has been applied to a variety of woody plant species in Australia and South Africa (Gill and McMahon [1986](#page-18-11); Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Harvey et al. [2017;](#page-19-9) Kraaij et al. [2013;](#page-19-8) McCaw [2008;](#page-19-10) Muir, Vesk, and Hepworth [2014](#page-19-11)). The juvenile period can be defined in a number of ways, including the time to first flowering or fruiting after fire in the most precocious individual, or the time to flowering or fruiting in a certain portion of the population, often 50% (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Kraaij et al. [2013\)](#page-19-8). While the first signs of reproduction may indicate the minimum time to maturity, several years of flowering and subsequent successful seed set may be required to accumulate a seed bank large enough for population replacement after fire, particularly for fire-killed species (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003\)](#page-17-5). A suggested rule of thumb, therefore, is that a fire interval equal to two times (or three times for particularly sensitive species) the juvenile period is the minimum period required for population persistence under average growing conditions (e.g., average post-fire rainfall) (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003;](#page-17-5) Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)). A rule of thumb applied in South African shrublands is that at least half a population must have flowered at least three times (Kraaij et al. [2013\)](#page-19-8). The juvenile period approach is specifically designed for fire-killed species where there is no persistence via resprouting, all individuals are normally killed by fire (i.e., fire is not patchy), there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment and seed banks are exhausted by fire (i.e., no residual seed bank) (Bell [2001\)](#page-17-6). While this approach is supported by a few single- or multi-species studies on post-fire maturation rates (Burrows and Wardell-Johnson [2003](#page-17-5); Treurnicht et al. [2016\)](#page-20-1), it was only originally intended to provide guidance until more detailed assessments were available (Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)), and there has been little critical evaluation of whether the 2×rule of thumb is appropriate across a wide range of species. Maximum tolerable fire intervals are not commonly defined, but can be identified from adult longevity (e.g., evidence of senescence) or a decline in reproductive output in the long absence of fire, where there is little or no inter-fire seedling recruitment to maintain populations in the absence of fire (Bond [1980](#page-17-7); Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013](#page-18-5)). Maximum tolerable intervals for resprouters probably even precede adult senescence as the stock of live buds required for resprouting declines with plant age such that plants approaching the end of their lifespan have decreasing probability of survival through fire (Enright et al. [2011\)](#page-18-4). Variation in post-fire juvenile periods at least partly depends on the mode of plant regeneration (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Harvey et al. [2017](#page-19-9)). The juvenile period for plants regenerating from seed after fire (termed the primary juvenile period) tends to be longer than that for plants resprouting or recovering vegetatively after fire (termed the secondary juvenile period) (Bradstock and Kenny [2003](#page-17-2); Zammit and Westoby [1987\)](#page-20-2). Given that fire-killed species typically recover entirely from seed, only the primary juvenile period is relevant, whereas postfire populations of resprouting species may contain a mix of resprouting individuals and post-fire seedlings so that both primary and secondary juvenile periods can be defined. In practice, reported juvenile periods for resprouting species are generally a composite value of both primary and secondary juvenile periods, but since new recruits are often infrequent, such estimates are best regarded as estimates of the secondary juvenile period (Enright and Goldblum [1999](#page-18-12)). Estimates of the primary juvenile period for resprouter species are rare due to sample size constraints associated with low rates of recruitment, and the usually much longer times to first reproduction (Keeley, Fotheringham, and Baer-Keeley [2006;](#page-19-12) Zammit and Westoby [1987](#page-20-2)). While the juvenile period approach largely focusses on fire-killed species, as {2} these are considered to be most sensitive to fire interval impacts (Bowman et al. [2014](#page-17-1); Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7); Harvey et al. [2017\)](#page-19-9), successful reproduction and seedling recruitment are also required for the long-term persistence of resprouting species (Enright et al. [2014\)](#page-18-7). Despite global applicability of the juvenile period approach for assessing immaturity risk and estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals, including widespread use in some regions, including southern Australia and South Africa, there has been limited evaluation of the relationship between the onset of flowering and seed bank accumulation for different species, or of the consequences of variation in environmental conditions or population size structure for sensitivities to shortened fire intervals (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) McCaw [2008;](#page-19-10) Treurnicht et al. [2016](#page-20-1); von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [2018](#page-20-3); Wooller, Wooller, and Brown [2002\)](#page-20-4). Variation in climate, herbivory and other environmental factors which affect plant growth and population structure can alter reproductive trajectories such that a single species-level juvenile period value may over- or under-estimate the fire-free period required for different populations (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Kraaij et al. [2013;](#page-19-8) McCaw [2008](#page-19-10); Morgan, McCarthy, and Willocks [2021](#page-19-13)). Longer juvenile periods are often associated with low-productivity environments, including sites with low average rainfall, or low rainfall in the few years following fire (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) McCaw [2008\)](#page-19-10). Low environmental productivity can act to delay maturation, reduce growth, flowering and seed set, and increase the seedbank required for replacement after subsequent fires (Enright et al. [2015\)](#page-18-1). High herbivore pressure may also delay or reduce flowering and seed production by reducing the size of plants and altering the resources available for reproduction, although these effects are less well documented (Brown, Paczkowska, and Gibson [2016\)](#page-17-8). While variation in reproductive attributes across sites or years will always be a confounding factor in defining tolerable fire intervals, understanding the causal relationships behind variation in reproductive trajectories is particularly important for the management of contemporary landscapes with warming and drying climates alongside ongoing fragmentation and other human disturbances. In this study, we used field data to model post-fire reproductive trajectories across varying environmental conditions for six woody plant species in fire-prone Banksia woodlands of southwestern Australia. Increasing understanding of fire intervalrelated population dynamics offers the opportunity to manage fire regimes for species conservation. We employed a space-fortime sampling approach to quantify reproduction (flowering rate, flower counts, and cone counts per plant) in co-occurring fire-killed and resprouting species along a post-fire chronosequence of 1–35 years since the last fire and across sites with varying rainfall and herbivory. Vegetation in this region regularly experiences fire, and native species exhibit a variety of firerelated traits and adaptation syndromes which we anticipate would be reflected in varying post-fire reproductive trajectories. Objectives for risk reduction through prescribed burning (managed fire intervals) indicate fire intervals of 13–33 years (Ritchie et al. [2021](#page-19-14)). Recent data show post-fire ages ranging from 1 to 56 years since the last fire, with some areas potentially older (Tangney et al. [2022\)](#page-20-5). During the period 1970–2009, median fire intervals (prescribed burns and wildfires combined) across the northern (drier) part of our study area was 9 years with an average of 37% of area burnt attributed to wildfires (Wilson et al. [2014](#page-20-6)). We aim to quantify post-fire juvenile periods (defined here as time to 50% flowering), estimate minimum tolerable fire intervals based on the '2 × juvenile period' rule of thumb guideline, explore whether this rule of thumb reflects sufficient flowering and canopy seed bank accumulation and quantify reproduction in the long absence of fire. We also aim to quantify reproductive patterns under varying rainfall and herbivory conditions and how this affects minimum tolerable fire interval estimates. Populations of fire-killed and resprouting species may also be multi-cohort (Hobbs and Atkins [1990\)](#page-19-15) which can complicate reproductive dynamics; therefore, we also aim to evaluate models of reproduction relative to plant size (as a surrogate for age or cohort) to investigate the causal relationship between size and reproduction and test the strength of time since fire as a predictor of reproduction commonly used to inform fire management. #### **2   |   Methods** ## **2.1   |   Study Area** This study was conducted in urban and peri-urban reserves in the Swan Coastal Plain bioregion of southwestern Australia. Low open Banksia woodlands are the dominant vegetation type in this region, with an estimated 50%–60% of their original extent having been cleared in recent decades for the rapid urbanisation of Western Australia's capital city of Perth (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14). Most remaining vegetation is restricted to a few large conservation areas on the city margins, and small urban and peri-urban reserves, but even in these areas, there is projected ongoing species loss associated with time-delayed effects of habitat loss and fragmentation (Fowler et al. [2023](#page-18-13)). In 2016, Banksia woodlands were recognised as a Threatened Ecological Community under Australia's national environmental law, and smaller portions have conservation listings at the state level (Commonwealth of Australia [2016;](#page-18-14) Ramalho et al. [2014](#page-19-16); Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14). Banksia woodlands are characterised by a low (4–8m height), open canopy of *Banksia* (Proteaceae) trees (predominantly the resprouters *B. attenuata* and *B. menziesii*, and fire-killed *B. prionotes*) and a species-rich understorey dominated by sclerophyllous shrubs in the plant families Dilleniaceae, Ericaceae, Fabaceae, Myrtaceae and Proteaceae (Dodd and Griffin [1989;](#page-18-15) Ritchie et al. [2021](#page-19-14)). The nutrient-poor, deep sandy soils of the Swan Coastal Plain are comprised largely of two major Pleistocene dune complexes (Bassendean and Spearwood), distinguished by their age of origin (Spearwood sands: 120k—500ka old, Bassendean sands: ~2ma old) and nutrient content (particularly nitrogen and phosphorus, declining with age) (Turner, Hayes, and Laliberté [2018](#page-20-7)). The region has a Mediterranean-type climate, with cool, wet winters and hot, dry summers, making vegetation highly fire-prone during the dry season (austral summer and autumn; December–May). Average annual precipitation ranges from approximately 800mm in the south to 550mm in the north, 80% of which falls between May and October (Tangney et al. [2022\)](#page-20-5) (Figure [S1\)](#page-20-8). {3} Fire is a regular occurrence on the Swan Coastal Plain, including low-moderate severity prescribed burning for risk reduction and conservation purposes during autumn and spring periods, and high severity wildfires mostly from human-caused ignitions during the hot, dry summer period (Densmore and Clingan [2019;](#page-18-16) Enright and Fontaine [2014;](#page-18-17) Howard et al. [2020](#page-19-17); Plucinski [2014\)](#page-19-18). The proximity of urban and peri-urban Banksia woodlands to human homes and infrastructure has placed substantial attention and importance on fire management in this ecosystem. While there are no direct estimates of historical or long-term fire intervals in Banksia woodlands that might suggest lower or upper limits to their adaptations, they share attributes (e.g., key plant functional types, surface and elevated fuel types) with surrounding vegetation types, including shrublands to the north and eucalypt forests to the east and south, where typical fire intervals have been estimated at 10–40+ years (shrublands) and 5–20 years (low severity, forest) or 20–100 years (high severity, forest) (Burrows, Ward, and Robinson [1995](#page-17-9); Enright et al. [2012;](#page-18-18) Enright and Thomas [2008](#page-18-19); Murphy et al. [2013\)](#page-19-19). Indigenous use of fire was widespread in the region prior to European colonisation but specific information regarding burning in Banksia woodlands is not clear (Lullfitz et al. [2020;](#page-19-20) Rodrigues et al. [2022](#page-20-9)). ## **2.2   |   Study Species** To explore fire interval effects on reproduction, we chose six woody plant species with a range of growth forms, fire response traits and seed bank storage modes across four common plant families (Table [1](#page-3-0)). All species are native, common and widespread in Banksia woodlands and considered indicators of the vegetation type; although varying in their abundance and distribution within the landscape (Gibson et al. [1994](#page-18-20)). Serotinous (canopy seed bank) species typically accumulate woody fruits containing seeds (hereafter cones) in the canopy over multiple years, therefore allowing assessment of cumulative reproductive output. In the study area, the two selected *Banksia* species are known to be weakly serotinous, with most seeds released from woody fruits (hereafter cones) within 1–2 years of cone maturity (Cowling and Lamont [1985](#page-18-21)). The dioecious shrub species *Allocasuarina humilis* is moderately serotinous with female plants retaining seeds in cones for up to 5 years (personal obs.). By pairing serotinous species with species with other seed storage modes, here specifically soil seed banks, we aim to gain an insight into the response of the broader plant community. ## **2.3   |   Site Selection** To assess varying fire intervals, we employed a space-for-time approach and selected sites with a broad range of recent fire histories (time since fire, TSF). We first interrogated fire history data for remnant vegetation in urban and peri-urban reserves across the study region to identify a set of candidate sites with a wide range of fire ages, suitable access (with permission from land managers) and appropriate vegetation type (i.e., not wetland, riparian, or limestone vegetation). Year of last fire for each site was determined from spatial data layers maintained by the Western Australian Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA-060, ); historical satellite and aerial imagery (Landgate, [https://map](https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html)[viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html](https://map-viewer-plus.app.landgate.wa.gov.au/index.html)); and local government records. Given limitations in fire history records and satellite and aerial imagery, we were unable to confirm exact ages for some sites beyond 35 years (occurring before approximately 1986). Sites with no assignable post-fire age are referred to here as long unburnt (LUB), and for analysis are given a notional age of 35 years. This produced a total of 34 sites across a fire interval chronosequence from 1 to 35years (or more), with each site containing one to five study species. The number of sites surveyed for each species ranged from 11 to 17, all spanning a similar post-fire chronosequence (Table [1\)](#page-3-0). Some sites were surveyed over two successive years, creating two nonindependent TSF samples. Sites were mostly (91%) located on Spearwood sands across a 100 km north–south extent of the Swan Coastal Plain (Figure [1](#page-4-0)). Mean annual rainfall ranged from 698 mm in the north (Muchea, 1971–2000) to 843 mm in the south (Halls Head, 1971–2000; Australian Bureau of Meteorology [2020](#page-17-10)) (Figure [S1\)](#page-20-8). All species except *B. prionotes* were sampled across the full extent of this rainfall gradient. *Banksia prionotes* was only found across a very narrow (negligible) range (30 mm mean annual rainfall difference) in the sampled study area, but occur more broadly in the region, as do the other study species. The presence (*n* = 19) or absence (*n* = 15) of kangaroos (western grey kangaroo, *Macropus fuliginosus*) as major herbivores was assessed at each site based on sightings of individuals or their scats as well as local knowledge and records (City of Joondalup [2015](#page-17-11); City of Nedlands [2014;](#page-17-12) Ecoscape (Australia Pty Ltd) [2008;](#page-18-22) Government of Western Australia [2000;](#page-19-21) Natural Area Consulting [2012](#page-19-22)). Where present in urban reserves, kangaroos (or signs of their presence) are easily observed, and populations often achieve high density. There was no discernible change in kangaroo abundance over the study period. #### **2.4   |   Field Surveys** At each site, data were collected on reproductive and size attributes for live individuals. Seedlings less than 1–2 years old in sites older than 4years since fire (inter-fire seedlings) were excluded as these individuals can have a low survival rate and therefore have little consequence for the reproductive status of populations. Data on the abundance of inter-fire seedlings from the same sites are presented in Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [\(2024](#page-19-23)). Seedlings were distinguished by the presence of cotyledons, lack of signs of current or past reproduction, and were generally <10–20 cm tall for shrub species or <30 cm tall for tree species. Estimates of seedling age were confirmed by observations of seedlings of known age in post-fire sites. Data were mostly collected within plots positioned to include as many of the target species as possible and ranging in size from 25 to 150 m2 as necessary to suit different species and plant densities, and to ensure sampling of at least 30 individuals. Plant densities were calculated from the number of individuals in each plot and scaled to the number of plants per hectare. Smaller plots were used for shrub species (density range 0.1–4.6 plants m−2), and larger plots for tree species (0.03–1.58 plants m−2). At least two plots were established at each site, but where plant density was particularly low, measurements were taken based on a nearest-neighbour search until a minimum of 30 plants were recorded. For some plotbased surveys, additional nearest plants outside of plots were measured to fulfil sample size criterion. Field surveys were undertaken from 2016 to 2018 during peak flowering times for each species (Table [1\)](#page-3-0). Measurements recorded for each individual included: (1) number of flowers (or inflorescences; all species), (2) number of mature cones with unopened follicles (canopy seed bank species only) and (3) size (all species). *Allocasuarina humilis* is a dioecious species and we identified and recorded attributes of male and female plants separately (only female plants produce cones). The number of cones recorded represents the cumulative canopy seed bank from all previous reproductive seasons excluding seed loss from seed predation, disease and spontaneous follicle opening, among other factors. Size was recorded as aboveground plant height (*Gompholobium tomentosum* and *Acacia pulchella*), canopy volume (*Hibbertia hypericoides* and *Allocasuarina humilis*) or stem diameter at breast height (DBH, 1.37m above the ground; *Banksia attenuata, B. prionotes*). These measurements were chosen to best represent how size relates to reproductive performance given each species' growth form. **FIGURE 1**    |    Locations of the 34 study sites in urban and peri-urban nature reserves on the Swan Coastal Plain around Perth, Western Australia. Canopy volume (*V*, m3 ) for *H. hypericoides* and *A. humilis* was calculated from maximum canopy height (*H*, m) and perpendicular canopy width measurements (*W1* and *W2*, m), using an ellipsoid form: #### **2.5   |   Data Analysis** ## **2.5.1   |   Post-Fire Reproductive Trajectories** To analyse post-fire reproductive trajectories, we evaluated generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) of TSF, herbivory and mean annual rainfall as a priori predictors of each of three population-level reproductive attributes: flowering rate (% individuals flowering), mean number of flowers per plant and mean number of closed cones per plant (for the three serotinous species only). Population-level attributes were calculated from all individuals surveyed, including resprouting and young (nonreproductive) plants, where present. We employed a model selection approach whereby we constructed a set of plausible models from subsets of the a priori predictors and compared these using Akaike's Information Criterion corrected for small sample size (AICc) and AICc model weights (ωAICc) which represent the probability or weight of evidence for each model (Burnham, Anderson, and Huyvaert [2011](#page-17-13); Hurvich and Tsai [1989\)](#page-19-25). Models with ΔAICc <5 generally represented a cumulative ωAICc of ≥0.95 and therefore are presented here as part of the 95% confidence set, following Symonds and Moussalli ([2011\)](#page-20-11). Models with ΔAICc<2 are considered to have substantial support (Burnham and Anderson [2002\)](#page-17-14). We conducted this analysis in *R* (version 4.0.3) (R Core Team [2020\)](#page-19-26) using the *FSSgam* package (Fisher et al. [2018\)](#page-18-23) which enables an all subsets approach and uses the *gam()* function from the *mgcv* package (Wood [2017\)](#page-20-12). Flowering rate, presented as proportions, was modelled using a binomial error distribution (logit link function) with data weighted by the number of individuals recorded per site. Mean number of flowers and cones per plant were modelled using a tweedie error distribution (log link function) to account for many zero values (i.e., non-flowering/non-fruiting individuals). TSF was logtransformed for analysis as responses are expected to change most rapidly in the first few years after fire, and to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range. TSF was included as a continuous smoother in the model set to allow for non-linear relationships with time. In all models, the smoothing parameter was limited to a simple spline (k=3) to avoid overfitting. Mean annual rainfall was included as a linear predictor in all models, and any effects were presented as predictions at the 10th and 90th percentile of mean annual rainfall across the TSF chronosequence, representing post-fire reproductive trajectories for 'low' (~720mm) and 'high' (~790mm) rainfall sites, respectively. Herbivory was included as a two-level factor variable (absence or presence of kangaroo herbivores) in model sets for shrub species only (i.e., excluding *B. attenuata* and *B. prionotes*) as we lacked a strong a priori expectation of the effects of herbivory from kangaroos (generally <2m tall) on tree species that are typically >4m tall at maturity. A two-way interaction between log-transformed TSF and herbivory was included in the model set for *G. tomentosum* only to explore if effects of herbivory varied by TSF. Replication of different herbivory levels across the range of log-transformed TSF was not considered to be adequate for the other shrub species and therefore was only included as an additive effect in other model sets. An identifier for the year of survey was included as a random smoother in all models for species where measurements were recorded in two successive years to account for repeat measures and any annual variation in environmental conditions (e.g., rainfall) other than an increase in TSF by 1year. Modelling of flowering rate and flower counts was conducted separately for male and female plants of the dioecious species *A. humilis*. Top-ranking model comparisons are presented for models on female data only. Only female plants produce cones and seeds and so modelling of cone counts was necessarily restricted to female plant data. Juvenile period was calculated from the flowering rate of female plants. The sex ratio was, on average, 45% females and 55% males across all populations (excluding non-reproductive individuals), or 49% females and 51% males after the post-fire maturation period (i.e., after 4years) (Figure [S2\)](#page-20-8). #### **2.5.2**|**Time Since Fire as a Predictor of Reproduction** To assess the strength of TSF as a predictor of reproduction, we compared GAMMs with single predictors of either TSF or plant size (height, canopy volume or effective DBH) for each of the three reproductive attributes measured. Models using plant size as the predictor represent the mechanistic relationship between TSF and reproduction, where the growth of plants following fire enables greater access to resources and an increase in reproductive output. For single-cohort populations (i.e., fire-killed species), we would expect that models using single predictors of TSF and plant size would explain similar amounts of variation (i.e., *R*2 ) and have a similar weight of evidence (i.e., AICc and ωAICc). However, for multi-cohort populations (usually resprouters, but also possible for some fire-killed species), we would expect that models using size would explain much more variation and have a much greater weight of evidence than models using TSF. GAMMs were constructed as outlined above, where models of TSF or size alone were compared using *FSSgam*. Size measurements (height, canopy volume, effective DBH) were log-transformed to optimise the distribution of values across the predictor range and improve model fit. For the dioecious species (*A. humilis*), modelling was conducted separately for male and female plants, with top-ranking model comparisons presented for female data only. #### **3   |   Results** ## **3.1   |   Flowering Rates and Juvenile Periods** TSF consistently appeared in top-ranked models of flowering rates for all species (Table [2](#page-6-0)). Flowering rate generally increased rapidly in the first few years after fire and stabilised thereafter (Figure [2](#page-6-1)). *Acacia pulchella* was the only species with an apparent decline in flowering rate in longer unburnt sites; in sites older than 30years, predicted flowering rate fell below 50%, however, *V* = 4 3 × *𝜋* × *H* 2 × *W*1 2 × *W*2 2 {6} confidence interval bands are wide at sites older than 20years and so this result is interpreted with caution (Figure [2A\)](#page-6-1). Predicted times to 50% flowering ranged from 1 to 4.4years, corresponding to minimum tolerable fire intervals (2×juvenile period rule of thumb) of 2 to 8.8years (Table [3\)](#page-7-0). Mean predicted juvenile period for fire-killed species (2.6±0.7years [SE]) was similar to that for resprouting species (3.0±1.0years; Table [3\)](#page-7-0). For all species other than the two resprouting shrubs, there was considerable site-tosite variation in flowering rate at any given TSF, as reflected in 95% confidence intervals (Figure [2A,C,D](#page-6-1)). [2017\)](#page-19-9), but we observed little difference. For example, resprouters may have a much lower maximum reproductive output at peak maturity compared to co-occurring fire-killed species owing to differences in resource allocation to reproduction versus energy storage (Enright and Lamont [1989\)](#page-18-26). Also, by the onset of reproductive maturity, resprouters have likely developed a strong resprouting capacity, potentially surviving through several fires before reaching a highly reproductive stage (Enright and Lamont [1992\)](#page-18-27), although resprouting and reproductive capacity may be eroded by a series of short fire intervals (Enright et al. [2011](#page-18-4); Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016](#page-18-8)). In contrast, fire-killed species may require several years after reaching reproductive maturity to develop adequate reproductive capacity for recovery after subsequent fires and therefore could be at risk of decline at the same intervals at which resprouters can readily resprout. There is an obvious advantage for fire-killed species in fire-prone habitats to reach maximum reproductive capacity as quickly as possible, and probably soon after the onset of reproduction, as indicated by our juvenile period data. 262 263 For the fire-killed species with the longest juvenile period studied here (*B. prionotes*), some plants produced cones following the first year of flowering (4 years post-fire), and the corresponding estimated minimum tolerable fire interval (8years) allowed populations to reach, on average, 56% of their maximum flower production and 91% of their maximum canopy seed bank size. Maximum predicted cone count for *B. prionotes* barely exceeded one cone per plant, although individuals held up to 10 cones (Figure [8B](#page-13-0)). ### **4   |   Discussion** ## **4.1   |   Juvenile Periods and Tolerable Fire Intervals** The shape of post-fire reproductive trajectories provides direct evidence of fire frequencies that permit species persistence and is critical information for the conservation and management of fire-prone ecosystems globally, especially with ongoing climate and fire regime change. We modelled reproduction in six woody plant species with a variety of fire-related traits across a range of fire ages in Banksia woodlands and found juvenile periods of 1–4 years, with little difference attributable to fire response type. Minimum tolerable fire intervals under average growing conditions based on primary juvenile periods for fire-killed species and a mix of primary and secondary juvenile periods for resprouters ranged from approximately 3–8 years and 2–9 years, respectively. Although there was some evidence of decline in reproduction in the oldest sites (>30 years since the last fire), reproductive capacity was likely still adequate for post-fire seedling recruitment after these long fire intervals. Variation in juvenile periods and reproductive output across all fire ages were associated with variation in growth forms and with changes in site productivity (rainfall) and herbivory. Taken together, our observations of rapid post-fire reproductive recovery and no fatal decline in reproduction in the long absence of fire are consistent with the suggestion that Banksia woodlands are adapted to mixed-severity fire regimes including widely varying intervals, where species have the capacity to cope with short and long fire intervals (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23). The species studied here, potentially representing a larger suite of Banksia woodland species with similar growth forms, fire response and seed bank storage modes, would all likely tolerate fire intervals of 10 years under average growing conditions, and the most rapidly maturing would likely tolerate intervals as short as 5 years under average growing conditions. While juvenile period data for resprouters is important for understanding effects on reproduction from seed, which is crucial for longterm population persistence, minimum tolerable fire intervals for resprouters based on the juvenile period method disregard the often-overriding contribution of resprouting to the post-fire recovery of species with this capability. Resprouters, therefore, may be able to tolerate even shorter intervals (i.e., less than 5 years) if resprouting capacity develops rapidly post-fire. However, several repeated short fire intervals (less than 5years) may preclude recruitment and erode adult resprouting capacity **FIGURE 7**    |    Relationships between plant size and flowering rate for all six study species. Maximum canopy height (cm), canopy volume (m3, ellipsoid form) or effective DBH (cm) was used as the best representative of size given each species' typical growth form. Solid black lines represent generalised additive mixed model fits, and shaded ribbons represent 95% confidence intervals. {13} (Enright et al. [2011;](#page-18-4) Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016\)](#page-18-8), acting as a separate mechanism of sensitivity to short fire intervals (i.e., separate to immaturity risk). Rather than resprouters, a more appropriate focus for understanding community-level minimum tolerable fire intervals is the slowest maturing, firekilled species (*B. prionotes*). *Banksia prionotes* likely requires longer intervals of at least 8–10 years for sufficient post-fire recruitment where it occurs, especially where low rainfall delays or reduces flowering and seed production. Current managed fire interval objectives of 13–33 years for risk reduction (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14) should, therefore, support the persistence of the woody plant functional types studied here; however, continued regional warming and drying associated with climate change may pose a threat of shortening wildfire intervals, consistent with the interval squeeze concept *sensu* (Enright et al. [2015](#page-18-1)). Our juvenile period and minimum tolerable fire interval findings are consistent with evidence from the region on the same or similar species (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7); Wilson et al. [2014\)](#page-20-6). However, corresponding minimum fire interval recommendations (8–16 years) suggested by Wilson et al. [\(2014](#page-20-6)) are based on population-level maturity of resprouters (a combination of primary and secondary juvenile periods) which, as explained above, are not the primary focus of the juvenile period approach as they largely recover via resprouting. Instead, minimum fire intervals based on juvenile period data for fire-killed species **FIGURE 8**    |    Relationships between (A) plant size and flower count, and (B) plant size and cone count (serotinous species only). Maximum canopy height (cm), canopy volume (m3, ellipsoid form) or effective DBH (cm) was used as the best representative of size given each species' typical growth form. Solid or dashed lines represent generalised additive mixed model fits, and shaded ribbons represent 95% confidence intervals. Relationships between plant size and flower count for *A. humilis*, a dioecious species, are presented separately for male and female plants. {14} presented in Wilson et al. [\(2014](#page-20-6)) are up to 8–10 years for the most sensitive, slow-maturing species, which is consistent with our findings. Suggested minimum tolerable fire intervals for fire-killed serotinous species (including *B. prionotes*) in drier (less productive) shrublands north of our study region range from 10 to 15 years for high versus low post-fire winter rainfall years, respectively (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7)). As our minimum tolerable interval estimates (2–9 years) suggest, minimum tolerable fire intervals should be somewhat shorter in the more productive (higher rainfall) Banksia woodlands. Consistent with this hypothesis, our estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals of around 3–5 years for fire-killed shrubs with soil seed banks are somewhat shorter than the equivalent 5–6 years reported in Enright et al. [\(2014\)](#page-18-7). Interestingly, however, estimates for resprouting shrubs show little difference between the two regions; resprouting shrubs with canopy seed banks showed minimum tolerable intervals of around 5–7 years and resprouting shrubs with soil seed banks showed little risk of even the shortest intervals sampled (Enright et al. [2014](#page-18-7)). Post-fire growth and maturation rates of fire-killed shrubs, which regenerate from seedlings, are strongly contingent on environmental productivity (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6), whereas post-fire growth rates in resprouting shrubs may be less contingent on environmental conditions during the post-fire period as already-established plants draw on stored energy reserves for post-fire growth and reproduction (Clarke et al. [2013](#page-18-24)), acknowledging again that seedling recruitment is not the major form of post-fire recovery for resprouters. A strength of the analysis of Enright et al. [\(2014\)](#page-18-7) is that estimates of minimum tolerable fire intervals were based on robust, direct measures of resprouter survival and seedling recruitment, and therefore we suggest that further targeted study of seed availability and subsequent postfire seedling recruitment at various fire intervals in Banksia woodlands is warranted to confirm minimum tolerable fire intervals and further explore variation along environmental gradients. Additional evidence is also needed to test the assumptions of the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum intervals, including whether the 2×rule of thumb (Gill and Nicholls [1989](#page-18-10)) adequately covers natural variation in (1) seed bank accumulation rates and (2) flowering, pollination and seed set for species with different traits. At our estimated minimum tolerable fire intervals, populations had reached 22%–84% of their predicted maximum flowering output, and serotinous species had produced cones over at least 3–4 years and had reached 45%–91% of their predicted maximum canopy seed bank accumulation. Variation in post-fire reproductive attributes among species potentially indicates that the efficacy of the 2×approximation of minimum tolerable fire intervals varies between species. Perhaps species with soil-stored seed banks might be more adequately covered by the 2×approximation than those with canopy seed banks, as species with soil-stored seed may possess a residual seed bank after fire (i.e., seed banks are not completely exhausted by fire) (Auld and Denham [2006](#page-17-15)) and do not have to produce a persistent woody fruit requiring resources like serotinous species (Cramer and Midgley [2009;](#page-18-25) Tonnabel et al. [2012\)](#page-20-13). Our results also demonstrate substantial variation in reproduction owing to varying environmental conditions, suggesting that, in some cases, the 2×approximation may be inadequate to account for delays in reproduction. For example, for *G. tomentosum*, the presence of herbivores and low mean annual rainfall delayed the juvenile period beyond the estimated minimum tolerable fire interval under average growing conditions. ## **4.2   |   Post-Fire Reproduction** Fire-killed species are generally considered to have longer primary juvenile periods than the secondary juvenile periods of cooccurring resprouters (Gosper, Prober, and Yates [2013;](#page-18-5) Harvey et al. [2017\)](#page-19-9), but we observed little difference. Similar juvenile periods for these species groups, however, do not necessarily mean that they have equivalent reproductive trajectories or would be expected to have similar fire interval responses given differences in other traits. For example, resprouters may have a much lower maximum reproductive output at peak maturity compared to co-occurring fire-killed species owing to differences in resource allocation to reproduction versus energy storage (Enright and Lamont [1989\)](#page-18-26). Also, by the onset of reproductive maturity, resprouters have likely developed a strong resprouting capacity, potentially surviving through several fires before reaching a highly reproductive stage (Enright and Lamont [1992\)](#page-18-27), although resprouting and reproductive capacity may be eroded by a series of short fire intervals (Enright et al. [2011](#page-18-4); Fairman, Nitschke, and Bennett [2016](#page-18-8)). In contrast, fire-killed species may require several years after reaching reproductive maturity to develop adequate reproductive capacity for recovery after subsequent fires and therefore could be at risk of decline at the same intervals at which resprouters can readily resprout. There is an obvious advantage for fire-killed species in fire-prone habitats to reach maximum reproductive capacity as quickly as possible, and probably soon after the onset of reproduction, as indicated by our juvenile period data. For the fire-killed species with the longest juvenile period studied here (*B. prionotes*), some plants produced cones following the first year of flowering (4 years post-fire), and the corresponding estimated minimum tolerable fire interval (8years) allowed populations to reach, on average, 56% of their maximum flower production and 91% of their maximum canopy seed bank size. For a related, fire-killed *Banksia* species, Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [\(1996](#page-18-9)) similarly showed that plants began producing cones after the first year of flowering and produced an increasing number of cones in the following few years. Despite being the slowest-maturing, fire-killed species in this study, and probably in Banksia woodlands generally, *B. prionotes* appears to have a relatively short juvenile period compared to other fire-killed species in southwestern Australia (Gosper et al. [2022](#page-18-6); Harvey et al. [2017](#page-19-9); Wooller, Wooller, and Brown [2002\)](#page-20-4). Populations of *B. prionotes* also often occur in discrete stands such that a conservative minimum interval of 10 years, under average growing conditions, may not necessarily be relevant to apply to the entire landscape, or where fires are sufficiently patchy or of low severity to allow established individuals to survive fire (Burrows and Middleton [2016](#page-17-16)). Intervals less than 10years are relatively rare on the Swan Coastal Plain, especially in areas with managed fire regimes, although changing climate regimes and increasing human disturbance do not necessarily preclude such intervals (Fontaine [2022\)](#page-18-28). {15} Our findings are consistent with previous efforts from the region in quantifying post-fire seed production in the resprouting *B. attenuata* in showing that mature trees are capable of producing cones in the first year or two after fire because they can resprout epicormically (Densmore and Clingan [2019;](#page-18-16) Valentine et al. [2014](#page-20-14)). Post-fire cone production is mediated by fire severity, where there are minimal interruptions to reproduction after low severity fire, but trees may take several years to regain the same level of cone production after high severity fire (Densmore and Clingan [2019](#page-18-16)). By the time of the species-specific minimum tolerable fire interval estimated here (~9 years), Valentine et al. [\(2014](#page-20-14)) estimated that mature adults (>2m tall) had accumulated, on average, approximately 6 cones per plant, which is higher than estimates presented here (~1 cone per plant). Our dataset includes smaller juvenile plants and a subset of our data on *B. attenuata* trees >2m tall shows cone counts across a similar range of values to Valentine et al. [\(2014\)](#page-20-14). Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016](#page-19-27)) and Densmore and Clingan [\(2019](#page-18-16)) report around 1.3 and 7 times higher estimates of *B. attenuata* mean canopy seed bank density (cones per ha), respectively, than we find here (mean 746 cones per ha; Figure [S3\)](#page-20-8). However, Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016\)](#page-19-27) included higher rainfall sites on the Swan Coastal Plain and Densmore and Clingan [\(2019](#page-18-16)) reported on the entire crop of cones for ease of recording regardless of whether they had closed follicles or not, where, in both cases, it would be reasonable to expect higher canopy seed bank estimates. Interestingly, the much higher estimates of cones per ha reported by Densmore and Clingan [\(2019\)](#page-18-16) can be explained by the weakly serotinous nature of *B. attenuata* in the region (Cowling and Lamont [1985](#page-18-21)), where most seeds are released from cones within two years of seed maturity, but opened cones are likely retained on the plant for many years, and could therefore give the impression of a much larger canopy seed bank. Johnston, Stock, and Mawson [\(2016](#page-19-27)) reported a similar trend of gradually increasing seed bank size with increasing time since fire for *B. attenuata* and a similar range of values for cones per ha for *B. prionotes*. We show that plants of fire-killed shrubs that regenerate via seed following fire gain reproductive capacity quickly. Likewise, Monk, Pate, and Loneragan [\(1981](#page-19-28)) observed that the fire-killed *A. pulchella* began producing flowers and seeds in the second year after fire, and achieved maximum seed production shortly thereafter (3–4 years post-fire). These observations differ from those for fire-killed Proteaceae shrubs from southeastern Australia where cone and seed production was not observed for a few years after first flowering, and was slower overall (Jenkins, Morrison, and Auld [2010](#page-19-29)). For fast-growing species such as *A. pulchella*, a doubling of the juvenile period as a general rule of thumb for estimating the minimum tolerable fire interval may be adequate to sustain populations under average growing conditions, even if this only allows for one or two additional years of seed production. Rapid post-fire reproductive maturity and abundant seed production are important mechanisms to cope with short fire intervals for species adapted to frequent canopy scorch, whether that be understorey shrubs scorched in all but the lowest severity fires, or trees burnt in crown fire regimes (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996;](#page-18-9) Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon [1996\)](#page-18-29). Likewise, soil-stored seed banks, variable seed dormancy and residual seedbanks are traits that allow species to cope with short fire intervals. Banksia woodlands may be adapted to mixed severity fire regimes where understorey and overstorey components experience a range of low, moderate and high severity fire at widely varying intervals, potentially as short as 5–10 years in the understorey (Hobbs and Atkins [1990](#page-19-15); Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23). Our findings for the resprouting shrub *A. humilis* are consistent with expectations for dioecious species in that patterns of postfire flowering appear to be driven by the costs of male versus female reproduction (Barrett and Hough [2012;](#page-17-17) Obeso [2002\)](#page-19-30). Flower and pollen production in male plants is less costly than flower, cone and seed production in female plants and so we would expect to observe precocious male flowering (Field, Pickup, and Barrett [2013](#page-18-30)). In comparison to female plants, male *A. humilis* plants had a shorter juvenile period (2.5 vs. 3.5years on average), produced more flowers per plant on average across all fire ages (927 vs. 269) and produced more flowers on average at any given plant size. Wilson et al. [\(2014\)](#page-20-6) provided an estimate of 40 years for the maximum tolerable fire interval for Banksia woodlands based on the maximum longevity of serotinous, fire-killed *Banksia* species. However, *Banksia* longevity was derived for a different species (*B. hookeriana*) from a nearby region with different climate and fire regimes, and for a species that grows as a tall shrub rather than a tree, and therefore presumably has a shorter lifespan (Cowling and Lamont [1985\)](#page-18-21). We expect *Banksia* tree longevity in the range of 40–60 years for *B. prionotes* (fire-killed) and to exceed 100 years for *B. attenuata* (resprouter). Over the approximately 35-year chronosequence studied here, we found no evidence of decline in reproduction for *B. attenuata*, but some evidence for a minor decline in reproduction in *B. prionotes* which appears primarily driven by a decline in plant density of mature stages with a minor contribution from a decline in reproductive output per plant. Although *B. prionotes* can have low levels of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), this input of non-reproductive individuals does not appear to have a noticeable effect on population-level reproduction (Figure [S5\)](#page-20-8). There is little evidence of major population senescence in *B. prionotes*, and therefore, maximum tolerable intervals are likely to exceed 40years, which are very rare regardless (Wilson et al. [2014](#page-20-6)). #### **4.3   |   Reproduction Under Varying Environmental and Demographic Conditions** Environmental productivity (mean annual rainfall) and the presence or absence of herbivory were found to be important factors associated with post-fire reproductive trajectories (Burrows, Wardell-Johnson, and Ward [2008;](#page-17-4) Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) McCaw [2008\)](#page-19-10). In sites with low mean rainfall (low productivity) or herbivore presence, predicted juvenile periods were delayed by up to 3 years, and therefore minimum tolerable fire intervals by up to 6 years for fire-killed understorey shrubs (*A. pulchella* and *G. tomentosum*). Low mean rainfall also decreased flower production by up to 61% for the same species. For short-lived species, this may represent a doubling (or more) of the minimum fire-free period required for population replacement, and potentially a reduction in lifetime reproductive output.

content.content: 278 279 {16} 280 281 While these data pertain to mean rainfall and the prevailing presence or absence of herbivores, our results suggest that delayed reproductive maturity and reduced reproductive output could occur under abrupt environmental changes such as the introduction of native or non-native herbivores, or the increasing severity of drought conditions associated with climate change (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Matusick et al. [2018\)](#page-19-31). Modelling suggests that primary juvenile periods for serotinous obligate seeders (here represented by *B. prionotes*) could more than double in the study area under 2050 climate change scenarios, including lower mean annual rainfall (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6), potentially requiring longer fire intervals to conserve vulnerable populations. In general, we sampled across a relatively narrow mean annual rainfall gradient (~150mm difference) compared to the variation present in the broader region, and in particular, our sampling of *B. prionotes* populations occurred across a very narrow range (30mm difference). It is not surprising, therefore, that we did not detect an effect of rainfall for *B. prionotes*; however, if sampling was repeated across a wider rainfall gradient (spatial or temporal), we would expect to detect slower maturity rates under low rainfall. This is a broad concern for fire-killed species which rely on post-fire recruitment from seeds for persistence, and is consistent with the concept of 'interval squeeze' where populations are vulnerable to decline with the simultaneous shortening of fire intervals and reduced seed production and post-fire recruitment associated with climate change impacts (Enright et al. [2015\)](#page-18-1). Invasive grassy weeds are also a significant threat in Banksia woodlands (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14), and may pose an additional limitation on population recovery if weeds reduce post-fire seedling recruitment or delay maturation and reproductive maturity. 282 283 The effects of varying mean annual rainfall on flowering rate (juvenile period) provided a curious result for *B. attenuata*, where populations in high mean rainfall sites appeared to mature more slowly than populations in low mean rainfall sites. Rather than higher rainfall delaying maturation, we believe this relates to differences in the demographic structure of populations under varying rainfall regimes altering population-level calculations. In the study area, higher rainfall and longer growing seasons likely facilitate higher rates of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), although not to a level that would result in densification or canopy closure that would, in turn, preclude recruitment of shade-intolerant seedlings and probably reduce reproductive output. Flowering rates reported here are a composite of reproduction (or lack thereof) in seedlings, juveniles and adults, and therefore a higher proportion of non-reproductive seedlings and juveniles resulting from higher recruitment will lower flowering rate estimates. 284 285 Canopy seed banks (closed cone counts per plant) for both *Banksia* species were very low, with *B. attenuata* generally having less than two seed-bearing cones per plant on average, and *B. prionotes* generally less than one. Low cone counts can be explained by a combination of the weakly serotinous nature of these *Banksia* species in the study area, and demographic structures with a high proportion of juvenile plants with little to no reproduction (Figures [S5](#page-20-8) and [S6](#page-20-8)). Cowling and Lamont [\(1985](#page-18-21)) reported a gradient in the degree of serotiny of *Banksia* species in the region with populations in our study area being weakly or non-serotinous, meaning that the majority of the accumulated canopy seed bank originates from the most recent seed crop minus any losses from 286 287 disease and predation. Whelan and Ayre [\(2020\)](#page-20-15) likewise reported very low canopy seed bank accumulation for a serotinous *Banksia* shrub species from southeastern Australia. Both weakly serotinous *Banksia* species studied here develop multi-cohort populations, especially in the absence of fire (Hobbs and Atkins [1990;](#page-19-15) Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024](#page-19-23)). Like the effect of rainfall on *B. attenuata* flowering rate noted above, a high proportion of non-reproductive juvenile plants lowers population-level seed bank size estimates which likely underestimates the reproductive potential of mature individuals. While mature individuals have the potential to contribute much larger seed banks, weak serotiny will ultimately limit the maximum size of the canopy seed bank. This contrasts with the seed bank dynamics of highly serotinous *Banksia* species in ecosystems with more regular crown fire regimes where canopy seed banks can accumulate over many years (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996\)](#page-18-9). 288 289 Top-ranked models explained up to 92% of variation in the data (mean=43%, inter-quartile range=30%–51%; Table [2,](#page-6-0) Table [5\)](#page-8-2), leaving, in some cases, substantial variation unexplained by the variables considered in this study. More detailed analyses of the effects of interannual weather variation and spatially varying site variables (e.g., soil type, aspect, elevation) could explain greater variation in the data and provide a deeper understanding of the drivers of reproduction. The analysis presented here using mean annual rainfall could also be extended to quantify the effects of varying rainfall at different demographic stages—for example, during seedling establishment (1–2years post-fire), floral initiation and fruit development—to assess the sensitivity of post-fire reproduction to extreme dry climate conditions. Such analyses could help predict scenarios or sites under which fire managers may need to consider longer managed fire intervals to accommodate delayed juvenile periods under increasingly common droughts and heatwave events (Matusick et al. [2018;](#page-19-31) Ruthrof et al. [2021\)](#page-20-16). 290 291 #### **4.4   |   Time Since Fire Versus Size as a Predictor of Reproduction** 292 293 While we found that TSF was a clear indicator of reproduction, we also show that plant size is a much stronger predictor of reproductive capacity as also reported elsewhere by Andrus et al. [\(2020\)](#page-17-18), Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon [\(1993](#page-18-31)) and von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [\(2018\)](#page-20-3). Many plant species that inhabit fire-prone environments (especially fire-killed species in stand-replacing fire regimes) are often assumed to follow a specific post-fire trajectory where a single, post-fire seedling cohort matures and grows larger at a similar rate (Gill and McMahon [1986](#page-18-11)). However, this assumption may weaken in noncrown fire regimes, or for multi-cohort populations resulting from inter-fire recruitment, post-fire resprouting, or both. Interfire recruitment is evident for most of the species studied here (Hobbs and Atkins [1990](#page-19-15); Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), and therefore, population-level metrics of reproduction may be more closely related to varying demographic structure or environmental conditions rather than TSF. 294 295 We acknowledge TSF and post-fire juvenile periods as simplistic yet useful indicators of post-fire reproductive maturity, but here we show that the effects of other environmental and demographic conditions can introduce substantial variation into species 296 297 {17} 298 299 responses, and therefore are important to consider when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence (Gosper et al. [2022](#page-18-6)). As originally recognised, the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals can provide rapid and low-cost guidance for fire management planning, but advances in ecological understanding and technology for measuring vegetation attributes should allow for the development of more sophisticated models for predicting variation in reproduction by including multiple environmental and demographic variables. Other metrics of species reproductive maturity and minimum tolerable fire intervals that may provide useful alternative or supplemental information for fire managers include the assessment of (1) the reproductive output (and density) of the largest individuals as the plants that contribute most to the reproductive capacity of the population and (2) average understorey plant height and litter cover as surrogates of plant growth and fuel accumulation. Ongoing advances in the mapping of vegetation structure from remote sensing data (e.g., through airborne or terrestrial laser scanning) (Moudrý et al. [2023;](#page-19-32) Turner et al. [2023](#page-20-17)) may provide an opportunity to measure plant size and density across large areas and combine with environmental and demographic data, such as that presented in this study, to calculate metrics of reproduction at a similar landscape scale to traditional fire age mapping currently used extensively in fire management planning. 300 301 #### **Author Contributions** 302 303 **Russell G. file.content: {16} While these data pertain to mean rainfall and the prevailing presence or absence of herbivores, our results suggest that delayed reproductive maturity and reduced reproductive output could occur under abrupt environmental changes such as the introduction of native or non-native herbivores, or the increasing severity of drought conditions associated with climate change (Gosper et al. [2022;](#page-18-6) Matusick et al. [2018\)](#page-19-31). Modelling suggests that primary juvenile periods for serotinous obligate seeders (here represented by *B. prionotes*) could more than double in the study area under 2050 climate change scenarios, including lower mean annual rainfall (Gosper et al. [2022\)](#page-18-6), potentially requiring longer fire intervals to conserve vulnerable populations. In general, we sampled across a relatively narrow mean annual rainfall gradient (~150mm difference) compared to the variation present in the broader region, and in particular, our sampling of *B. prionotes* populations occurred across a very narrow range (30mm difference). It is not surprising, therefore, that we did not detect an effect of rainfall for *B. prionotes*; however, if sampling was repeated across a wider rainfall gradient (spatial or temporal), we would expect to detect slower maturity rates under low rainfall. This is a broad concern for fire-killed species which rely on post-fire recruitment from seeds for persistence, and is consistent with the concept of 'interval squeeze' where populations are vulnerable to decline with the simultaneous shortening of fire intervals and reduced seed production and post-fire recruitment associated with climate change impacts (Enright et al. [2015\)](#page-18-1). Invasive grassy weeds are also a significant threat in Banksia woodlands (Ritchie et al. [2021\)](#page-19-14), and may pose an additional limitation on population recovery if weeds reduce post-fire seedling recruitment or delay maturation and reproductive maturity. The effects of varying mean annual rainfall on flowering rate (juvenile period) provided a curious result for *B. attenuata*, where populations in high mean rainfall sites appeared to mature more slowly than populations in low mean rainfall sites. Rather than higher rainfall delaying maturation, we believe this relates to differences in the demographic structure of populations under varying rainfall regimes altering population-level calculations. In the study area, higher rainfall and longer growing seasons likely facilitate higher rates of inter-fire seedling recruitment (Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), although not to a level that would result in densification or canopy closure that would, in turn, preclude recruitment of shade-intolerant seedlings and probably reduce reproductive output. Flowering rates reported here are a composite of reproduction (or lack thereof) in seedlings, juveniles and adults, and therefore a higher proportion of non-reproductive seedlings and juveniles resulting from higher recruitment will lower flowering rate estimates. Canopy seed banks (closed cone counts per plant) for both *Banksia* species were very low, with *B. attenuata* generally having less than two seed-bearing cones per plant on average, and *B. prionotes* generally less than one. Low cone counts can be explained by a combination of the weakly serotinous nature of these *Banksia* species in the study area, and demographic structures with a high proportion of juvenile plants with little to no reproduction (Figures [S5](#page-20-8) and [S6](#page-20-8)). Cowling and Lamont [\(1985](#page-18-21)) reported a gradient in the degree of serotiny of *Banksia* species in the region with populations in our study area being weakly or non-serotinous, meaning that the majority of the accumulated canopy seed bank originates from the most recent seed crop minus any losses from disease and predation. Whelan and Ayre [\(2020\)](#page-20-15) likewise reported very low canopy seed bank accumulation for a serotinous *Banksia* shrub species from southeastern Australia. Both weakly serotinous *Banksia* species studied here develop multi-cohort populations, especially in the absence of fire (Hobbs and Atkins [1990;](#page-19-15) Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024](#page-19-23)). Like the effect of rainfall on *B. attenuata* flowering rate noted above, a high proportion of non-reproductive juvenile plants lowers population-level seed bank size estimates which likely underestimates the reproductive potential of mature individuals. While mature individuals have the potential to contribute much larger seed banks, weak serotiny will ultimately limit the maximum size of the canopy seed bank. This contrasts with the seed bank dynamics of highly serotinous *Banksia* species in ecosystems with more regular crown fire regimes where canopy seed banks can accumulate over many years (Enright, Lamont, and Marsula [1996\)](#page-18-9). Top-ranked models explained up to 92% of variation in the data (mean=43%, inter-quartile range=30%–51%; Table [2,](#page-6-0) Table [5\)](#page-8-2), leaving, in some cases, substantial variation unexplained by the variables considered in this study. More detailed analyses of the effects of interannual weather variation and spatially varying site variables (e.g., soil type, aspect, elevation) could explain greater variation in the data and provide a deeper understanding of the drivers of reproduction. The analysis presented here using mean annual rainfall could also be extended to quantify the effects of varying rainfall at different demographic stages—for example, during seedling establishment (1–2years post-fire), floral initiation and fruit development—to assess the sensitivity of post-fire reproduction to extreme dry climate conditions. Such analyses could help predict scenarios or sites under which fire managers may need to consider longer managed fire intervals to accommodate delayed juvenile periods under increasingly common droughts and heatwave events (Matusick et al. [2018;](#page-19-31) Ruthrof et al. [2021\)](#page-20-16). #### **4.4   |   Time Since Fire Versus Size as a Predictor of Reproduction** While we found that TSF was a clear indicator of reproduction, we also show that plant size is a much stronger predictor of reproductive capacity as also reported elsewhere by Andrus et al. [\(2020\)](#page-17-18), Gauthier, Bergeron, and Simon [\(1993](#page-18-31)) and von Takach Dukai, Lindenmayer, and Banks [\(2018\)](#page-20-3). Many plant species that inhabit fire-prone environments (especially fire-killed species in stand-replacing fire regimes) are often assumed to follow a specific post-fire trajectory where a single, post-fire seedling cohort matures and grows larger at a similar rate (Gill and McMahon [1986](#page-18-11)). However, this assumption may weaken in noncrown fire regimes, or for multi-cohort populations resulting from inter-fire recruitment, post-fire resprouting, or both. Interfire recruitment is evident for most of the species studied here (Hobbs and Atkins [1990](#page-19-15); Miller, Enright, Fontaine et al. [2024\)](#page-19-23), and therefore, population-level metrics of reproduction may be more closely related to varying demographic structure or environmental conditions rather than TSF. We acknowledge TSF and post-fire juvenile periods as simplistic yet useful indicators of post-fire reproductive maturity, but here we show that the effects of other environmental and demographic conditions can introduce substantial variation into species {17} responses, and therefore are important to consider when making decisions about fire intervals that may impact species persistence (Gosper et al. [2022](#page-18-6)). As originally recognised, the juvenile period approach for estimating minimum tolerable fire intervals can provide rapid and low-cost guidance for fire management planning, but advances in ecological understanding and technology for measuring vegetation attributes should allow for the development of more sophisticated models for predicting variation in reproduction by including multiple environmental and demographic variables. Other metrics of species reproductive maturity and minimum tolerable fire intervals that may provide useful alternative or supplemental information for fire managers include the assessment of (1) the reproductive output (and density) of the largest individuals as the plants that contribute most to the reproductive capacity of the population and (2) average understorey plant height and litter cover as surrogates of plant growth and fuel accumulation. Ongoing advances in the mapping of vegetation structure from remote sensing data (e.g., through airborne or terrestrial laser scanning) (Moudrý et al. [2023;](#page-19-32) Turner et al. [2023](#page-20-17)) may provide an opportunity to measure plant size and density across large areas and combine with environmental and demographic data, such as that presented in this study, to calculate metrics of reproduction at a similar landscape scale to traditional fire age mapping currently used extensively in fire management planning. #### **Author Contributions** **Russell G.
