{0} #### **Abstract** **Question:** What is the role of dispersal, persistent soil seed banks and seedling recruitment in population persistence of fleshy-fruited obligate seeding plant species in fire-prone habitats? **Location:** Southeastern Australia. **Methods:** We used a long-term study of a shrubby, fleshy-fruited *Persoonia* species (*Proteaceae*) to examine (1) seed removal from beneath the canopy of adult plants; (2) seedling recruitment after fire; (3) the magnitude and location of the residual soil seed bank; and (4) the implications for fire management of obligate seeding species. We used demographic sampling techniques combined with Generalised Linear Modelling and regression to quantify population changes over time. **Results:** Most of the mature fruits (90%) on the ground below the canopy of plants were removed by *Wallabia bicolor* (Swamp wallaby) with 88% of seeds extracted from *W. bicolor* scats viable and dormant. Wallabies play an important role in moving seeds away from parent plants. Their role in occasional long distance dispersal events remains unknown. We detected almost no seed predation *in situ* under canopies (< 1%). Seedling recruitment was cued to fire, with post-fire seedling densities 6-7 times pre-fire adult densities. After fire, a residual soil seed bank was present, as many seeds (77-100%) remained dormant and viable at a soil depth where successful future seedling emergence is possible (0-5 cm). Seedling survival was high (> 80%) with most mortality within 2 years of emergence. Plant growth averaged 17 cm per year. The primary juvenile period of plants was 7-8 years, within the period of likely return fire intervals in the study area. We predicted that the study population increased some five-fold after the wildfire at the site. **Conclusions**: Residual soil seed banks are important, especially in species with long primary juvenile periods, to buffer the populations against the impact of a second fire occurring before the seed bank is replenished. **Keywords:** Fire frequency; Macropod; Mammal; Obligate seeder; Soil seed bank. **Nomenclature:** Harden, G.J. (1990-1992). # **Dispersal and recruitment dynamics in the fleshy-fruited** *Persoonia lanceolata* **(Proteaceae)** **Auld, Tony D.**1\***; Denham, Andrew J.**1,2 **& Turner, Ken**3 1*Biodiversity Science, Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW), PO Box 1967, Hurstville NSW 2220 Australia;* 2*E-Mail andrew.denham@environment.nsw.gov.au;* 3*Native Vegetation Science, Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW), PO Box 867 Wollongong, NSW 2520 Australia; E-mail ken.turner@dnr.nsw.gov.au \*Corresponding author; E-mail tony.auld@environment.nsw.gov.au* ## **Introduction** Persistence of plant populations is influenced by a range of factors (Harper 1977). Ultimately, all plant populations rely on recruitment from seed to compensate for the death of individuals. For plants that occur in fireprone habitats and are killed by fire (obligate seeders), recruitment is often linked to the passage of fire (Keeley 1991; Tyler 1995; Whelan 1995). The abundance and distribution of new recruits in such plant populations is controlled by a combination of factors. These include: (1) amount of seed produced (e.g. Enright & Lamont 1989); (2) seed dispersal to safe sites (Hughes & Westoby 1992; Lamont et al. 1993); (3) factors that govern the breaking of seed dormancy and promote seed germination (Auld & O'Connell 1991; Baskin & Baskin 1998; Keeley & Fotheringham 2000; Ooi et al. 2006); and (4) early seedling survival (Tyler 1995, 1996). As adults of obligate seeding species are killed by fire, sufficient time between fires is needed to replenish seed banks. Fire regimes that allow fires to repeatedly occur before seed banks are replenished may cause population declines or local extinction. Avoiding such fire regimes is necessary in order to manage fire-prone habitats for the conservation of biodiversity (Bradstock et al. 1998; Keeley & Fotheringham 2000; Gill 2001; Keith et al. 2002; Whelan 2002). An understanding of the dynamics of seed dispersal and factors influencing recruitment is necessary to determine how obligate seeding species respond to changes in fire regimes that result from direct human activities and climate change (Whelan 1986). Seed dispersal of woody species in many fire-prone habitats can be limited, as indicated by the predominance of myrmecochory in SE and SW Australia (Berg 1975; Rice & Westoby 1981) and elsewhere (Gomez & Espadaler 1998). For such species, the capacity to reoccupy sites should a species be adversely affected by fire regimes is limited (Whelan 1986, 1995), especially where habitats are highly fragmented by urban and rural development. For some species, there is a greater {1} capacity for dispersal, through either wind dispersal of small seeds or dispersal by animal vectors. Fleshyfruited species that may be moved by vertebrates are a small component of the heath and woodland flora of southeastern Australia (French & Westoby 1996) and other fire-prone floras (Bullock 1978; Milewski & Bond 1981; Keeley 1991). This may be the result of the low soil fertility that characterises the vegetation in these areas (Westoby et al. 1990). We estimate, based on seed morphology characteristics, that in the Sydney region, only some 9 % of species (in 57 genera) that occur in fire-prone heaths, woodlands and dry forest habitats have fleshy fruits that are likely to be dispersed by vertebrates. The most abundant groups are from two diverse families, *Persoonia* in the Proteaceae (29 taxa) and *Acrotriche*, *Astroloma, Brachyloma*, *Leucopogon, Lissanthe, Melichrus*, *Monotoca* and *Styphelia* in the *Ericaceae* (formerly included in the Epacridaceae, 43 taxa). The role of seed dispersal in maintaining populations or in moving seeds between populations in such taxa is poorly known. *Persoonia* is an endemic Australian genus of ca. 100 species (Weston 2002), with two main centres of radiation, southeastern and southwestern Australia. Obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp. may have long primary juvenile periods, relative to the average inter-fire interval (Benson 1985; Auld unpubl.) and a number are threatened in the Sydney Basin of southeastern Australia (Rymer 2006). Such species are at risk of decline if fire frequencies are increased via arson, climate change or burning for protection of life and property. In this paper we report on a long-term study of one obligate seeding shrub species, *Persoonia lanceolata* Andrews, that is common in eastern Australia and is a significant structural component of vegetation in heaths and woodlands. We ask: - 1. Is seed removed or eaten from beneath the canopy of adult plants? - 2. What agents are involved in seed removal or seed predation? - 3. What is the magnitude of seedling recruitment after fire? Does this suggest population stability under the current fire regime? - 4. What is the magnitude and location of the residual soil seed bank? How is this related to the pre-fire seed density? and - 5. What are the implications for fire management of obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp.? ## **Methods** #### *Study species and site* *Persoonia lanceolata* is a bushy shrub that grows to 3 m high. It is a fire sensitive obligate seeder, common in the understorey in heath and woodlands along the east coast and ranges of New South Wales, Australia (Weston 2002). Flowering occurs in summer (December to February) with mature fruits ripening in the following spring (September to October, Benson & McDougall 2000). The fruit of *Persoonia* species is a drupe (Weston 2002) of approximately 1300 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990), with a pulpy flesh surrounding a hard woody pyrene. There is mostly one seed per pyrene in *P. lanceolata* (Westoby et al. 1990; pers. obs.). Seed dispersal is thought to be mostly by mammals and birds (Benson & McDougall 2000). We examined a population of *P. lanceolata* at one site within Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park 20 km north of Sydney (33°53' E, 151°13' S) southeastern Australia. Annual precipitation for Sydney is around 1300 mm, while the average monthly maximum/minimum temperatures are 26/18 °C in summer and 16/8 °C in winter. The area of the site was ca. 2 ha and contained a dense mature population of *P. lanceolata* occurring in a periodically wet heathland. *Persoonia lanceolata* was one of the dominant shrubs along with *Angophora crassifolia*, *Eucalyptus stricta* and *Hakea teretifolia.* There was a range of smaller shrub species (0.5 - 2 m), particularly members of the *Proteaceae* and *Fabaceae* (common species include: *Banksia oblongifolia, Boronia pinnata, Dillwynia floribunda, Epacris pulchella, Grevillea speciosa, Hakea dactyloides, Leptospermum squarrosum, Mirbelia rubiifolia, Persoonia pinifolia, Pultenaea elliptica* and *Xanthorrhoea* spp.) and a ground cover of sedges, grasses, and herbs (common species include: *Actinotus minor, Anisopogon avenaceus, Bauera rubioides, Cyathochaeta diandra, Lindsaea linearis, Lomandra cylindrica, L. glauca, Mitrasacme polymorpha, Patersonia* sp.*, Restio* spec.). The site was burnt by an extensive summer (January) wildfire in 1994 that burnt all the surrounding habitat. It had previously been burnt in a summer wildfire 15 years prior. #### *Seed dispersal and predation* Prior to the wildfire, we established plots under randomly selected mature *P. lanceolata* plants over two consecutive fruiting seasons. In the first season, we established five plots in a pilot experiment that ran for 12 days. In the second season, we established ten plots and followed the fates of seeds for 40 days. At each plot we established two treatments; {2} (1) a cache of 10 mature fruits; and (2) a cache of 10 mature fruits covered by a wire mesh cage (mesh 1 cm × 1 cm), cage 15 cm by 15 cm by 6 cm high. Each cage was placed over a petri dish and secured with wire stakes. These cages excluded vertebrates. All caches were placed in 9 cm diameter petri dishes to avoid fruits being washed away in storms. The fate of seeds in caches was checked twice daily for 4 days then daily for 10 days and then 2-3 times per week. Searches were made around the caches for fruits or fruit/seed remains if seeds were removed from the caches. Where mammals were suspected of taking seeds (where pieces of seed testa were found or whole seeds were removed overnight) additional trials were established to identify the likely animals responsible. Adhesive tape was placed on the edges of petri dishes containing seeds and hair samples of the mammal species removing seeds were collected. These animal hairs were identified by B. Triggs. Field trapping using Elliott type A aluminium folding box traps was conducted to determine which small mammal species were present at the site. A 2-factor GLIM was used to compare the proportion of caches where fruit were removed in the first 12 days in the caged and uncaged treatments, across two years (12 days being the length of time the experiment was run in the first season). A separate 1-factor GLIM examined the proportion of caches where fruit removal occurred across treatments at the end of the second season. In both cases a binomial error structure was used. We also searched the surrounding habitat for any scats that contained pyrenes or fruits. We collected numerous scats and removed the pyrenes from them. For 10 replicate samples of 10 pyrenes from these scats we estimated the non-dormant seed fraction by placing replicate batches of seeds into 9-cm diameter petri dishes on Whatmans Grade 1 filter paper at room temperatures. Distilled water was added to ensure the filter paper remained moist and germination was followed for 2 months after which seeds were extracted from pyrenes and tested for viability using tetrazolium (Lakon 1949). #### *Seedling recruitment, survival and growth after fire* After the 1994 wildfire, we established 23 permanent 1-m2 quadrats within the population using a randomised grid. Within each quadrat we scored the number of dead adults that were rooted in the quadrat and tagged new emerging seedlings of *P. lanceolata* for a period of 12 years. New seedlings (71) were identified by their distinctive cotyledons. At each sampling, we scored plant survivorship, assessed whether the plants had reached maturity (as indicated by the production of flowers and then fruits), and measured the height of all tagged *P. lan-* *ceolata* plants as an indicator of their growth to maturity. The time to first flowering was recorded for all seedlings and the magnitude of fruit production estimated in several flowering seasons by counting large (near mature) fruits on all tagged plants. The rate of growth of plants was examined using non-linear regression (power function) of plant height (lognormal transformed) against plant age. As plants were repeatedly sampled, we also carried out an Analysis of Covariance with previous sample plant height as a covariate. We also compared the pre-fire density of plants with the post-fire seedling density as an estimate of population turnover after the fire. #### *Residual soil seed bank* Within a randomly chosen subset (8) of the 23 available 1-m2 quadrats described above to follow seedling emergence, survival and growth, we examined the residual soil seed bank. In 2003, 9 years after the 1994 fire (after seedlings had had their first flowering, but before the first post-fire seed fall) we excavated the soil in each of the 8 (1-m2) plots. All the soil in each plot was excavated in two parts, i.e. 0 to 5 cm and 5-10 cm depths. Pyrenes were extracted by sieving. Samples were wet sieved by washing through firstly a 6.3 mm followed by a 4.2 mm sieve. The retained parts were allowed to dry and hand sorted. Pyrenes passed through the first sieve and were retained by the second. Intact pyrenes were opened to determine if the fruit contained a viable seed (filled, firm and white). ## **Results** #### *Seed dispersal and predation* Seed removal outside cages after 12 days occurred in both sampled seasons (GLIM Δ dev = 14.1, 1 df, *P* < 0.005), with no interaction between years and treatment (GLIM Δ dev = 0.0, 1 df, *P* > 0.05) and no year effect (GLIM Δ dev = 0.1, 1 df, *P* > 0.05). Averaged across the two years some 17% of seed was removed (removal occurring in 53 % of seed caches) in 12 days (Fig. 1). At the end of the second sample season, where we followed the fate of seeds for 40 days, the treatment effect was again significant (GLIM Δ dev = 16.9, 1 df, *P <* 0.005), with an average of 90% of fruits removed in the open (removal occurring in 100 % of seed caches). The rate of seed removal outside the cages was slow but continued over the 40 day trial (Fig. 1). Inside cages, there was occasional consumption of the flesh around pyrenes, and occasionally whole fruits were removed. Outside of cages most losses were fruit removals, although in a very few cases the pyrene was removed and the flesh remained. {3} #### *Seedling recruitment, survival and growth after fire* Most seedlings emerged in the first 10 months after the 1994 fire (the time of our first sample). There was only limited emergence after this (Table 1), but occasional seedlings appeared until 6 years post-fire. This subsequent emergence was not confined to any particular season (summer 11, autumn 6, winter 3 seedlings, respectively), and declined in magnitude over time. Seedling survival was high with most observed mortality in the first 1-2 years after seedlings were tagged (Fig. 2). Our sampling did not allow us to detect mortality in the first 10 months post-fire. The post-fire seedling density was 6-7 times greater than the pre-fire adult density (0.5 vs. 3.3/m2). Seedlings reached a height of ca. 1 m (range 0.10 - 1.7m) at 6-7 years old, growing at an average rate of 0.17m per year (Fig. 3). Age was a good predictor of plant **Fig. 1.** Seed removal rates over two annual fruit-crops in *Persoonia lanceolata*, (**a**) year 1; (**b**) year 2. Treatments are: caged for vertebrate exclusion (filled circles); uncaged (open triangles). Error bars are 1 SE. **Fig. 2.** Survival of seedlings of *Persoonia lanceolata* over time. **Table 1.** Fecundity data for maturing juveniles of *Persoonia lanceolata.*

Only two fruits in the experiment in the first year were observed to have been eaten *in situ*. Where whole seed removals occurred, two lines of evidence suggested that the fruits were eaten by the macropod *Wallabia bicolor* (swamp wallaby). Hair samples from around batches of seeds were identified as this species and scats of the species frequently contained *Persoonia* pyrenes. Field trapping of small mammals using Elliott Traps showed that only *Rattus fuscipes* and *Antechinus* sp. (a marsupial mouse) were commonly trapped at the site. Neither species is known to remove large fleshy fruits. For the pyrenes extracted from *Wallabia bicolor* (Swamp Wallaby) scats we found high seed viability (88 ± 3%), but all viable seeds were still dormant. {4} height with a power function of log height accounting for some 87% of the variation in mean plant height. The Analysis of Covariance showed a significant effect of both plant age (*P* < 0.001) and previous plant height (*P* < 0.001), suggesting that although a number of smaller plants persist for a while (see Fig. 3), the height of a plant at a particular age was not simply dependent on its previous height. No plants flowered until 6 years after the fire. At this time only 13% of plants were mature and resultant fruit production was very low (Table 1). The proportion of plants that reproduced increased over time up to 92% 12 years after the fire. The magnitude of fruit production also increased markedly from the first to the second fruiting season and in subsequent seasons (Table 1). #### *Residual soil seed bank* Residual seeds in the soil were found in all sampled quadrats, independent of whether or not above ground seedlings were present at the time of sampling (Fig. 4). The density of seeds in the soil (21.2 ± 5.1 seeds/m2) was some 6-7 times greater than the density of seedlings that emerged after fire. On a 1-m2 plot basis, we estimate that between 72-100% of the available soil seed bank did not germinate after the wildfire. This may be an overestimate, as some seeds that germinated may not have been observed as seedlings at our first census 10 months after the fire. Most of the residual soil seed bank was in the top 5 cm of soil (90%). ## **Discussion** Fire plays an important part in the life cycle of many plant species, including woody *Persoonia* species. Like many other obligate seeders, for the common *P. lanceolata*, fire caused population-scale adult mortality and promoted the recruitment of new plants. Population persistence in this obligate seeding species will be influenced by fire frequency, fire patchiness and the dispersal capability of seeds. After a single fire, most seedling recruitment was confined to the first 1-2 years, suggesting that seeds of this species respond to fire cues and/or that the post-fire environment provides favourable conditions for seedling establishment. For obligate seeding shrubs in general, recruitment is often linked to the first 12 months after fire, e.g. southeastern Australia (Purdie 1977; Auld & Tozer 1995; Benwell 1998); Spanish matorral (Fernández-Santos & Gómez-Guitérrez 1994); Florida sand pine scrub (Carrington 1999); Californian chaparral and sage brush (Keeley et al. 2006). However, there was no seasonal component observed in seedling emergence after the initial flush (in comparison to Auld et al. 2000; Ooi et al. 2004). Some continued seedling recruitment occurred for up to 6 years post-fire. The number of seedlings recruited post-fire exceeded pre-fire adult numbers by 6-7 times. The likely change in population abundance after the wildfire can be compared using an estimate of pre-fire adults to post-fire seedlings, and incorporating estimated subsequent seedling mortality levels. This included mortality prior to plants reaching maturity (Fig. 2, ca. 14 (± 4)% after 7.5 years) and an estimate of the likely subsequent adult mortality in the following 7.5 years (to allow equivalent populations estimates for a 15-year old stand). We assumed mortality from 7.5-15 years post-fire matched that of the 2-12 year old plants in the study (Fig. 2). Based on these estimates, we predict that the population density 15 years after the **Fig. 3.** Plant height against age for seedlings of *Persoonia lanceolata*. The line refers to the power function: Ln(plant height) = 2.215\*(plant age)0.367; *R*2 = 0.87). **Fig. 4.** Magnitude of the residual soil seed bank in *Persoonia lanceolata* in 1-m2 quadrats. {5} 1994 wildfire would be some 5 × that of the pre-fire density. Few comparable examples of quantitative estimates of population change in response to fire are available. Keeley et al. (2006) observed an increase in abundance in obligate seeding shrubs in the first five years postfire in southern California, whilst Auld & Scott (2004) showed that the ratio of pre vs. post-fire plant abundance in obligate seeders was dependent upon the time since the previous fire (i.e. pre-fire plant ages). This general lack of data in fire-prone habitats limits quantitative comparison of the impact of varying fire regimes on persistence of obligate seeding plants. Survival of new seedlings of *P. lanceolata* is of a Deevey Type III (*sensu* Harper 1977), with highest mortality when plants are young and small, and reduced mortality once the seedlings are established and grow. This matches the pattern for seedlings in other fireprone habitats (Fernández-Santos & Gómez-Guitérrez 1994; Whelan 1995). Plant growth is relatively slow compared to co-habiting obligate seeding shrubs and in this study, flowering did not occur until 6 years after the fire. As it takes over 6 months for fruits to mature and as the first flowering effectively produced almost no seed, we consider the first effective fruit set was some 7-8 years after the fire. This relatively long primary juvenile period has been noted at other sites for this species (Benson & McDougall 2000; Auld unpubl.), although it has also been observed to be slightly shorter (Benson & McDougall 2000). It is also typical of other co-habiting, obligate seeding *Persoonia* spp. such as *P. pinifolia* and *P. isophylla* (Benson & McDougall 2000; Auld unpubl.). Fires may readily re-occur in the habitat of *P. lanceolata* every 5-10 years, with most (75%) areas in nearby comparable vegetation having a current fire return interval of 7-17 years (Bradstock & Kenny 2003). Consequently, the species may be at risk of population declines unless either a significant proportion of the soil seed bank remains available after a fire (as a residual seed bank), or seeds can readily disperse back into the population from unburnt populations. We found considerable residual seed at our study site and much of this lay in the top 5 cm of the soil, the area most likely to be influenced by fire-related germination cues such as heat (Bradstock & Auld 1995), and possibly smoke. These buried seeds are unlikely to be killed by the lethal heating effects of a fire. Seeds in the top 5 cm will also be least affected by limitations to successful emergence due to depth constraints (Bond et al. 1999). Residual seed values varied, but all greatly exceeded those of some other obligate seeders that co-occur with *P. lanceolata* (Auld & Denham 2006). However, even the residual soil seed bank detected in this study does not ensure there will be population level replacement should a fire occur before there has been replenishment of the soil seed bank. The magnitude of any germination event will be governed by factors relating to the fire itself (heat and smoke output) and post-fire rainfall levels. Removal of fruits from below parent shrubs by Swamp Wallabies was common. In contrast, removal by invertebrates was uncommon, as observed for this species at other sites by French & Westoby (1996). Very few seeds were consumed below canopies. In contrast to some other members of the *Proteaceae* such as *Grevillea* (Auld & Denham 1999), seed removal does not seem to be a mechanism for seed escape from seed predators. Rather, seed removal by Swamp Wallabies would likely reduce future seedling densities adjacent to pre-fire parent plants. Seeds that were removed passed though the gut of animals in a viable and dormant state. Hence, Swamp Wallabies are likely to be an effective dispersal agent for *Persoonia* spp., in agreement with Rymer (2006). Most seeds are likely to be deposited within a population, as evidenced by numerous scats containing seeds in the population. The question remains as to whether these dispersal agents have the ability to move seeds between populations, especially in order to prevent local population extinctions under a regime of too frequent fire. It has been suggested that vertebrate dispersal of *Persoonia* seeds may be a mechanism for gene flow between populations (Rymer & Ayre 2006) or for re-establishment of populations after local extinction (French & Westoby 1996). The long-term nature of this study allowed us to quantify population processes and changes over time. Such studies are a trade off between parameter estimation and predictability across the landscape (Silvertown & Lovett Doust 1983; Whelan 1995). The utility of these data for making predictions about other populations of *Persoonia lanceolata* remains to be investigated. ## **Conclusions** The observed maintenance of a large post-fire residual soil seed bank was potentially an effective means of buffering the population from local extinction if fires occasionally re-occur at short intervals. A long-term high frequency fire regime that prevents the replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to lead to population declines and possible local extinction. We suggest that a sound understanding of how fire impacts on obligate seeding species, such as *Persoonia,* will be best developed by a combination of long-term studies at particular sites combined with detailed multi-site or multi-species comparisons of key demographic attributes, e.g. seed germination, seed dispersal patterns, residual soil seed banks. {6} **Acknowledgements.** We thank Lisa Metcalfe and Mark Ooi for valuable assistance in the field and in soil sieving. 1	*Journal of Ecology* 1998, **86**, 946–959
2	
3	# The ecological significance of canopy seed storage in fire-prone environments: a model for non-sprouting shrubs
4	
5	NEAL J. ENRIGHT\*†, RALF MARSULA‡, BYRON B. LAMONT† and CHRISTIAN WISSEL‡
6	
7	\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville 3052, Australia; †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth 6001, Australia; and ‡Department of Ecological Modelling, UFZ Centre for Environmental Research, Leipzig-Halle, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, D-04301 Leipzig, Germany
8	
9	# Summary
10	
11	1 A comprehensive data set on age, survival and reproduction for the non-sprouting (fire-killed) shrub *Banksia hookeriana*, encompassing 13 years of measurements at 15 sites in south-western Australia, and including 10 fires, was used to parameterize a computer model to investigate optimum plant life-history strategies in a fire-prone environment. Parameter ranges encompassed life-history information for other non-sprouting Banksia species from the same region.
12	
13	2 The relationship between fire interval and level of canopy seed storage (serotiny) was analysed to identify the circumstances under which serotiny is favoured, and what degree of serotiny maximizes potential population growth rate. In addition to deterministic versions of the model, stochasticity in fire interval and conditions for recruitment were analysed.
14	
15	3 The deterministic model indicated a maximum finite rate of natural increase (λ = 1.15) when the fire interval was 16 years and all seeds were retained on the plant until fire occurred. Although the model failed to predict the intermediate degrees of serotiny present in nature, it supported the optimum fire interval predicted from canopy seed bank dynamics.
16	
17	4 Changes to biological attributes associated with timing of reproduction and longevity shifted the optimum fire interval and estimated rate of population growth, but did not alter the conclusions concerning serotiny. Although shorter seed longevity and increased rates of predation and/or decay reduced the value of serotiny, even very low levels of canopy seed storage increased species fitness under intermediate fire frequencies (10–20 years).
18	
19	5 If the probability of inter-fire recruitment and survival was increased, optimum growth shifted from strong serotiny under a regime of frequent fire (<20 year interval), to weak (or no) serotiny where the interval between successive fires was long (>40 year interval).
20	
21	6 Stochasticity around mean fire interval resulted in intermediate to strong (but not complete) serotiny being predicted as optimal once the CV for fire interval approached 100%. This result is interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy whereby spontaneous release of some seeds during the inter-fire period permits recruitment on rare occasions where fire interval approaches or exceeds the species longevity.
22	
23	*Keywords: Banksia*, computer models, fire regime, optimum life-history strategies, serotiny, stochastic effects, woody plants
24	
25	*Journal of Ecology* (1998) **86**, 946–959
26	
27	946 Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright (fax 61 3 9344 4972; e-mail enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au).
28	
29	
30	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
31	
32	947 *N.J. Enright* et al.
33	
34	# Introduction
35	
36	Plants in fire-prone environments are often characterized by biological attributes that increase the probability of survival and/or recruitment following disturbance by fire. Among these are the ability of individuals to regrow from protected buds either above- or below-ground (resprouting), fire-stimulated flowering and seed production, and fire-triggered germination of seeds stored either in the soil or in the plant canopy (Gill 1981). Since species that resprout after fire commonly co-exist in fire-prone environments (e.g. mediterranean-type shrublands) with those that are killed by fire (non-sprouters), a frequent question concerns the circumstances under which one or other strategy is favoured (e.g. Keeley & Zedler 1978; Keeley 1986; Hilbert 1987). Beyond this simple dichotomous division into resprouters and non-sprouters, fire-prone communities may contain an array of (sometimes congeneric) species showing consistent variation in the amount of resprouting after fire, the extent to which seeds are stored in the soil or on the plant, and in other biological attributes (e.g. longevity, age to reproduction, level of seed production).
37	
38	It is important to determine the biological attributes that influence demographic behaviour and to establish which attributes confer the greatest fitness advantage on a species in relation to particular fire regimes. As well as revealing information on the selective pressures acting on species in fire-prone environments, the answers aid conservation and management of species in relation to human-imposed fire regimes.
39	
40	This paper presents a computer model of population dynamics for a non-sprouting woody perennial in a fire-prone environment, and the results of simulations which sought to reveal the optimum level of on-plant seed storage (serotiny) in relation to fire interval. Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits or cones within the crown for more than 1 year and is common in species from a number of important families in fire-prone areas of Australia (Proteaceae, Myrtaceae, Cupressaceae, Casuarinaceae), South Africa (Proteaceae, Bruniaceae) and North America (Pinaceae) (Lamont et al. 1991a). It can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds once mature (no seed storage). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released spontaneously (in the absence of fire) within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where most seeds are held in the canopy for many years (e.g. >10 years in some species of Pinus and Banksia).
41	
42	The ecological and evolutionary significance of serotiny seems clear: where fire is the most common cause of ecosystem disturbance, cued release of canopy-stored seeds by fire (and their germination in the first growing season after fire) maximizes plant age and therefore seed available for the next generation by the time of the next fire. Seeds released, and seedlings established, later during the inter-fire period have a lower probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987). They will be younger and will thus have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs, and so are less fit (sensu Stearns 1992). It would therefore appear that very strong serotiny should represent the optimum strategy for perennial plants in fire-prone environments. However, a range of degrees of serotiny may be encountered within the same plant community (e.g. Cowling et al. 1987; Enright & Lamont 1989a,b) or even within the same species. In the latter case, variations have been found in relation to environmental gradients, e.g. lower serotiny in less fire-prone parts of the species’ geographical range for *Banksia attenuata* in Australia (Cowling & Lamont 1985), and in relation to time since last fire, e.g. inter-fire recruits show lower serotiny than immediate post-fire recruits of *Pinus banksiana* in boreal forests of southern Quebec (Gautier et al. 1996). Lamont et al. (1991a) note that some fire regimes and growth forms apparently foster incomplete serotiny, but that ‘degree of serotiny has received little formal treatment, and the empirical subtleties of such relationships remain largely unexplored’.
43	
44	The model described here is based on field data collected over 13 years from 15 sites and including 10 different fires (up to two at the same site) for *B. hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae), a non-sprouting woody shrub of mediterranean-type shrublands in south-western Australia (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a,b; Enright et al. 1996). Nevertheless, the model is likely to have a more general application since parameter values can readily be changed to match the known life-history attributes of other serotinous, non-sprouting perennial plants. By basing the model and its parameter values on those measured over an extended period of time (and at a number of sites) for a real plant species the model described here avoids many of the criticisms levelled at population models. For example, Cousens (1995) argues that the results of simulation studies for hypothetical species are often determined largely by the structure of the models themselves and provide little insight into real population dynamic behaviour and, further, that many models based on real data are flawed since the data are derived from glasshouse experiments or from density studies that exclude stochastic year-to-year variations in factors unrelated to density (e.g. weather).
45	
46	
47	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
48	
49	948 Canopy seed storage in non-sprouting shrubs
50	
51	#### Ecological and biological attributes of *B. hookeriana*
52	
53	#### FIELD DATA COLLECTION
54	
55	*Banksia hookeriana* is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (non-sprouting) woody shrub that grows up to 2.5 m in height, which is restricted to the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia (centred on 29°30′S, 115°15′E) about 250–330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seed production and plant survivorship were estimated for sample populations of different ages (i.e. time since last fire). Sites covering the whole range of possible plant ages could not be located, and fires during the course of remeasurements returned some sites to zero age. Fifteen sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area, and ranging in age from 1 to 16 years at the start of the study, were established and censused annually in June (i.e. at the end of the summer–autumn period of peak plant mortality) from 1986 to 1996.
56	
57	The onset and level of flowering (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded for all individuals within five replicate 25 m<sup>2</sup> subplots per plot for stands <8 years old, and annual cone production followed for a random sample of 10 individuals for older stands. Fertile cones typically carry 5–15 woody follicles arranged around a central rachis, each follicle holding two seeds. Cones arise terminally at the beginning of each growing season, and node scars and branching pattern clearly mark the boundary between successive years of vegetative growth. Thus plant age and individual cone age can be determined with only a small likelihood of error. Complete cone crops were harvested from 20 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants in 1986, and cones were aged so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. The numbers of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds in closed follicles were determined by cone age, and viability of firm seeds was assessed by germination testing (full details are provided in Enright et al. 1996). Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class that remained closed in the absence of fire (following Lamont et al. 1991a).
58	
59	The total number of cones per plant was quantified for all plants in plots affected by wild fires during the course of the field study. The number of follicles opened by fire was enumerated for a random sample of 10 cones on each of 10 plant skeletons per plot, and the number of viable seeds released per plant estimated using data for seeds from harvested cones.
60	
61	Plant survivorship was recorded annually for 10 randomly chosen individuals within each subplot where plant age was <8 years, and in the whole plot for older stands. The number of seeds released following fire, the number of seedlings established in the first winter, and number of survivors at each age was used to produce survivorship trajectories. These trajectories described the number of seeds required to produce a new individual of any particular age.
62	
63	Data for three other non-sprouting Banksia species (*B. prionotes* Lindley, *B. leptophylla* A.S. George and *B. lanata* A.S. George) provided information on ranges for parameter values for modelling purposes. Up to six Banksia species (a mixture of resprouters and non-sprouters) co-occurred in some of the field sites. The biological attributes of these species are described in Cowling et al. (1987), Enright & Lamont (1989a) and Enright & Lamont (1992a).
64	
65	#### SPECIES ATTRIBUTES
66	
67	Seed production typically commences when plants are 5 years old and fluctuates widely around a mean of about 200 viable seeds per year from 15 years onwards (Enright et al. 1996). While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout their life. Few seeds are released except when fire causes the follicles on cones to open. Once released, seeds either germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish (Enright & Lamont 1989a). Enright et al. (1996) describe in detail the mean rate of accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy in relation to plant age. On average, 17% of embryos abort; seed losses due to spontaneous release in the absence of fire average 4% per annum; while predation and decay of seeds stored in closed follicles increases by 4% per annum from the first year.
68	
69	From 3% to 27% of seeds released following fires in the period 1985–93 produced seedlings in the first winter (Enright & Lamont 1989a; N. J. Enright, unpublished data). Plant survivorship is lowest in the first year and quickly increases such that there is little mortality (<1% year<sup>−1</sup>) in plants older than 8 years. While no plants older than 25 years have been observed in the field, the continuing survival of most individuals in our oldest study site (N. J. Enright, unpublished data) indicates that longevity may be 30–40 years in the absence of fire. Large, old plants may succumb to drought over summer, and are prone to collapse due to the heavy load of seed-bearing cones on old branches, and this suggests an increased mortality rate for old plants.
70	
71	In the absence of fire, some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the probability of germination and survival of recruits to reproductive age is extremely low. Seedlings are occasionally encountered in stands >15 years old, but so far no such recruits have been recorded to survive to reproductive age. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to assume that occasionally these inter-fire recruits might grow to maturity and contribute to future generations. The low chance of establishment, combined with low rates of seed release when the degree of serotiny is high, means that very few recruits are likely via this pathway.
72	
73	
74	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
75	
76	949 *N.J. Enright* et al.
77	
78	Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissues due to drought stress and plant senescence, but is incomplete relative to seed release after fire (Witkowski et al. 1991). The canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, both because even if seeds are released they will have a low probability of establishment, and because dead plants are usually completely incinerated by fire so that any seeds still held in the crown will perish (Lamont & Barker 1988). The woody stems and cones on living shrubs burn less intensely due to a higher moisture content, and although the stems are killed they remain standing and the cones are opened but not consumed. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, a population is threatened with local extinction.
79	
80	### WEATHER AND FIRE
81	
82	Mediterranean-type climate regions are characterized by cool, moist winters and hot, dry summers. In the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia, winter rains are highly predictable and will almost always provide sufficient moisture to allow seedling establishment after fire. However, the extent of summer drought is more variable. One-hundred and ten years of rainfall records for nearby Dongara (Western Australian Bureau of Meteorology climate station 8044; 29°15′S, 114°56′E, mean annual rainfall of 471 mm for the period 1884–1993) show that about 80% of summers have the typical mediterranean-type pattern of low to very low rainfall. In the other 20% of years, tropical storms punctuate the summer with heavy rainfall events and drought stress on plants is greatly reduced (Enright & Lamont 1992a).
83	
84	Summer weather conditions are important in determining levels of seedling survival in the first year following fire. Survivorship of seedlings is highest in wet summers and lowest in dry summers (Enright & Lamont 1992a). There was no relationship between rainfall in the previous summer and subsequent inflorescence production for plants >15 years old. However, there was a significant positive relationship between total rainfall in one year and inflorescence production in the next (log<sub>10</sub> cones = 5.45 × log<sub>10</sub> annual rainfall – 13.80; d.f. = 16, F = 10.50, P < 0.05, r<sup>2</sup> = 0.36). This non-linear relationship suggests reduced inflorescence production following years of lower than average rainfall, but little increase above average levels of production following wet years.
85	
86	Risk of fire is high every summer and there is no obvious relationship between rainfall and fire: of nine wild fires recorded in the vicinity of the field area since 1967, four occurred in wetter than average years, and four in years with very dry summers (one of which followed a wet winter). However, the timing of fire in relation to rainfall in the first few years after fire (especially unusually wet or dry summers) is important since seedling mortality is highest during this period (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a). Stands burned within the last 5 years are unlikely to have accumulated sufficient biomass to carry a fire. The shortest recorded fire interval in relation to the nine fires noted above was 7 years.
87	
88	# Methods
89	
90	### THE MODEL
91	
92	The computer model, written in C++, describes the population dynamics of a serotinous, non-sprouting woody perennial that is subject to disturbance by fire. We chose an age-based approach to characterize the population: the model traces the number of x-year-old plants, N(x), and the number of seeds stored on an x-year-old plant, S(x), for each age x. Changes in N(x) and S(x) are caused by plant death, seed production, seed loss, seed release, germination and establishment of seedlings. These processes are described by the functional relationships detailed below, and illustrated conceptually in Fig. 1. The model begins with a post-fire population of 100 viable seeds and calculates their survivorship and reproduction in relation to age until fire causes plant death and seed release. Fire kills all individuals, and recruitment following fire is solely from seeds.
93	
94	Germination, establishment and survivorship of plants depend on the growing conditions (especially summer rainfall), and the model uses the fits derived from field data on survivorship, and illustrated in Fig. 2, to describe these rates. The probability of germination of seeds and establishment of seedlings in the first year is the inverse of the observed number of seeds required for self-replacement of a 1-year-old plant. In the same way, the probability p(x) that a plant survives until it is x years old is the inverse of the number of seeds required for self-replacement of a plant at age x. Thus, the probability p(x, x + 1) to survive from year x to year x + 1 can be calculated
95	
96	Diagram boxes: Fire; Seed release; Germination and plant survival; Seed production; Seed loss due to predation and rotting; Seed storage; Inter-fire seed release.
97	
98	Fig. 1 Summary flow diagram of the main processes built into the computer model for a serotinous, non-sprouting perennial plant. Note this is not a complete flow diagram of the model. Full model details are described in the text.
99	
100	
101	<!-- PAGE BREAK -->
102	
103	950 Canopy seed storage in non-sprouting shrubs
104	
105	Fig. 2 The mean number of viable seeds required to produce a new plant of given age, over plant ages 0–10 years, for *B. hookeriana*, and the best-fit regression lines describing (a) good, (b) average, (c) bad and (d) very bad recruitment, respectively. Regression model details in the text.
106	
107	as the ratio p (x, x + 1) = p (x + 1)/p (x). The best fit regression line describing recruitment under average conditions is: number of viable seeds required per recruit = 69.03 × log(age) + 23.60) (d.f. = 1,72, F = 39.1, P < 0.001). Other functions are: in good weather, number of viable seeds = 26.54 × log (age) + 23.03; in bad weather, number of viable seeds = 116.53 × log(age) + 82.16; and, in very bad weather, number of viable seeds = 451.72 × log (age) + 17.67. These fits encompass a broader range of measured field recruitment responses than would be the case if regression model (95% or 99%) confidence limits were used to define good and bad recruitment, and are argued to reflect more realistically the natural variation in recruitment in relation to variation in summer rainfall. The impacts that climate have on population growth rate are based on the classification of post-fire years as good (>40 mm summer rainfall), average (10–40 mm), bad (1–10 mm) and very bad (0 mm).
108	
109	At each time step the plants get 1 year older. The model calculates the age class distribution of the individuals as well as their seed production in that year and accumulated seed storage in the plant canopy. Plants have an increased risk of mortality once an age of 25 years is exceeded. This mortality rate increases from 0 to 0.1 by steps of 0.01 per year such that <20% of plants alive at age 25 years are still alive at age 40 years. Maximum plant longevity is described by the parameter A4 (Table 1).
110	
111	Juvenile plants commence seed production at plant age A2 years. Seed production increases linearly up to age A3, after which it remains constant at Fm seeds per year. Most seeds are stored in the plant canopy, but the seeds in a proportion, Lv, of follicles are lost each year due to predation and rotting, while a further proportion, r, open each year in the absence of fire and release their seeds (inter-fire release). 1/r (the inverse of r) describes the degree of serotiny. Thus, a value of 1 for serotiny means that all seeds are released by the end of the year in which they were produced (i.e. the plant is not serotinous), while a value of 1000 means that, on average, only 0.1% of the seed crop is released per year and nearly all of the seed crop (regardless of seed age) is held on the plant until fire triggers seed release. This definition of serotiny follows that proposed by Lamont (1991). The degree of serotiny can theoretically range from 1 (0% serotiny) to infinity (100% serotiny) but most recorded values (e.g. for Banksia species) fall between 10 and 100 (Table 2).
112	
113	Seeds have a longevity of Vm years on the plant. Seeds released during the inter-fire period have a lower probability of germination and establishment than seeds released in response to fire (post-fire release). The model takes this into account: the probability of germination and establishment for seeds released in any inter-fire year is only Postint of that of the post-fire released seeds. For a given released seed, we estimate the probability of inter-fire recruitment (expressed as a proportion) to be c. 0.05 that of post-fire recruitment. When a plant dies during the inter-fire period all seeds stored on that plant are lost. When a fire occurs all remaining plants are killed, and all of their stored seeds are released.
114	
115	The mean fitness of the population (sensu Stearns 1992) in relation to any set of life-history parameters and environmental factors is estimated using the finite rate of natural increase (λ). This is calculated as:
116	
117	λ = <sup>n</sup>√(N<sub>t+n</sub>/N<sub>t</sub>),
118	
119	where n is the number of years between two fires (i.e. represents the fire interval), t is an arbitrary point in time during the simulation and N<sub>t</sub> is the number of individuals at time t. Thus, N<sub>t</sub> and N<sub>t+n</sub> represent the number of individuals for two equivalent points (i.e. same plant age) after successive fires.
120	
121	The model is deterministic in its simplest form. Mean values for life history and environmental parameters, based on information for *B. hookeriana*, were used as the initial settings. Parameter values and ranges used in the model are listed in Table 1. The model is generalized by examining the effects on λ of fire interval and degree of serotiny across the ranges 6–60 years and 1–1000, respectively. 203	#### DETERMINISTIC ANALYSES
204	
205	Deterministic analysis with parameters set to those for *B. hookeriana* reveals a broad peak in the estimated finite rate of natural increase (λ) for fire intervals of 12–25 years, with a maximum (λ = 1.15) at 16 years (Fig. 3a). λ increases with degree of serotiny to a peak at maximum serotiny (i.e. 1000; no seeds released except as caused by fire), with the rate of increase in λ greatest as degree of serotiny rises from 1 to 10. Population decline (extinction) is predicted at very short fire intervals, with the risk of extinction greater for non-serotinous (intervals ≤11 years), than for highly serotinous (intervals ≤8 years), plants. At very long fire intervals (>40 years) extreme serotiny is a disadvantage.

266	### DETERMINISTIC MODEL
267	
268	The optimum fire interval of 16 years obtained from the deterministic model for the *B. hookeriana* parameter set agrees with predictions made by Enright et al. (1996) based on the dynamics of the canopy seed store alone. Extinction is predicted where fire occurs before the plants reach reproductive age or when they have not had time to accumulate a sufficient canopy seed store to ensure successful recruits following fire: this point is frequently made in the fire ecology literature (e.g. Gill 1981; Lamont et al. 1991a). A fire interval in excess of 40 years also leads to extinction if degree of serotiny is close to 1000, since the longevity of plants is exceeded and few or no seeds have been released prior to plant death. This result is consistent with the findings of Bond (1980), who documented the decline of serotinous Proteaceae populations in South African fynbos that had remained unburned for 30–65 years. However, we have no field evidence for the behaviour of stands >25 years old and so there is uncertainty surrounding the parameter values selected to describe population behaviour in this area of the environmental space. The predicted optimum mean return interval for fire (16 years) is greater than that recorded within the geographical range of *B. hookeriana* and other parts of the northern sandplain heaths of western Australia (Van der Moezel et al. 1987; and history of fires reported in the present study). # The ecological significance of canopy seed storage in fire-prone environments: a model for non-sprouting shrubs

NEAL J. ENRIGHT\*†, RALF MARSULA‡, BYRON B. LAMONT† and CHRISTIAN WISSEL‡

\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville 3052, Australia; †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth 6001, Australia; and ‡Department of Ecological Modelling, UFZ Centre for Environmental Research, Leipzig-Halle, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, D-04301 Leipzig, Germany

# Summary

1 A comprehensive data set on age, survival and reproduction for the non-sprouting (fire-killed) shrub *Banksia hookeriana*, encompassing 13 years of measurements at 15 sites in south-western Australia, and including 10 fires, was used to parameterize a computer model to investigate optimum plant life-history strategies in a fire-prone environment. Parameter ranges encompassed life-history information for other non-sprouting Banksia species from the same region.

2 The relationship between fire interval and level of canopy seed storage (serotiny) was analysed to identify the circumstances under which serotiny is favoured, and what degree of serotiny maximizes potential population growth rate. In addition to deterministic versions of the model, stochasticity in fire interval and conditions for recruitment were analysed.

3 The deterministic model indicated a maximum finite rate of natural increase (λ = 1.15) when the fire interval was 16 years and all seeds were retained on the plant until fire occurred. Although the model failed to predict the intermediate degrees of serotiny present in nature, it supported the optimum fire interval predicted from canopy seed bank dynamics.

4 Changes to biological attributes associated with timing of reproduction and longevity shifted the optimum fire interval and estimated rate of population growth, but did not alter the conclusions concerning serotiny. Although shorter seed longevity and increased rates of predation and/or decay reduced the value of serotiny, even very low levels of canopy seed storage increased species fitness under intermediate fire frequencies (10–20 years).

5 If the probability of inter-fire recruitment and survival was increased, optimum growth shifted from strong serotiny under a regime of frequent fire (<20 year interval), to weak (or no) serotiny where the interval between successive fires was long (>40 year interval).

6 Stochasticity around mean fire interval resulted in intermediate to strong (but not complete) serotiny being predicted as optimal once the CV for fire interval approached 100%. This result is interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy whereby spontaneous release of some seeds during the inter-fire period permits recruitment on rare occasions where fire interval approaches or exceeds the species longevity.

*Keywords: Banksia*, computer models, fire regime, optimum life-history strategies, serotiny, stochastic effects, woody plants

*Journal of Ecology* (1998) **86**, 946–959

<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

947 *N.J. Enright* et al.

# Introduction

Plants in fire-prone environments are often characterized by biological attributes that increase the probability of survival and/or recruitment following disturbance by fire. Among these are the ability of individuals to regrow from protected buds either above- or below-ground (resprouting), fire-stimulated flowering and seed production, and fire-triggered germination of seeds stored either in the soil or in the plant canopy (Gill 1981). Since species that resprout after fire commonly co-exist in fire-prone environments (e.g. mediterranean-type shrublands) with those that are killed by fire (non-sprouters), a frequent question concerns the circumstances under which one or other strategy is favoured (e.g. Keeley & Zedler 1978; Keeley 1986; Hilbert 1987). Beyond this simple dichotomous division into resprouters and non-sprouters, fire-prone communities may contain an array of (sometimes congeneric) species showing consistent variation in the amount of resprouting after fire, the extent to which seeds are stored in the soil or on the plant, and in other biological attributes (e.g. longevity, age to reproduction, level of seed production).

It is important to determine the biological attributes that influence demographic behaviour and to establish which attributes confer the greatest fitness advantage on a species in relation to particular fire regimes. As well as revealing information on the selective pressures acting on species in fire-prone environments, the answers aid conservation and management of species in relation to human-imposed fire regimes.

This paper presents a computer model of population dynamics for a non-sprouting woody perennial in a fire-prone environment, and the results of simulations which sought to reveal the optimum level of on-plant seed storage (serotiny) in relation to fire interval. Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits or cones within the crown for more than 1 year and is common in species from a number of important families in fire-prone areas of Australia (Proteaceae, Myrtaceae, Cupressaceae, Casuarinaceae), South Africa (Proteaceae, Bruniaceae) and North America (Pinaceae) (Lamont et al. 1991a). It can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds once mature (no seed storage). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released spontaneously (in the absence of fire) within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where most seeds are held in the canopy for many years (e.g. >10 years in some species of Pinus and Banksia).

The ecological and evolutionary significance of serotiny seems clear: where fire is the most common cause of ecosystem disturbance, cued release of canopy-stored seeds by fire (and their germination in the first growing season after fire) maximizes plant age and therefore seed available for the next generation by the time of the next fire. Seeds released, and seedlings established, later during the inter-fire period have a lower probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987). They will be younger and will thus have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs, and so are less fit (sensu Stearns 1992). It would therefore appear that very strong serotiny should represent the optimum strategy for perennial plants in fire-prone environments. However, a range of degrees of serotiny may be encountered within the same plant community (e.g. Cowling et al. 1987; Enright & Lamont 1989a,b) or even within the same species. In the latter case, variations have been found in relation to environmental gradients, e.g. lower serotiny in less fire-prone parts of the species’ geographical range for *Banksia attenuata* in Australia (Cowling & Lamont 1985), and in relation to time since last fire, e.g. inter-fire recruits show lower serotiny than immediate post-fire recruits of *Pinus banksiana* in boreal forests of southern Quebec (Gautier et al. 1996). Lamont et al. (1991a) note that some fire regimes and growth forms apparently foster incomplete serotiny, but that ‘degree of serotiny has received little formal treatment, and the empirical subtleties of such relationships remain largely unexplored’.

The model described here is based on field data collected over 13 years from 15 sites and including 10 different fires (up to two at the same site) for *B. hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae), a non-sprouting woody shrub of mediterranean-type shrublands in south-western Australia (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a,b; Enright et al. 1996). Nevertheless, the model is likely to have a more general application since parameter values can readily be changed to match the known life-history attributes of other serotinous, non-sprouting perennial plants. By basing the model and its parameter values on those measured over an extended period of time (and at a number of sites) for a real plant species the model described here avoids many of the criticisms levelled at population models. For example, Cousens (1995) argues that the results of simulation studies for hypothetical species are often determined largely by the structure of the models themselves and provide little insight into real population dynamic behaviour and, further, that many models based on real data are flawed since the data are derived from glasshouse experiments or from density studies that exclude stochastic year-to-year variations in factors unrelated to density (e.g. weather).


<!-- PAGE BREAK -->

948 Canopy seed storage in non-sprouting shrubs

#### Ecological and biological attributes of *B. hookeriana*

#### FIELD DATA COLLECTION

*Banksia hookeriana* is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (non-sprouting) woody shrub that grows up to 2.5 m in height, which is restricted to the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia (centred on 29°30′S, 115°15′E) about 250–330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seed production and plant survivorship were estimated for sample populations of different ages (i.e. time since last fire). Sites covering the whole range of possible plant ages could not be located, and fires during the course of remeasurements returned some sites to zero age. Fifteen sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area, and ranging in age from 1 to 16 years at the start of the study, were established and censused annually in June (i.e. at the end of the summer–autumn period of peak plant mortality) from 1986 to 1996.

The onset and level of flowering (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded for all individuals within five replicate 25 m<sup>2</sup> subplots per plot for stands <8 years old, and annual cone production followed for a random sample of 10 individuals for older stands. Fertile cones typically carry 5–15 woody follicles arranged around a central rachis, each follicle holding two seeds. Cones arise terminally at the beginning of each growing season, and node scars and branching pattern clearly mark the boundary between successive years of vegetative growth. Thus plant age and individual cone age can be determined with only a small likelihood of error. Complete cone crops were harvested from 20 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants in 1986, and cones were aged so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. The numbers of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds in closed follicles were determined by cone age, and viability of firm seeds was assessed by germination testing (full details are provided in Enright et al. 1996). Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class that remained closed in the absence of fire (following Lamont et al. 1991a).

The total number of cones per plant was quantified for all plants in plots affected by wild fires during the course of the field study. The number of follicles opened by fire was enumerated for a random sample of 10 cones on each of 10 plant skeletons per plot, and the number of viable seeds released per plant estimated using data for seeds from harvested cones.

Plant survivorship was recorded annually for 10 randomly chosen individuals within each subplot where plant age was <8 years, and in the whole plot for older stands. The number of seeds released following fire, the number of seedlings established in the first winter, and number of survivors at each age was used to produce survivorship trajectories. These trajectories described the number of seeds required to produce a new individual of any particular age.

Data for three other non-sprouting Banksia species (*B. prionotes* Lindley, *B. leptophylla* A.S. George and *B. lanata* A.S. George) provided information on ranges for parameter values for modelling purposes. Up to six Banksia species (a mixture of resprouters and non-sprouters) co-occurred in some of the field sites. The biological attributes of these species are described in Cowling et al. (1987), Enright & Lamont (1989a) and Enright & Lamont (1992a).

#### SPECIES ATTRIBUTES

Seed production typically commences when plants are 5 years old and fluctuates widely around a mean of about 200 viable seeds per year from 15 years onwards (Enright et al. 1996). While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout their life. Few seeds are released except when fire causes the follicles on cones to open. Once released, seeds either germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish (Enright & Lamont 1989a). Enright et al. (1996) describe in detail the mean rate of accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy in relation to plant age. On average, 17% of embryos abort; seed losses due to spontaneous release in the absence of fire average 4% per annum; while predation and decay of seeds stored in closed follicles increases by 4% per annum from the first year.

From 3% to 27% of seeds released following fires in the period 1985–93 produced seedlings in the first winter (Enright & Lamont 1989a; N. J. Enright, unpublished data). Plant survivorship is lowest in the first year and quickly increases such that there is little mortality (<1% year<sup>−1</sup>) in plants older than 8 years. While no plants older than 25 years have been observed in the field, the continuing survival of most individuals in our oldest study site (N. J. Enright, unpublished data) indicates that longevity may be 30–40 years in the absence of fire. Large, old plants may succumb to drought over summer, and are prone to collapse due to the heavy load of seed-bearing cones on old branches, and this suggests an increased mortality rate for old plants.

In the absence of fire, some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the probability of germination and survival of recruits to reproductive age is extremely low. Seedlings are occasionally encountered in stands >15 years old, but so far no such recruits have been recorded to survive to reproductive age. Nevertheless, it is reasonable to assume that occasionally these inter-fire recruits might grow to maturity and contribute to future generations. The low chance of establishment, combined with low rates of seed release when the degree of serotiny is high, means that very few recruits are likely via this pathway.

Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissues due to drought stress and plant senescence, but is incomplete relative to seed release after fire (Witkowski et al. 1991). The canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, both because even if seeds are released they will have a low probability of establishment, and because dead plants are usually completely incinerated by fire so that any seeds still held in the crown will perish (Lamont & Barker 1988). The woody stems and cones on living shrubs burn less intensely due to a higher moisture content, and although the stems are killed they remain standing and the cones are opened but not consumed. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, a population is threatened with local extinction.

### WEATHER AND FIRE

Mediterranean-type climate regions are characterized by cool, moist winters and hot, dry summers. In the northern sandplain heaths of south-western Australia, winter rains are highly predictable and will almost always provide sufficient moisture to allow seedling establishment after fire. However, the extent of summer drought is more variable. One-hundred and ten years of rainfall records for nearby Dongara (Western Australian Bureau of Meteorology climate station 8044; 29°15′S, 114°56′E, mean annual rainfall of 471 mm for the period 1884–1993) show that about 80% of summers have the typical mediterranean-type pattern of low to very low rainfall. In the other 20% of years, tropical storms punctuate the summer with heavy rainfall events and drought stress on plants is greatly reduced (Enright & Lamont 1992a).

Summer weather conditions are important in determining levels of seedling survival in the first year following fire. Survivorship of seedlings is highest in wet summers and lowest in dry summers (Enright & Lamont 1992a). There was no relationship between rainfall in the previous summer and subsequent inflorescence production for plants >15 years old. However, there was a significant positive relationship between total rainfall in one year and inflorescence production in the next (log<sub>10</sub> cones = 5.45 × log<sub>10</sub> annual rainfall – 13.80; d.f. = 16, F = 10.50, P < 0.05, r<sup>2</sup> = 0.36). This non-linear relationship suggests reduced inflorescence production following years of lower than average rainfall, but little increase above average levels of production following wet years.

Risk of fire is high every summer and there is no obvious relationship between rainfall and fire: of nine wild fires recorded in the vicinity of the field area since 1967, four occurred in wetter than average years, and four in years with very dry summers (one of which followed a wet winter). However, the timing of fire in relation to rainfall in the first few years after fire (especially unusually wet or dry summers) is important since seedling mortality is highest during this period (Enright & Lamont 1989a, 1992a). Stands burned within the last 5 years are unlikely to have accumulated sufficient biomass to carry a fire. The shortest recorded fire interval in relation to the nine fires noted above was 7 years.

# Methods

### THE MODEL

The computer model, written in C++, describes the population dynamics of a serotinous, non-sprouting woody perennial that is subject to disturbance by fire. We chose an age-based approach to characterize the population: the model traces the number of x-year-old plants, N(x), and the number of seeds stored on an x-year-old plant, S(x), for each age x. Changes in N(x) and S(x) are caused by plant death, seed production, seed loss, seed release, germination and establishment of seedlings. These processes are described by the functional relationships detailed below, and illustrated conceptually in Fig. 1. The model begins with a post-fire population of 100 viable seeds and calculates their survivorship and reproduction in relation to age until fire causes plant death and seed release. Fire kills all individuals, and recruitment following fire is solely from seeds.

Germination, establishment and survivorship of plants depend on the growing conditions (especially summer rainfall), and the model uses the fits derived from field data on survivorship, and illustrated in Fig. 2, to describe these rates. The probability of germination of seeds and establishment of seedlings in the first year is the inverse of the observed number of seeds required for self-replacement of a 1-year-old plant. In the same way, the probability p(x) that a plant survives until it is x years old is the inverse of the number of seeds required for self-replacement of a plant at age x. Thus, the probability p(x, x + 1) to survive from year x to year x + 1 can be calculated

The best fit regression line describing recruitment under average conditions is: number of viable seeds required per recruit = 69.03 × log(age) + 23.60) (d.f. = 1,72, F = 39.1, P < 0.001). Other functions are: in good weather, number of viable seeds = 26.54 × log (age) + 23.03; in bad weather, number of viable seeds = 116.53 × log(age) + 82.16; and, in very bad weather, number of viable seeds = 451.72 × log (age) + 17.67. The impacts that climate have on population growth rate are based on the classification of post-fire years as good (>40 mm summer rainfall), average (10–40 mm), bad (1–10 mm) and very bad (0 mm).

At each time step the plants get 1 year older. The model calculates the age class distribution of the individuals as well as their seed production in that year and accumulated seed storage in the plant canopy. Plants have an increased risk of mortality once an age of 25 years is exceeded. This mortality rate increases from 0 to 0.1 by steps of 0.01 per year such that <20% of plants alive at age 25 years are still alive at age 40 years. Maximum plant longevity is described by the parameter A4 (Table 1).

Juvenile plants commence seed production at plant age A2 years. Seed production increases linearly up to age A3, after which it remains constant at Fm seeds per year. Most seeds are stored in the plant canopy, but the seeds in a proportion, Lv, of follicles are lost each year due to predation and rotting, while a further proportion, r, open each year in the absence of fire and release their seeds (inter-fire release). 1/r (the inverse of r) describes the degree of serotiny. Thus, a value of 1 for serotiny means that all seeds are released by the end of the year in which they were produced (i.e. the plant is not serotinous), while a value of 1000 means that, on average, only 0.1% of the seed crop is released per year and nearly all of the seed crop (regardless of seed age) is held on the plant until fire triggers seed release. This definition of serotiny follows that proposed by Lamont (1991). The degree of serotiny can theoretically range from 1 (0% serotiny) to infinity (100% serotiny) but most recorded values (e.g. for Banksia species) fall between 10 and 100 (Table 2).

Seeds have a longevity of Vm years on the plant. Seeds released during the inter-fire period have a lower probability of germination and establishment than seeds released in response to fire (post-fire release). The model takes this into account: the probability of germination and establishment for seeds released in any inter-fire year is only Postint of that of the post-fire released seeds. For a given released seed, we estimate the probability of inter-fire recruitment (expressed as a proportion) to be c. 0.05 that of post-fire recruitment. When a plant dies during the inter-fire period all seeds stored on that plant are lost. When a fire occurs all remaining plants are killed, and all of their stored seeds are released.

The mean fitness of the population (sensu Stearns 1992) in relation to any set of life-history parameters and environmental factors is estimated using the finite rate of natural increase (λ). This is calculated as:

λ = <sup>n</sup>√(N<sub>t+n</sub>/N<sub>t</sub>),

where n is the number of years between two fires (i.e. represents the fire interval), t is an arbitrary point in time during the simulation and N<sub>t</sub> is the number of individuals at time t. Thus, N<sub>t</sub> and N<sub>t+n</sub> represent the number of individuals for two equivalent points (i.e. same plant age) after successive fires.

The model is deterministic in its simplest form. Mean values for life history and environmental parameters, based on information for *B. hookeriana*, were used as the initial settings. Parameter values and ranges used in the model are listed in Table 1. The model is generalized by examining the effects on λ of fire interval and degree of serotiny across the ranges 6–60 years and 1–1000, respectively. Changes to other parameters allowed exploration of a broad range of life histories (representing additional species) and environmental conditions (representing good and bad conditions for recruitment, survival and reproduction).

Stochastic versions of the model were also analysed. A truncated, normal sampling distribution was used to select ignition times around specified mean fire intervals, giving an increasing probability of disturbance with time elapsed since last fire. Simulations were repeated 1000–5000 times for each parameter set to provide a stable mean population growth surface (±SD) in relation to fire interval and degree of serotiny. Ignition events selected at random from the sampling distributions resulted in fires only when stand age was >5 years. This resulted in a systematic difference between the mean of the sampled distribution and the resultant mean fire interval. That is (for example), if the mean fire interval for a run was 10 years and the standard deviation was 5 (CV = 50%), then c. 68% of ignition times fell between 5 and 15 years. About 16% of ignition times, in the lower tail of the sampling distribution, were rejected (ignitions for stand ages <5 years) and new ignition times selected. The mean of the ignition times actually resulting in fires was thus greater than the mean of the theoretical distribution from which values were chosen. This difference is systematic and requires the addition of a correction factor that ranges from 4 to 6 years as fire interval increases from 6 to 20 years. Results are presented for the corrected mean fire interval.
